title: al-Muqaddima al-Ājurrūmiyya
author: Ibn Ājurrūm
subject: nahw
summary: The short prose introduction to naḥw by Ibn Ājurrūm of Fez (d. 723/1323): the first grammar book of the North-African madrasas, and of many others from West Africa to the pesantren of Indonesia, learnt by heart and then read with a commentary. In twenty-six brief chapters it defines speech and the three kinds of word, sets out iʿrāb and its signs, the verb and what puts it in naṣb and jazm, and then the nouns in rafʿ, in naṣb and in khafḍ. The lessons follow the vowelled print of J. J. S. Perowne (Cambridge, 1852) a chapter or two at a time: the passage and its translation, an explanation with worked examples, exercises with model answers, and a short test.

lessons.title: Speech and its three parts
body: The Ājurrūmiyya begins at once with its first definition, and the madrasa student learns it by heart before anything else. A definition in the grammar books is built so that each word does work: it lets something in and keeps something out. Speech (kalām) is “an utterance, compound, conveying a meaning, by convention”: four conditions, and only what meets all four is kalām in the grammarians' sense. In everyday Arabic kalām is simply “talk”; here it is a technical word, the complete statement.

Utterance (lafẓ) is a sound made with the mouth that contains letters, so a gesture or a piece of writing is not kalām, however clear it is. Compound (murakkab) means made of two words or more: a single word such as zaydun, “Zayd”, is not kalām. Conveying a meaning (mufīd) means a meaning the listener can rest on, without waiting for more: qāma Zaydun, “Zayd stood”, is complete, but in qāma Zaydun, “if Zayd stood…”, is compound and still not kalām, because the hearer waits for the rest. By convention (bi-l-waḍʿ): the commentators read it in two ways, as “by the convention of the Arabs”, so that only Arabic words count, or as “with intent”, so that the words of a sleeper or a parrot do not count.

The smallest kalām is therefore two words: two nouns, as in Zaydun qāʾimun, “Zayd is standing”, or a verb and a noun, as in qāma Zaydun. Everything longer is built on these two shapes, which the later chapters name: the nominal sentence and the verbal sentence.

Then come the parts of which kalām is made, the three kinds of word: the noun (ism), the verb (fiʿl), and the particle (ḥarf) “that came for a meaning”. That last phrase matters. The word ḥarf also names a letter of the alphabet, such as the zāy of Zayd, which has no meaning of its own; the particle meant here, such as fī, “in”, or in, “if”, has one, though it shows it only together with other words. Nothing in Arabic falls outside these three kinds, and the next lesson gives the signs by which each is known.

terms.en: speech: a compound utterance that conveys a complete meaning
utterance: a sound with letters
compound: made of two words or more
conveying a meaning the listener can rest on
convention (the Arabs' coining of words), or intent
the particle, which came for a meaning

examples.en: qāma Zaydun, “Zayd stood”: a verb and a noun, complete: kalām
Zaydun qāʾimun, “Zayd is standing”: two nouns, complete: kalām
in qāma Zaydun, “if Zayd stood…”: compound, but the meaning is not complete: not kalām

tasks.prompt: Is each of these kalām in the sense of the Ājurrūmiyya? If not, say which condition it lacks: (a) zaydun alone; (b) qāma Zaydun; (c) in qāma Zaydun; (d) a nod of the head meaning “yes”.
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ — قَامَ زَيْدٌ — إِنْ قَامَ زَيْدٌ
tasks.answer: (a) Not kalām: one word, so it is not compound (murakkab). (b) Kalām: an utterance, compound of a verb and a noun, with a complete meaning, in Arabic. (c) Not kalām: it is compound, but not mufīd, since the listener waits for what follows “if”. (d) Not kalām: a gesture is not an utterance (lafẓ).

tasks.prompt: Go through the four words of the definition one by one and say what each keeps out.
tasks.answer: Lafẓ (utterance) keeps out gestures and writing. Murakkab (compound) keeps out the single word. Mufīd (conveying a meaning) keeps out compounds that leave the listener waiting, such as a condition without its answer. Bi-l-waḍʿ (by convention) keeps out words not coined by the Arabs, or, on the other reading, words said without intent, as by a sleeper.

tasks.prompt: Name the three kinds of word and give one example of each from this lesson.
tasks.answer: The noun (ism): zaydun. The verb (fiʿl): qāma, “he stood”. The particle (ḥarf): in, “if”.

tasks.prompt: Why does Ibn Ājurrūm say “a particle that came for a meaning” and not simply “a particle”?
tasks.answer: Because the word ḥarf also means a letter of the alphabet, such as the zāy or the dāl of Zayd, which has no meaning of its own. The particle that is a kind of word, such as fī or in, came for a meaning, which it shows together with other words.

quiz.prompt: How does the Ājurrūmiyya define speech (kalām)?
options: Any single word that has a meaning
An utterance, compound, conveying a meaning, by convention
A sentence that begins with a verb
quiz.explanation: Four conditions: lafẓ, murakkab, mufīd, bi-l-waḍʿ. Only what meets all four is kalām.

quiz.prompt: Is zaydun, said on its own, kalām?
options: Yes: it is a noun with a meaning
No: it is not an utterance
Yes, if it is said with intent
quiz.explanation: Kalām needs at least two words. A single word is a kalima, not kalām.

quiz.prompt: “In qāma Zaydun”, “if Zayd stood…”, lacks which condition of kalām?
options: Lafẓ: it is not an utterance
Murakkab: it is a single word
Mufīd: the meaning is not complete
quiz.explanation: It is compound, but the listener waits for the answer to “if”: it conveys no meaning he can rest on.

quiz.prompt: Why is a nod of the head not kalām, though it is understood?
quiz.explanation: Lafẓ is a sound with letters. Gestures and writing are left out by this first condition.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of word does the book name?
options: Four: noun, verb, particle and sentence
Five, with the pronoun and the article
quiz.explanation: Kalām is made of three kinds of word, and nothing falls outside them.

quiz.prompt: What does “that came for a meaning” keep out?
options: The letters of the alphabet, which are also called ḥarf
quiz.explanation: A letter such as the zāy of Zayd has no meaning of its own; the particle that is a kind of word has one.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the smallest kalām?
options: A particle with a verb, as in qāma
A verb with a noun, as qāma Zaydun
quiz.explanation: The smallest kalām is two words: two nouns, or a verb and a noun.

text.original: الْكَلَامُ هُوَ اللَّفْظُ الْمُرَكَّبُ الْمُفِيدُ بِالْوَضْعِ، وَأَقْسَامُهُ ثَلَاثَةٌ: اسْمٌ وَفِعْلٌ وَحَرْفٌ جَاءَ لِمَعْنًى.
text.en: Speech (kalām) is an utterance (lafẓ), compound (murakkab), conveying a complete meaning (mufīd), by convention (bi-l-waḍʿ). Its divisions are three: the noun (ism), the verb (fiʿl), and the particle (ḥarf) that comes for a meaning.

lessons.title: How a noun, a verb and a particle are known
body: Ibn Ājurrūm does not define the noun and the verb; he gives their signs (ʿalāmāt), things you can see or hear on a word that tell you its kind. That is the beginner's way: you sort a word by testing it. One sign is enough. A noun need not show all its signs, and some of them never come together: the article al- and tanwīn exclude each other, so one says rajulun, “a man”, or al-rajulu, “the man”, but never both at once.

The noun has four signs. Khafḍ, the ending in -i that a governor causes, as in bi-Zaydin, “with Zayd”. Tanwīn, the -n heard after the last vowel, as in zaydun or kitābun. The article al-, as in al-rajulu. And the particles of khafḍ that come before it: min (from), ilā (to), ʿan (away from), ʿalā (on), fī (in), rubba (many a), bi- (with), ka- (like), li- (for), and the particles of the oath, wa-, bi- and ta-, as in wa-llāhi, “by God”. Khafḍ and the particles of khafḍ are two signs, not one: a word can be in khafḍ with no particle (ghulāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's servant”), and a particle can show a noun whose ending never changes, as in min hādhā, “from this”.

The verb has four signs too: qad, which comes before the past and the present (qad ḍaraba, “he has struck”); the sīn and sawfa, which come only before the present and give it a future sense (sawfa yaktubu, “he will write”); and the feminine tāʾ with sukūn, which comes only on the past: ḍarabat, “she struck”. That tāʾ must be quiescent: the moving tāʾ of a noun, as in qāʾimatun, or the pronoun tāʾ of ḍarabtu, “I struck”, is something else.

The particle has no sign of its own: it is the word with which no sign of the noun and no sign of the verb is fit. Teachers compare it to the letter ḥāʾ (ح), known among jīm (ج) and khāʾ (خ) by having no dot at all. Hal (is it?), fī (in) and lam (not) take neither tanwīn nor al-, neither qad nor the tāʾ, and so they are particles.

One gap is worth knowing: none of these signs fits the imperative, such as iḍrib, “strike!”. The Ājurrūmiyya counts it among the verbs (lesson 9) without giving its sign; later books such as Ibn Hishām's Qaṭr al-nadā add one: it asks for an act and accepts the yāʾ of the woman addressed, as in iḍribī.

terms.en: a sign by which the kind of a word is known
the -n after the last vowel of a noun
the -i state of a noun (later books: jarr)
the particles that put a noun in khafḍ
the particles of the oath: wa-, bi-, ta-
the quiescent feminine -t of the past verb

examples.en: bi-Zaydin, “with Zayd”: a particle of khafḍ and the khafḍ itself, two signs of the noun
al-rajulu, “the man”: the article, a sign of the noun
qad ḍaraba, “he has struck”: qad, a sign of the verb
sawfa yaktubu, “he will write”: sawfa, a sign of the present verb
ḍarabat, “she struck”: the quiescent tāʾ, a sign of the past verb

diagram.caption: One sign is enough to know the kind of a word.

tasks.prompt: Sort these words into nouns, verbs and particles, and give the sign that shows it: kitābun, fī, yaktubu, al-qalami, ḍarabat, hal.
tasks.arabic: كِتَابٌ — فِي — يَكْتُبُ — الْقَلَمِ — ضَرَبَتْ — هَلْ
tasks.answer: Kitābun: a noun (tanwīn). Fī: a particle (it accepts no sign of the noun or the verb). Yaktubu: a verb (it accepts sawfa and qad: sawfa yaktubu). Al-qalami: a noun (the article, and the khafḍ). Ḍarabat: a verb (the quiescent feminine tāʾ). Hal: a particle (no sign).

tasks.prompt: Which sign of the noun does each phrase show? (a) bi-Zaydin; (b) rajulun; (c) al-ghulāmu; (d) wa-llāhi.
tasks.answer: (a) The particle of khafḍ bi-, and the khafḍ (-in) with tanwīn. (b) Tanwīn. (c) The article al-. (d) The particle of the oath wa-, and the khafḍ of the name.

tasks.prompt: Which signs of the verb come before the past, and which before the present (muḍāriʿ)?
tasks.answer: Qad comes before both (qad ḍaraba, qad yaḍribu). The sīn and sawfa come only before the present (sawfa yaktubu). The quiescent feminine tāʾ comes only on the past (ḍarabat).

tasks.prompt: A student writes al-rajulun for “the man”. What is wrong?
tasks.answer: The article al- and tanwīn never come together on one noun. With the article it is al-rajulu; without it, rajulun, “a man”.

quiz.prompt: How many signs of the noun does the Ājurrūmiyya give?
options: Three: tanwīn, the article and qad
Four: khafḍ, tanwīn, the article, the particles of khafḍ
None: the noun is known by its meaning
quiz.explanation: Khafḍ, tanwīn, the entering of al-, and the entering of the particles of khafḍ (and of the oath).

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a sign of the verb?
quiz.explanation: Qad, the sīn, sawfa and the quiescent feminine tāʾ are the verb's signs; the other three belong to the noun.

quiz.prompt: How is the particle known?
options: No sign of the noun or of the verb fits it
It has at least three letters
quiz.explanation: The particle has no sign of its own: it is the word with which neither the noun's signs nor the verb's are fit, as the letter ḥāʾ is known by having no dot.

quiz.prompt: Ḍarabat, “she struck”, is known to be a verb by…
options: the particle of khafḍ before it
quiz.explanation: The tāʾ with sukūn at the end of a past verb marks the feminine doer; it is a sign of the verb.

quiz.prompt: Why is al-rajulun wrong?
options: A noun cannot take the article
The article and tanwīn never come together
Tanwīn is a sign of the verb
quiz.explanation: A noun shows one sign or several, but al- and tanwīn exclude each other: al-rajulu or rajulun.

quiz.prompt: Which signs come only before the present verb (muḍāriʿ)?
quiz.explanation: Sa- and sawfa give the present a future sense and enter it alone; qad enters the past and the present, the tāʾ only the past.

quiz.prompt: Which kind of word has no sign given for it in the Ājurrūmiyya, though the book counts it as a verb?
quiz.explanation: None of the four signs fits iḍrib, “strike!”. Later books add one: it asks for an act and takes the yāʾ of the woman addressed (iḍribī).

text.original: فَالِاسْمُ يُعْرَفُ بِالْخَفْضِ وَالتَّنْوِينِ وَدُخُولِ الْأَلِفِ وَاللَّامِ، وَحُرُوفِ الْخَفْضِ، وَهِيَ: مِنْ، وَإِلَى، وَعَنْ، وَعَلَى، وَفِي، وَرُبَّ، وَالْبَاءُ، وَالْكَافُ، وَاللَّامُ، وَحُرُوفِ الْقَسَمِ، وَهِيَ: الْوَاوُ، وَالْبَاءُ، وَالتَّاءُ.
text.en: The noun is known by khafḍ, by tanwīn, by the coming of the alif and lām [the article al-] upon it, and by the particles of khafḍ, which are: min “from”, ilā “to”, ʿan “away from”, ʿalā “on”, fī “in”, rubba “many a”, bi- “with, by”, ka- “like” and li- “for”; and by the particles of oath, which are: wa-, bi- and ta- (“by …”).

text.original: وَالْفِعْلُ يُعْرَفُ بِقَدْ وَالسِّينِ وَسَوْفَ وَتَاءِ التَّأْنِيثِ السَّاكِنَةِ. وَالْحَرْفُ مَا لَا يَصْلُحُ مَعَهُ دَلِيلُ الِاسْمِ وَلَا دَلِيلُ الْفِعْلِ.
text.en: The verb is known by qad [“already”], by sa- and sawfa [“will”], and by the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine [-at]. The particle is that with which neither the sign of the noun nor the sign of the verb is fitting.

lessons.title: Iʿrāb: the change of the ending
body: Iʿrāb is “the change of the endings of words because of the different governors that enter on them, in pronunciation or by assumption”. Take one noun in three sentences: jāʾa Zaydun, “Zayd came”; raʾaytu Zaydan, “I saw Zayd”; marartu bi-Zaydin, “I passed by Zayd”. The word is the same; only its last vowel changes, -un, -an, -in. That change at the end is iʿrāb. A change inside the word, as from ḍaraba to yaḍribu, belongs to ṣarf, not to iʿrāb.

The change has a cause: the governor (ʿāmil) that “enters on” the word. In the first sentence the verb jāʾa governs Zayd as its doer, in the second the verb raʾaytu governs him as its object, in the third the particle bi- governs him. In the madrasa no ending is left without its governor: the student who reads a sentence asks of every word what put its ending there. That question runs through the whole of naḥw, and through al-Birgivī's ʿAwāmil, which lists the governors one by one.

In pronunciation (lafẓan) or by assumption (taqdīran): some words cannot show the change. Al-fatā, “the young man”, ends in an alif that carries no vowel, so in jāʾa al-fatā, raʾaytu al-fatā and marartu bi-l-fatā it sounds the same; the grammarians say that its rafʿ, naṣb and khafḍ are there by assumption (muqaddar). The rule is the same as for Zayd; only the sound is missing.

Iʿrāb has four kinds (states): rafʿ, naṣb, khafḍ and jazm. Rafʿ and naṣb are shared by nouns and verbs; khafḍ belongs to nouns only, jazm to verbs only. So yaḍribu, “he strikes”, is in rafʿ; lan yaḍriba, “he will not strike”, in naṣb; lam yaḍrib, “he did not strike”, in jazm; but a verb is never in khafḍ, and a noun never in jazm. Khafḍ is the word of the Ājurrūmiyya; most later books call it jarr.

Two traps. Iʿrāb is the change, not the vowel: the ḍamma is the sign of rafʿ, and the next lessons show that rafʿ can have other signs. And not every word takes iʿrāb: the past verb, the particles and some nouns (hādhā, “this”) keep one ending whatever governs them; that fixed ending is called bināʾ. In the madrasa, “doing the iʿrāb” of a sentence also means parsing it aloud, word by word, with each word's state and its governor.

terms.en: the change of a word's ending caused by its governor
the governor: what causes the ending
assumed: an ending that is there but cannot be heard
the -u state, in nouns and verbs
the -i state, in nouns only (jarr)
the state of the verb with sukūn, in verbs only

examples.arabic: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ — رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
examples.en: jāʾa Zaydun, raʾaytu Zaydan, marartu bi-Zaydin: one noun, three governors, three endings
jāʾa al-fatā, “the young man came”: rafʿ by assumption on the alif
yaḍribu, lan yaḍriba, lam yaḍrib: the present verb in rafʿ, naṣb and jazm

tasks.prompt: Give the state of Zayd in each sentence and the governor that caused it.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ — رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
tasks.answer: Jāʾa Zaydun: rafʿ, governed by the verb jāʾa, whose doer he is. Raʾaytu Zaydan: naṣb, governed by the verb raʾaytu, whose object he is. Marartu bi-Zaydin: khafḍ, governed by the particle bi-.

tasks.prompt: Is each change iʿrāb or ṣarf? (a) yaḍribu → lam yaḍrib; (b) ḍaraba → yaḍribu.
tasks.answer: (a) Iʿrāb: only the ending changes, because the governor lam entered. (b) Ṣarf: the form of the word changes (past to present), not because of a governor.

tasks.prompt: In jāʾa al-fatā, where is the iʿrāb of al-fatā, and why can it not be heard?
tasks.answer: Al-fatā is in rafʿ as the doer of jāʾa, but its ending is an alif, which cannot carry a vowel. The ḍamma is assumed (muqaddar) on the alif: the iʿrāb is there by assumption, not in pronunciation.

tasks.prompt: Which states are shared by nouns and verbs, and which belongs to each alone?
tasks.answer: Rafʿ and naṣb are shared. Khafḍ belongs to nouns alone, jazm to verbs alone.

quiz.prompt: What changes in iʿrāb?
options: The first letter of the word
The vowel of the middle letter
quiz.explanation: Iʿrāb is the change of the endings (awākhir) of words; changes inside the word belong to ṣarf.

quiz.prompt: What causes the change of iʿrāb?
options: The governors (ʿawāmil) that enter on the word
The meaning of the word alone
quiz.explanation: Each ending is caused by a governor, such as a verb or a particle, that enters on the word.

quiz.prompt: Which state is found in nouns but never in verbs?
quiz.explanation: Nouns take rafʿ, naṣb and khafḍ; verbs take rafʿ, naṣb and jazm.

quiz.prompt: Which state is found in verbs but never in nouns?
quiz.explanation: There is no jazm in nouns, as the book says: lā jazma fīhā.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾa al-fatā the ending of al-fatā cannot be heard. What do the grammarians say?
options: It has no iʿrāb at all
It is in naṣb, since it ends in alif
Its rafʿ is there by assumption (taqdīran)
quiz.explanation: The alif cannot carry a vowel, so the sign of rafʿ is assumed on it: iʿrāb by assumption.

quiz.prompt: How many states (kinds) of iʿrāb are there?
quiz.explanation: Rafʿ, naṣb, khafḍ and jazm.

quiz.prompt: Ḍaraba becomes yaḍribu. Is this iʿrāb?
options: Yes: the ending changed from -a to -u
No: the form changes, not the ending through a governor
quiz.explanation: Past to present is a change of form, the business of ṣarf. Iʿrāb is the ending changed by a governor, as in yaḍribu → lam yaḍrib.

text.original: الْإِعْرَابُ هُوَ تَغْيِيرُ أَوَاخِرِ الْكَلِمِ لِاخْتِلَافِ الْعَوَامِلِ الدَّاخِلَةِ عَلَيْهَا لَفْظًا أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا.
text.en: Iʿrāb is the change of the endings of words because of the differing governors (ʿawāmil) that come upon them, either audibly or as implied (taqdīran).

text.original: وَأَقْسَامُهُ أَرْبَعَةٌ: رَفْعٌ وَنَصْبٌ وَخَفْضٌ وَجَزْمٌ. فَلِلْأَسْمَاءِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الرَّفْعُ وَالنَّصْبُ وَالْخَفْضُ، وَلَا جَزْمَ فِيهَا، وَلِلْأَفْعَالِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الرَّفْعُ وَالنَّصْبُ وَالْجَزْمُ، وَلَا خَفْضَ فِيهَا.
text.en: Its divisions are four: rafʿ, naṣb, khafḍ and jazm. Of these, the nouns have rafʿ, naṣb and khafḍ, and there is no jazm in them; and the verbs have rafʿ, naṣb and jazm, and there is no khafḍ in them.

lessons.title: The four signs of rafʿ
body: Each state of iʿrāb has an original sign and signs that stand in for it. For rafʿ the original sign is the ḍamma; the wāw, the alif and the nūn stand in for it. The book gives every sign with the places where it is found, and the madrasa learns them as a table: sign, then places, then an example.

The ḍamma marks rafʿ in four places. The singular noun (al-ism al-mufrad): here “singular” means not dual, not plural and not one of the five nouns, as in qāma Zaydun. The broken plural (jamʿ al-taksīr), whose singular is broken up inside: rijālun, “men”, from rajulun. The sound feminine plural, made with -āt: muslimātun. And the present verb with nothing attached to its end: yaḍribu, “he strikes”.

The wāw marks rafʿ in two places. The sound masculine plural, made with -ūna: qāma al-Zaydūna, “the Zayds stood”. And the five nouns: abūka (your father), akhūka (your brother), ḥamūka (your in-law), fūka (your mouth) and dhū mālin (a man of wealth). The book gives them with -ka, “your”, for a reason: they take letters only when they are joined to a word after them. Without it, akhun, “a brother”, takes the ḍamma like any singular noun.

The alif marks rafʿ in the dual of nouns only (khāṣṣatan): qāma al-Zaydāni, “the two Zayds stood”. The word “only” answers a trap: in the verb yaḍribāni, “the two strike”, there is an alif too, but it is the pronoun of the two doers, not a sign of rafʿ.

The nūn marks rafʿ in the present verb when there is attached to it the pronoun of two, the pronoun of a plural, or the pronoun of the woman addressed: yaḍribāni, yaḍribūna, taḍribīna. In these the sign of rafʿ is the nūn that stays at the end; lesson 8 calls them the five verbs. So the sign of rafʿ can be a vowel or a letter, and a learner reading a word asks first which kind of word it is.

terms.en: the -u vowel, original sign of rafʿ
the singular noun: not dual, not plural
the broken plural (rijāl from rajul)
the sound feminine plural in -āt
the sound masculine plural in -ūna
the five nouns: abū, akhū, ḥamū, fū, dhū

examples.en: yaqūmu Zaydun, “Zayd stands”: the ḍamma on the present verb and on the singular noun
qāma al-Zaydūna, “the Zayds stood”: the wāw of the sound masculine plural
qāma akhūka, “your brother stood”: the wāw of the five nouns
qāma al-Zaydāni, “the two Zayds stood”: the alif of the dual
yaḍribāni, “the two strike”: the nūn is the sign of rafʿ; the alif is the pronoun

tasks.prompt: Give the sign of rafʿ in each word and say which place of the book it belongs to: al-muslimūna, abūka, al-kutubu, taḍribīna, al-Zaydāni, al-muslimātu.
tasks.arabic: الْمُسْلِمُونَ — أَبُوكَ — الْكُتُبُ — تَضْرِبِينَ — الزَّيْدَانِ — الْمُسْلِمَاتُ
tasks.answer: Al-muslimūna: the wāw (sound masculine plural). Abūka: the wāw (the five nouns). Al-kutubu: the ḍamma (broken plural of kitāb). Taḍribīna: the nūn (present verb with the pronoun of the woman addressed). Al-Zaydāni: the alif (dual). Al-muslimātu: the ḍamma (sound feminine plural).

tasks.prompt: In yaḍribāni there is an alif and a nūn. Which is the sign of rafʿ, and what is the other?
tasks.answer: The nūn is the sign of rafʿ. The alif is the pronoun of the two doers; the book says the alif is a sign of rafʿ in the dual of nouns only.

tasks.prompt: Say “your brother stood” and “a brother stood”, and explain the difference of the signs.
tasks.answer: Qāma akhūka: akh is joined to -ka, so it is one of the five nouns and takes the wāw. Qāma akhun: not joined to a word after it, so it is an ordinary singular noun with the ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: What is the original sign of rafʿ?
quiz.explanation: The ḍamma is the original sign; the wāw, the alif and the nūn stand in for it.

quiz.prompt: Al-Zaydūna is in rafʿ. What is its sign?
quiz.explanation: The sound masculine plural takes the wāw in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: What is the sign of rafʿ in al-rijālu, “the men”?
options: The ḍamma, as a broken plural
quiz.explanation: A broken plural takes the vowels like a singular noun: the ḍamma in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: Why does the book add “only” (khāṣṣatan) to the alif of the dual?
options: The alif is also a sign of khafḍ
The alif of a verb like yaḍribāni is not a sign of rafʿ
quiz.explanation: In the verb the alif is the pronoun of the doers; the sign of rafʿ there is the nūn.

quiz.prompt: What is the sign of rafʿ in taḍribīna, “you (woman) strike”?
quiz.explanation: The yāʾ is the pronoun of the woman addressed; the staying of the nūn is the sign of rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: Which is one of the five nouns?
quiz.explanation: The five nouns are abū, akhū, ḥamū, fū and dhū; they take letters when joined to a word after them.

quiz.prompt: In yaḍribu, “he strikes”, the sign of rafʿ is…
quiz.explanation: The present verb with nothing attached to its end takes the ḍamma in rafʿ.

text.original: لِلرَّفْعِ أَرْبَعُ عَلَامَاتٍ: الضَّمَّةُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْأَلِفُ وَالنُّونُ. فَأَمَّا الضَّمَّةُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلرَّفْعِ فِي أَرْبَعَةِ مَوَاضِعَ: فِي الِاسْمِ الْمُفْرَدِ، وَجَمْعِ التَّكْسِيرِ، وَجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ، وَالْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ الَّذِي لَمْ يَتَّصِلْ بِآخِرِهِ شَيْءٌ.
text.en: Rafʿ has four signs: the ḍamma, the wāw, the alif and the nūn. As for the ḍamma, it is a sign of rafʿ in four places: in the singular noun, in the broken plural, in the sound feminine plural, and in the muḍāriʿ verb to whose end nothing is attached.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْوَاوُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلرَّفْعِ فِي مَوْضِعَيْنِ: فِي جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ، وَفِي الْأَسْمَاءِ الْخَمْسَةِ، وَهِيَ: أَبُوكَ، وَأَخُوكَ، وَحَمُوكَ، وَفُوكَ، وَذُو مَالٍ.
text.en: As for the wāw, it is a sign of rafʿ in two places: in the sound masculine plural, and in the five nouns, which are: abūka “your father”, akhūka “your brother”, ḥamūka “your father-in-law”, fūka “your mouth” and dhū mālin “possessor of wealth”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْأَلِفُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلرَّفْعِ فِي تَثْنِيَةِ الْأَسْمَاءِ خَاصَّةً. وَأَمَّا النُّونُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلرَّفْعِ فِي الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ إِذَا اتَّصَلَ بِهِ ضَمِيرُ تَثْنِيَةٍ، أَوْ ضَمِيرُ جَمْعٍ، أَوْ ضَمِيرُ الْمُؤَنَّثَةِ الْوَاحِدَةِ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ.
text.en: As for the alif, it is a sign of rafʿ in the dual of nouns only. As for the nūn, it is a sign of rafʿ in the muḍāriʿ verb when there is attached to it a pronoun of the dual, a pronoun of the plural, or the pronoun of the single feminine person addressed.

lessons.title: The five signs of naṣb
body: Naṣb has five signs: the fatḥa, the original one, and the alif, the kasra, the yāʾ and the dropping of the nūn, which stand in for it. They fall on the same words as the signs of rafʿ, so it helps to read this lesson beside the last one: each word that took a substitute in rafʿ takes a substitute in naṣb too.

The fatḥa marks naṣb in three places: the singular noun (raʾaytu Zaydan, “I saw Zayd”), the broken plural (raʾaytu al-rijāla, “I saw the men”), and the present verb with nothing attached to its end when a governor of naṣb (nāṣib) enters on it: lan yaḍriba, “he will not strike”. The sound feminine plural is missing from this list, which was four places in rafʿ; it comes back under the kasra.

The alif marks naṣb in the five nouns: raʾaytu abāka wa-akhāka, “I saw your father and your brother”. The kasra marks naṣb in the sound feminine plural: raʾaytu al-muslimāti, “I saw the Muslim women”. This is the beginner's trap: the word ends in -i and looks like khafḍ, but after raʾaytu it is the object, and the kasra here is a sign of naṣb.

The yāʾ marks naṣb in “the dual and the plural”, the plural meaning the sound masculine plural. Both end in yāʾ and nūn, and are told apart by the vowels around them: the dual has a fatḥa before the yāʾ and a kasra on the nūn (raʾaytu al-Zaydayni, “I saw the two Zayds”), the plural a kasra before the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the nūn (raʾaytu al-Zaydīna, “I saw the Zayds”).

The dropping of the nūn marks naṣb in the verbs whose rafʿ is by the nūn staying, the five verbs of the last lesson: yaḍribāni becomes lan yaḍribā, yaḍribūna becomes lan yaḍribū, taḍribīna becomes lan taḍribī. What was the sign of rafʿ disappears, and its absence is the sign of naṣb.

terms.en: the -a vowel, original sign of naṣb
a governor that puts a word in naṣb
the -i vowel; in naṣb, the sign of the sound feminine plural
the dual
the dropping of the nūn
the staying of the nūn, sign of rafʿ in the five verbs

examples.en: raʾaytu Zaydan, “I saw Zayd”: the fatḥa on the singular noun
lan yaḍriba, “he will not strike”: the fatḥa on the present verb after a nāṣib
raʾaytu abāka wa-akhāka, “I saw your father and your brother”: the alif of the five nouns
raʾaytu al-muslimāti, “I saw the Muslim women”: the kasra standing for the fatḥa
lan yaḍribū, “they will not strike”: the nūn of yaḍribūna is dropped

tasks.prompt: Put each noun after raʾaytu, “I saw”, and name the sign of naṣb: Zaydun, al-Zaydāni, al-Zaydūna, akhūka, al-muslimātu.
tasks.answer: Raʾaytu Zaydan (fatḥa); raʾaytu al-Zaydayni (yāʾ of the dual); raʾaytu al-Zaydīna (yāʾ of the plural); raʾaytu akhāka (alif of the five nouns); raʾaytu al-muslimāti (kasra for the sound feminine plural).

tasks.prompt: Put each verb after lan, “will not”, and name the sign of naṣb: yaḍribu, yaḍribāni, yaḍribūna, taḍribīna.
tasks.answer: Lan yaḍriba (fatḥa); lan yaḍribā, lan yaḍribū, lan taḍribī (the dropping of the nūn).

tasks.prompt: How do you tell al-Zaydayni (dual) from al-Zaydīna (plural) when both are in naṣb?
tasks.answer: By the vowels: the dual has a fatḥa before the yāʾ (-ay-) and a kasra on the nūn (-ni); the sound masculine plural has a kasra before the yāʾ (-ī-) and a fatḥa on the nūn (-na).

tasks.prompt: Raʾaytu al-muslimāti ends in -i. Why is al-muslimāti in naṣb and not in khafḍ?
tasks.answer: It is the object of the verb raʾaytu, a governor of naṣb, and no particle of khafḍ comes before it. The sound feminine plural takes the kasra in naṣb in place of the fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: How many signs of naṣb does the book give?
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa, the alif, the kasra, the yāʾ and the dropping of the nūn.

quiz.prompt: What is the sign of naṣb in raʾaytu abāka?
quiz.explanation: Abū is one of the five nouns: wāw in rafʿ, alif in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: In raʾaytu al-muslimāti, the kasra is the sign of…
quiz.explanation: The sound feminine plural takes the kasra in naṣb in place of the fatḥa; here it is the object of raʾaytu.

quiz.prompt: Lan yaḍribū comes from yaḍribūna. What is the sign of naṣb?
quiz.explanation: The five verbs are in rafʿ by the nūn staying and in naṣb by its dropping.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a dual in naṣb?
quiz.explanation: Fatḥa before the yāʾ and kasra on the nūn: the dual. Al-Zaydīna is the plural in naṣb; the other two are in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: Which kind of word takes the fatḥa in naṣb?
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa marks naṣb in the singular noun, the broken plural and the present verb after a nāṣib.

quiz.prompt: When does the present verb with nothing attached take the fatḥa?
options: When it is in the past
When a particle of khafḍ enters on it
When a governor of naṣb enters on it
quiz.explanation: It is in rafʿ until a nāṣib (lan, an…) enters on it; then it takes the fatḥa.

text.original: وَلِلنَّصْبِ خَمْسُ عَلَامَاتٍ: الْفَتْحَةُ وَالْأَلِفُ وَالْكَسْرَةُ وَالْيَاءُ وَحَذْفُ النُّونِ. فَأَمَّا الْفَتْحَةُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلنَّصْبِ فِي ثَلَاثَةِ مَوَاضِعَ: فِي الِاسْمِ الْمُفْرَدِ، وَجَمْعِ التَّكْسِيرِ، وَالْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ الَّذِي لَمْ يَتَّصِلْ بِآخِرِهِ شَيْءٌ وَإِذَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ نَاصِبٌ.
text.en: Naṣb has five signs: the fatḥa, the alif, the kasra, the yāʾ and the dropping of the nūn. As for the fatḥa, it is a sign of naṣb in three places: in the singular noun, in the broken plural, and in the muḍāriʿ verb to whose end nothing is attached, when a governor of naṣb comes upon it.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْأَلِفُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلنَّصْبِ فِي الْأَسْمَاءِ الْخَمْسَةِ، نَحْوُ: رَأَيْتُ أَبَاكَ وَأَخَاكَ، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ. وَأَمَّا الْكَسْرَةُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلنَّصْبِ فِي جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ.
text.en: As for the alif, it is a sign of naṣb in the five nouns, as raʾaytu abāka wa-akhāka “I saw your father and your brother”, and the like. As for the kasra, it is a sign of naṣb in the sound feminine plural.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْيَاءُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلنَّصْبِ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ وَالْجَمْعِ. وَأَمَّا حَذْفُ النُّونِ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلنَّصْبِ فِي الْأَفْعَالِ الَّتِي رَفْعُهَا بِثَبَاتِ النُّونِ.
text.en: As for the yāʾ, it is a sign of naṣb in the dual and the plural. As for the dropping of the nūn, it is a sign of naṣb in the verbs whose rafʿ is by keeping the nūn.

lessons.title: The signs of khafḍ and of jazm
body: Khafḍ has three signs: the kasra, the original, and the yāʾ and the fatḥa in its place. The kasra marks khafḍ in the singular noun and the broken plural, provided they are munṣarif, and in the sound feminine plural: marartu bi-Zaydin, bi-l-rijāli, bi-l-muslimāti. Munṣarif (fully declinable) is a noun that takes tanwīn and the kasra; the book names the condition here because some nouns do not.

The yāʾ marks khafḍ in the five nouns (marartu bi-abīka, “I passed by your father”), in the dual (bi-l-Zaydayni) and in the sound masculine plural (bi-l-Zaydīna). The dual and the plural therefore have the same form in naṣb and in khafḍ, as the last lesson showed.

The fatḥa marks khafḍ in the noun that is not munṣarif, the diptote: marartu bi-Aḥmada, “I passed by Aḥmad”, with -a after bi-, and no tanwīn. Which nouns are diptotes, the Ājurrūmiyya does not say; later books (Qaṭr al-nadā, the Alfiyya) give their causes. For now, know two common kinds: names on the pattern afʿal, such as Aḥmad, and plurals such as masājid, “mosques”. With the article or joined to a word after them, they take the kasra again: fī al-masājidi, “in the mosques”.

Jazm has two signs: the sukūn and the dropping. The sukūn marks jazm in the present verb whose last letter is sound: lam yaḍrib, “he did not strike”. The dropping marks jazm in the present verb whose last letter is weak (wāw, yāʾ or alif), which loses that letter, and in the five verbs, which lose their nūn: lam yaḍribā, lam yaḍribū, lam taḍribī. The Qurʾān gives the weak verbs in jazm: fa-l-yadʿu nādiyahu (96:17), wa-lam yakhsha illā llāha (9:18), wa-lā tamshi fī al-arḍi maraḥan (17:37): the wāw, the alif and the yāʾ of the verb have dropped.

Count the signs and you have fourteen: four of rafʿ, five of naṣb, three of khafḍ, two of jazm. Four of them are originals, one for each state: ḍamma, fatḥa, kasra, sukūn. The madrasa student recites them in this order until he can say, for any word, its state and its sign.

terms.en: fully declinable: takes tanwīn and the kasra
the diptote: no tanwīn, fatḥa in khafḍ
the absence of a vowel, original sign of jazm
dropping: of a weak last letter or of the nūn
a verb whose last letter is sound
a verb whose last letter is wāw, yāʾ or alif

examples.en: marartu bi-abīka, “I passed by your father”: the yāʾ of the five nouns
marartu bi-Aḥmada, “I passed by Aḥmad”: the fatḥa of the diptote
lam yaḍrib, “he did not strike”: the sukūn
wa-lā tamshi fī al-arḍi maraḥan, “and do not walk on the earth exultantly” (Q 17:37): the yāʾ of the verb dropped in jazm
lam yaḍribū, “they did not strike”: the nūn dropped

tasks.prompt: Put each noun after bi-, “with, by”, and name the sign of khafḍ: abūka, al-Zaydāni, al-muslimūna, Aḥmadu, al-rijālu.

tasks.prompt: Put each verb after lam, “did not”, and name the sign of jazm: yaktubu, yaktubāni, taktubīna, yaktubūna.
tasks.answer: Lam yaktub (sukūn: the last letter is sound); lam yaktubā, lam taktubī, lam yaktubū (the dropping of the nūn).

tasks.prompt: In fa-l-yadʿu nādiyahu, “so let him call his council” (Q 96:17), the verb is in jazm after the lām of command. What is the sign of its jazm?
tasks.answer: The dropping of its last letter: the verb ends in a weak letter (wāw), and in jazm that wāw is dropped, leaving yadʿu with a short ḍamma.

tasks.prompt: Name the four original signs, one for each state, and say how many signs there are in all.
tasks.answer: Ḍamma for rafʿ, fatḥa for naṣb, kasra for khafḍ, sukūn for jazm. Fourteen in all: four of rafʿ, five of naṣb, three of khafḍ, two of jazm.

quiz.prompt: Marartu bi-Aḥmada: what is the sign of khafḍ?
options: The fatḥa, since Aḥmad is a diptote
There is no khafḍ after bi-
quiz.explanation: The noun that is not munṣarif takes the fatḥa in khafḍ, and no tanwīn.

quiz.prompt: What is the sign of khafḍ in bi-abīka?
quiz.explanation: The five nouns: wāw in rafʿ, alif in naṣb, yāʾ in khafḍ.

quiz.prompt: What are the two signs of jazm?
quiz.explanation: The sukūn in the verb with a sound last letter; the dropping in the verb with a weak last letter and in the five verbs.

quiz.prompt: Lam yaḍribā comes from yaḍribāni. What is the sign of jazm?
quiz.explanation: The five verbs are in jazm, as in naṣb, by the dropping of their nūn.

quiz.prompt: Which nouns take the kasra in khafḍ only if they are munṣarif?
options: The singular noun and the broken plural
quiz.explanation: The book adds “munṣarif” to the singular and the broken plural; the diptotes among them take the fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: How many signs of iʿrāb are there in all?
quiz.explanation: Four of rafʿ, five of naṣb, three of khafḍ and two of jazm.

quiz.prompt: Al-masājid, “the mosques”, is a diptote. What is its ending in fī al-masājid?
options: Kasra: with the article it takes the kasra again
quiz.explanation: A diptote takes the fatḥa in khafḍ only without the article and not joined to a word after it.

text.original: وَلِلْخَفْضِ ثَلَاثُ عَلَامَاتٍ: الْكَسْرَةُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْفَتْحَةُ. فَأَمَّا الْكَسْرَةُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلْخَفْضِ فِي ثَلَاثَةِ مَوَاضِعَ: فِي الِاسْمِ الْمُفْرَدِ الْمُنْصَرِفِ، وَجَمْعِ التَّكْسِيرِ الْمُنْصَرِفِ، وَجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ.
text.en: Khafḍ has three signs: the kasra, the yāʾ and the fatḥa. As for the kasra, it is a sign of khafḍ in three places: in the singular noun that takes tanwīn (munṣarif), in the broken plural that takes tanwīn, and in the sound feminine plural.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْيَاءُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلْخَفْضِ فِي ثَلَاثَةِ مَوَاضِعَ: فِي الْأَسْمَاءِ الْخَمْسَةِ، وَالتَّثْنِيَةِ، وَالْجَمْعِ. وَأَمَّا الْفَتْحَةُ فَتَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلْخَفْضِ فِي الِاسْمِ الَّذِي لَا يَنْصَرِفُ.
text.en: As for the yāʾ, it is a sign of khafḍ in three places: in the five nouns, in the dual and in the plural. As for the fatḥa, it is a sign of khafḍ in the noun that does not take tanwīn (mā lā yanṣarif).

text.original: وَلِلْجَزْمِ عَلَامَتَانِ: السُّكُونُ وَالْحَذْفُ. فَأَمَّا السُّكُونُ فَيَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلْجَزْمِ فِي الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ الصَّحِيحِ الْآخِرِ، وَأَمَّا الْحَذْفُ فَيَكُونُ عَلَامَةً لِلْجَزْمِ فِي الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ الْمُعْتَلِّ الْآخِرِ، وَفِي الْأَفْعَالِ الَّتِي رَفْعُهَا بِثَبَاتِ النُّونِ.
text.en: Jazm has two signs: the sukūn and dropping. As for the sukūn, it is a sign of jazm in the muḍāriʿ verb whose last letter is sound; as for dropping, it is a sign of jazm in the muḍāriʿ verb whose last letter is weak, and in the verbs whose rafʿ is by keeping the nūn.

lessons.title: What is inflected by vowels
body: The last chapter went through the states one by one and gave each its signs. This chapter, “the inflected words” (al-muʿrabāt), turns the same facts the other way round: it starts from the kinds of word and says how each one is inflected. The repetition is deliberate. A student who has learnt both tables can begin from the word in front of him as easily as from the state he expects.

The inflected words fall into two groups: those inflected by vowels (ḥarakāt; the sukūn of jazm is counted with them) and those inflected by letters (ḥurūf). By vowels go four kinds: the singular noun, the broken plural, the sound feminine plural, and the present verb with nothing attached to its end. The rule for all four is the simple one: ḍamma for rafʿ, fatḥa for naṣb, kasra for khafḍ, sukūn for jazm, each in its own domain, since nouns have no jazm and verbs no khafḍ.

Three things leave the rule (kharaja ʿan dhālika). The sound feminine plural takes the kasra in naṣb: raʾaytu al-muslimāti. The diptote takes the fatḥa in khafḍ: marartu bi-Aḥmada. And the present verb with a weak last letter is in jazm by the dropping of that letter, not by the sukūn. Everything else in these four kinds follows the vowels.

One condition in the list hides more than it says: “the present verb with nothing attached to its end”. The commentaries explain what it keeps out. With the pronouns of two, of a plural or of the woman addressed it becomes one of the five verbs, inflected by letters (next lesson). With the nūn of the feminine plural, yaḍribna, “they (women) strike”, it is not inflected at all: its ending is fixed, and the same is true when the nūn of emphasis is joined directly to it.

terms.en: the inflected words
the vowels (with the sukūn)
here: letters standing for the vowels
what leaves the rule: the exceptions

examples.arabic: قَامَ زَيْدٌ — رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
examples.en: qāma Zaydun, raʾaytu Zaydan, marartu bi-Zaydin: the singular noun by the vowels
raʾaytu al-muslimāti: the first exception, kasra for naṣb
marartu bi-Aḥmada: the second exception, fatḥa for khafḍ
yaḍribna, “they (women) strike”: a present verb with the nūn of the feminine plural, its ending fixed

tasks.prompt: Give the three states (rafʿ, naṣb, khafḍ) of rijālun, muslimātun and Aḥmadu, and point out the exceptions.
tasks.answer: Rijālun, rijālan, rijālin (regular). Muslimātun, muslimātin, muslimātin (naṣb by the kasra: the first exception). Aḥmadu, Aḥmada, Aḥmada (khafḍ by the fatḥa, and no tanwīn: the second exception).

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of word and its state in each: lam yaktub; bi-l-kutubi; raʾaytu al-muslimāti; lan yaktuba.
tasks.arabic: لَمْ يَكْتُبْ — بِالْكُتُبِ — رَأَيْتُ الْمُسْلِمَاتِ — لَنْ يَكْتُبَ
tasks.answer: Lam yaktub: present verb, jazm by the sukūn. Bi-l-kutubi: broken plural, khafḍ by the kasra. Al-muslimāti: sound feminine plural, naṣb by the kasra. Lan yaktuba: present verb, naṣb by the fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Name the three exceptions to the rule of the vowels, with an example of each.
tasks.answer: The sound feminine plural in naṣb takes the kasra (raʾaytu al-muslimāti); the diptote in khafḍ takes the fatḥa (marartu bi-Aḥmada); the present verb with a weak last letter is in jazm by dropping that letter (wa-lā tamshi, Q 17:37).

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of word are inflected by vowels?
quiz.explanation: The singular noun, the broken plural, the sound feminine plural and the present verb with nothing attached.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is inflected by vowels?
quiz.explanation: The dual, the sound masculine plural, the five nouns and the five verbs are inflected by letters.

quiz.prompt: Which exception concerns the sound feminine plural?
options: It takes the fatḥa in khafḍ
It takes the kasra in naṣb
It takes the wāw in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: Raʾaytu al-muslimāti: the kasra stands for the fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: Which exception concerns the diptote?
options: It takes the kasra in naṣb
It takes the fatḥa in khafḍ
It takes the yāʾ in khafḍ
quiz.explanation: Marartu bi-Aḥmada: the fatḥa stands for the kasra.

quiz.prompt: Why does the book look at the same facts twice, by state and by kind of word?
options: Because the second is about verbs only
Because the first chapter was incomplete
So the student can start from the word or from the state
quiz.explanation: The second table turns the first round: from the kind of word to its signs.

quiz.prompt: What is the ending of yaḍribna, “they (women) strike”?
options: Fixed: the nūn of the feminine plural makes it uninflected
Rafʿ by the nūn, as a five verb
quiz.explanation: The present verb is inflected only with nothing attached; with the nūn of the feminine plural its ending is fixed (mabnī).

quiz.prompt: The present verb with a weak last letter is in jazm by…
quiz.explanation: It is the third exception to the rule of the vowels: wa-lā tamshi (Q 17:37).

text.original: الْمُعْرَبَاتُ قِسْمَانِ: قِسْمٌ يُعْرَبُ بِالْحَرَكَاتِ، وَقِسْمٌ يُعْرَبُ بِالْحُرُوفِ. فَالَّذِي يُعْرَبُ بِالْحَرَكَاتِ أَرْبَعَةُ أَنْوَاعٍ: الِاسْمُ الْمُفْرَدُ، وَجَمْعُ التَّكْسِيرِ، وَجَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ، وَالْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ الَّذِي لَمْ يَتَّصِلْ بِآخِرِهِ شَيْءٌ، وَكُلُّهَا تُرْفَعُ بِالضَّمَّةِ، وَتُنْصَبُ بِالْفَتْحَةِ، وَتُخْفَضُ بِالْكَسْرَةِ، وَتُجْزَمُ بِالسُّكُونِ.
text.en: The inflected words (muʿrabāt) are of two divisions: a division that is inflected by vowels and a division that is inflected by letters. That which is inflected by vowels is of four kinds: the singular noun, the broken plural, the sound feminine plural, and the muḍāriʿ verb to whose end nothing is attached. All of them take rafʿ by the ḍamma, naṣb by the fatḥa, khafḍ by the kasra and jazm by the sukūn.

text.original: وَخَرَجَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْيَاءَ: جَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ يُنْصَبُ بِالْكَسْرَةِ، وَالِاسْمُ الَّذِي لَا يَنْصَرِفُ يُخْفَضُ بِالْفَتْحَةِ، وَالْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ الْمُعْتَلُّ الْآخِرِ يُجْزَمُ بِحَذْفِ آخِرِهِ.
text.en: Three things are outside this: the sound feminine plural takes naṣb by the kasra; the noun that does not take tanwīn takes khafḍ by the fatḥa; and the muḍāriʿ verb whose last letter is weak takes jazm by the dropping of its last letter.

lessons.title: What is inflected by letters
body: Four kinds of word are inflected by letters: the dual, the sound masculine plural, the five nouns, and the five verbs. The five verbs are named by their pattern on faʿala, as the grammarians name forms: yafʿalāni, tafʿalāni, yafʿalūna, tafʿalūna, tafʿalīna. Any present verb of these shapes belongs to them: yaḍribāni, taḍribāni, yaḍribūna, taḍribūna, taḍribīna.

The dual takes the alif in rafʿ and the yāʾ in naṣb and khafḍ: al-Zaydāni, al-Zaydayni. The sound masculine plural takes the wāw in rafʿ and the yāʾ in naṣb and khafḍ: al-Zaydūna, al-Zaydīna. The five nouns are the only kind with three letters for the three states: the wāw in rafʿ, the alif in naṣb, the yāʾ in khafḍ: abūka, abāka, abīka.

The five verbs take the nūn in rafʿ and drop it in naṣb and jazm: yaḍribūna, lan yaḍribū, lam yaḍribū. Here the nūn is the sign itself: the alif, the wāw and the yāʾ before it are pronouns, the doers of the verb, and they stay in every state.

Look at the pairs and a pattern appears. In the dual, the plural and the sound feminine plural, naṣb takes the same form as khafḍ. In the five verbs, naṣb takes the same form as jazm. Teachers put it as a rule: in nouns naṣb follows khafḍ, in verbs naṣb follows jazm; only the five nouns and the words with vowels keep naṣb apart.

With this the first half of the book is done: what speech is, the kinds of word, iʿrāb, its signs and the words that take them. Everything after it applies these tables. When the book says that the doer is in rafʿ, the student must be able to say at once: zaydun with the ḍamma, al-Zaydāni with the alif, al-Zaydūna with the wāw, akhūka with the wāw.

terms.en: the five verbs: yafʿalāni … tafʿalīna
the dual (the book: al-tathniya)
the five nouns: wāw, alif, yāʾ
the pronoun: in the five verbs, the alif, wāw or yāʾ

examples.en: al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni, “the two Zayds are standing”: two duals in rafʿ by the alif
raʾaytu abāka, “I saw your father”: the alif of the five nouns in naṣb
lan taḍribī, “you (woman) will not strike”: the nūn dropped in naṣb
lam yaḍribū, “they did not strike”: the nūn dropped in jazm

tasks.prompt: Give al-muʿallimūna, “the teachers”, al-kitābāni, “the two books”, and akhūka in the three states of the noun.
tasks.answer: Al-muʿallimūna, al-muʿallimīna, al-muʿallimīna (wāw, yāʾ, yāʾ). Al-kitābāni, al-kitābayni, al-kitābayni (alif, yāʾ, yāʾ). Akhūka, akhāka, akhīka (wāw, alif, yāʾ).

tasks.prompt: Write the five verbs of kataba in the present, then after lan and after lam.
tasks.answer: Rafʿ: yaktubāni, taktubāni, yaktubūna, taktubūna, taktubīna. After lan: yaktubā, taktubā, yaktubū, taktubū, taktubī. After lam: the same as after lan, yaktubā, taktubā, yaktubū, taktubū, taktubī (the nūn is dropped in both).

tasks.prompt: In which kinds of word does naṣb take the form of khafḍ, and in which the form of jazm?
tasks.answer: In nouns, naṣb takes the form of khafḍ in the dual, the sound masculine plural (yāʾ in both) and the sound feminine plural (kasra in both). In verbs, naṣb takes the form of jazm in the five verbs (the nūn dropped in both).

tasks.prompt: In yaḍribūna, which letter is the sign of rafʿ, and what is the wāw?
tasks.answer: The nūn is the sign of rafʿ (it is dropped in naṣb and jazm). The wāw is the pronoun of the plural doers and stays in every state.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is inflected by letters?
quiz.explanation: The dual, the sound masculine plural, the five nouns and the five verbs are inflected by letters.

quiz.prompt: What are the signs of the dual?
options: Wāw in rafʿ, yāʾ in naṣb and khafḍ
Alif in rafʿ, yāʾ in naṣb and khafḍ
Alif in rafʿ and naṣb, yāʾ in khafḍ
Nūn in rafʿ, dropping it in naṣb
quiz.explanation: Al-Zaydāni in rafʿ, al-Zaydayni in naṣb and khafḍ.

quiz.prompt: Which kind has a different letter for each of its three states?
quiz.explanation: Abūka, abāka, abīka: wāw, alif, yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is one of the five verbs?
quiz.explanation: The five verbs are yafʿalāni, tafʿalāni, yafʿalūna, tafʿalūna and tafʿalīna; taktubīna is tafʿalīna.

quiz.prompt: Lam yaktubā and lan yaktubā look the same. Why?
options: In the five verbs naṣb and jazm are both by dropping the nūn
Lam and lan mean the same
One of them is a mistake
quiz.explanation: In the five verbs naṣb follows jazm: both drop the nūn.

quiz.prompt: In the sound masculine plural, naṣb has the same form as…
quiz.explanation: Al-Zaydīna in both naṣb and khafḍ: in nouns, naṣb follows khafḍ.

quiz.prompt: What is the sign of rafʿ in al-Zaydāni?
quiz.explanation: The dual is in rafʿ by the alif; the nūn after it is not the sign of iʿrāb in a noun.

text.original: وَالَّذِي يُعْرَبُ بِالْحُرُوفِ أَرْبَعَةُ أَنْوَاعٍ: التَّثْنِيَةُ، وَجَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ، وَالْأَسْمَاءُ الْخَمْسَةُ، وَالْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ، وَهِيَ: يَفْعَلَانِ، وَتَفْعَلَانِ، وَيَفْعَلُونَ، وَتَفْعَلُونَ، وَتَفْعَلِينَ.
text.en: That which is inflected by letters is of four kinds: the dual, the sound masculine plural, the five nouns, and the five verbs, which are: yafʿalāni “they two do”, tafʿalāni “you two do”, yafʿalūna “they do”, tafʿalūna “you (pl.) do” and tafʿalīna “you (f.) do”.

text.original: فَأَمَّا التَّثْنِيَةُ فَتُرْفَعُ بِالْأَلِفِ، وَتُنْصَبُ وَتُخْفَضُ بِالْيَاءِ. وَأَمَّا جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ فَيُرْفَعُ بِالْوَاوِ، وَتُنْصَبُ وَتُخْفَضُ بِالْيَاءِ. وَأَمَّا الْأَسْمَاءُ الْخَمْسَةُ فَتُرْفَعُ بِالْوَاوِ، وَتُنْصَبُ بِالْأَلِفِ، وَتُخْفَضُ بِالْيَاءِ. وَأَمَّا الْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ فَتُرْفَعُ بِالنُّونِ، وَتُنْصَبُ وَتُجْزَمُ بِحَذْفِهَا.
text.en: As for the dual, it takes rafʿ by the alif, and naṣb and khafḍ by the yāʾ. As for the sound masculine plural, it takes rafʿ by the wāw, and naṣb and khafḍ by the yāʾ. As for the five nouns, they take rafʿ by the wāw, naṣb by the alif and khafḍ by the yāʾ. As for the five verbs, they take rafʿ by the nūn, and naṣb and jazm by its dropping.

lessons.title: The three verbs and the present
body: The verbs are three: the past (māḍī), the present (muḍāriʿ) and the imperative (amr). The book gives them on one root, as the madrasa always does: ḍaraba, “he struck”; yaḍribu, “he strikes”; iḍrib, “strike!”. Learning the three together on one verb is the first habit of ṣarf, and al-Amthila and the other ṣarf primers build their tables the same way.

Then comes the ending of each. The past is “always with fatḥa at its end”: ḍaraba. This is a fixed ending (bināʾ), not iʿrāb: no governor changes it. The commentaries meet the obvious objection, ḍarabū and ḍarabtu, in two ways: some say the fatḥa is still there by assumption, others, as most later books, that the past is fixed on the ḍamma before the wāw of the plural and on the sukūn before the moving pronouns. The imperative is “always in jazm”: iḍrib. That is the view of the Kūfan grammarians, which Ibn Ājurrūm follows here as in calling the -i state khafḍ; the Baṣrans, and most later books, say the imperative is fixed on the sukūn, not majzūm.

The present is the verb that begins with one of four added letters, gathered in the word anaytu: the hamza (aḍribu, “I strike”), the nūn (naḍribu, “we strike”), the yāʾ (yaḍribu, “he strikes”) and the tāʾ (taḍribu, “you strike” or “she strikes”). The letter must be added, not part of the root: akrama, “he honoured”, begins with a hamza but is a past verb; its present is yukrimu.

The present is “always in rafʿ until a governor of naṣb or of jazm enters on it”. It is the only verb with iʿrāb at all. What puts it in rafʿ, the book does not say; many later grammarians answer that it is its being free of every governor of naṣb and jazm. The next two lessons list those governors: ten of naṣb, eighteen of jazm.

Two small traps. The tāʾ serves two persons, so taḍribu alone is “you (man) strike” or “she strikes”, and only the context decides. And the vowel of the added letter is fatḥa in the bare verb (yaḍribu) but ḍamma in the four-letter verb (yukrimu): ṣarf gives the rule, and it is not a sign of iʿrāb.

terms.en: the past verb: fixed on the fatḥa
the present verb: in rafʿ unless governed
the imperative: majzūm in this book
the four added letters of the present: anaytu
the fixed ending, which no governor changes

examples.en: ḍaraba, yaḍribu, iḍrib: the three verbs on one root, as the book gives them
aḍribu, naḍribu, yaḍribu, taḍribu: the four letters of anaytu
akrama, yukrimu: the hamza of akrama is not a sign of the present

tasks.prompt: Which of these are present verbs, and what is the added letter? aktubu, akrama, naktubu, taktubīna, kataba.
tasks.answer: Aktubu: present, the hamza (I write). Akrama: past; its hamza belongs to the pattern afʿala, not to anaytu. Naktubu: present, the nūn (we write). Taktubīna: present, the tāʾ (you, a woman, write). Kataba: past.

tasks.prompt: Give the past, the present and the imperative of naṣara, fataḥa and jalasa.
tasks.answer: Naṣara, yanṣuru, unṣur; fataḥa, yaftaḥu, iftaḥ; jalasa, yajlisu, ijlis.

tasks.prompt: The book says the imperative is “always in jazm”. What do most later books say, and whose view does the Ājurrūmiyya follow?
tasks.answer: Most later books, following the Baṣrans, say the imperative is fixed (mabnī) on the sukūn, not in jazm. The Ājurrūmiyya follows the Kūfans here.

tasks.prompt: Taḍribu has two possible meanings. Give them and say why.
tasks.answer: “You (a man) strike” and “she strikes”. The tāʾ of anaytu serves both the second person and the feminine third person; the context decides.

quiz.prompt: What does the word anaytu gather?
options: The four added letters of the present verb
quiz.explanation: Hamza, nūn, yāʾ and tāʾ: one of them begins every present verb.

quiz.prompt: According to the book, how does the past verb end?
options: With ḍamma in rafʿ, fatḥa in naṣb
quiz.explanation: “The past is always with fatḥa at its end”: a fixed ending, not iʿrāb.

quiz.prompt: What does the Ājurrūmiyya say about the imperative?
quiz.explanation: It follows the Kūfan view; most later books say it is fixed on the sukūn.

quiz.prompt: Akrama begins with a hamza. Is it a present verb?
options: No: its hamza is part of its pattern, not the hamza of anaytu
Yes: every verb with a hamza is present
quiz.explanation: The added letter must be the letter of the present. Akrama is the past of the pattern afʿala; its present is yukrimu.

quiz.prompt: When is the present verb in rafʿ?
options: Always, until a governor of naṣb or jazm enters on it
Only when it has a doer
quiz.explanation: The present is in rafʿ until a nāṣib or a jāzim enters on it.

quiz.prompt: Which of the three verbs changes its ending with the governors that enter on it?
quiz.explanation: The past is always with fatḥa and the imperative always in jazm; only the present is in rafʿ, naṣb or jazm according to its governor.

quiz.prompt: Naḍribu means…
quiz.explanation: The nūn of anaytu is the speaker with others: “we”.

text.original: الْأَفْعَالُ ثَلَاثَةٌ: مَاضٍ، وَمُضَارِعٌ، وَأَمْرٌ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ، وَيَضْرِبُ، وَاضْرِبْ. فَالْمَاضِي مَفْتُوحُ الْآخِرِ أَبَدًا، وَالْأَمْرُ مَجْزُومٌ أَبَدًا.
text.en: The verbs are three: the past (māḍī), the present–future (muḍāriʿ) and the imperative (amr), as ḍaraba “he struck”, yaḍribu “he strikes” and iḍrib “strike!”. The māḍī always has a fatḥa at its end, and the amr is always majzūm.

text.original: وَالْمُضَارِعُ مَا كَانَ فِي أَوَّلِهِ إِحْدَى الزَّوَائِدِ الْأَرْبَعِ يَجْمَعُهَا قَوْلُكَ: أَنَيْتُ، وَهُوَ مَرْفُوعٌ أَبَدًا حَتَّى يَدْخُلَ عَلَيْهِ نَاصِبٌ أَوْ جَازِمٌ.
text.en: The muḍāriʿ is that which has at its beginning one of the four added letters, which are gathered in your saying anaytu. It is always marfūʿ, until a governor of naṣb or a governor of jazm comes upon it.

lessons.title: The governors of naṣb
body: Ten words put the present verb in naṣb: an, lan, idhan, kay, the lām of kay, the lām of denial, ḥattā, and the answer with the fāʾ, the wāw and aw. After any of them the verb takes the sign of naṣb: the fatḥa (lan yaḍriba) or, in the five verbs, the dropping of the nūn (lan taḍribū, “you will not strike”).

An, “that”, turns the verb into the meaning of a verbal noun: aradta an taqūla, “you wanted to say”, is “you wanted saying”. Lan negates the future: lan yaḍriba, “he will not strike”. Idhan, “then, in that case”, answers someone: to “I will visit you” one says idhan ukrimaka, “then I will honour you”. Kay, “so that”, gives the purpose: jalastu kay aktuba, “I sat down so that I might write”.

The lām of kay is the li- of purpose with the same meaning: jalastu li-aktuba. The lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd) is the li- that follows a negated kāna: wa-mā kāna llāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum, “God was not going to punish them” (Q 8:33). Ḥattā, “until”, gives the end of something: ajlisu ḥattā takhruja, “I stay sitting until you go out”.

The answer with the fāʾ, the wāw and aw is a verb that comes after a demand or a negation, joined by one of these three: uktub fa-taḥfaẓa, “write, and so you will remember”, where taḥfaẓa is in naṣb because it answers the command. With the wāw the meaning is “and at the same time”: wa-lammā yaʿlami llāhu alladhīna jāhadū minkum wa-yaʿlama al-ṣābirīna, “while God has not yet known those of you who strove, and known the steadfast” (Q 3:142). With aw it is “until” or “unless”.

The madrasa adds a point the book leaves out. The Baṣran grammarians, and most books after them, hold that only four of these govern by themselves, an, lan, idhan and kay; after the others (the two lāms, ḥattā, and the fāʾ, wāw and aw of the answer) the verb is in naṣb by an an that is understood and not said. The Ājurrūmiyya counts all ten as governors, which is easier for the beginner; the result, the naṣb of the verb, is the same.

terms.en: the governors that put the present verb in naṣb
the li- of purpose: “so that”
the lām of denial, after a negated kāna
the answer with fa- to a demand or a negation
an understood, not said (the Baṣran view)

idhan ukrimaka, “then I will honour you”: idhan answering what was said
jalastu li-aktuba, “I sat down to write”: the lām of kay
wa-mā kāna llāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum (Q 8:33): the lām of denial after a negated kāna

tasks.answer: Lan taktuba (fatḥa); kay najlisa (fatḥa); lan taktubū (the nūn dropped); an taftaḥī (the nūn dropped).

tasks.prompt: Find the governor of naṣb in wa-mā kāna llāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum (Q 8:33), say which of the ten it is, and give the sign of naṣb.
tasks.answer: The li- before yuʿadhdhiba: the lām of denial, because it follows a negated kāna (mā kāna). Yuʿadhdhiba is in naṣb by the fatḥa; -hum is its object.

tasks.prompt: In uktub fa-taḥfaẓa, “write, and so you will remember”, why is taḥfaẓa in naṣb?
tasks.answer: It answers a demand (the command uktub) and is joined to it by the fāʾ of the answer, one of the ten. Without the command before it, taḥfaẓu would be in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Which four of the ten govern by themselves on the Baṣran view, and what do the Baṣrans say of the others?
tasks.answer: An, lan, idhan and kay. After the lām of kay, the lām of denial, ḥattā and the fāʾ, wāw and aw of the answer, they say the verb is in naṣb by an understood an.

quiz.prompt: How many governors of naṣb does the Ājurrūmiyya list?
quiz.explanation: An, lan, idhan, kay, the lām of kay, the lām of denial, ḥattā, and the answer with fa-, wa- and aw.

quiz.prompt: What does lan do?
options: It negates the past and puts the verb in jazm
It forbids and puts the verb in jazm
It negates the future and puts the verb in naṣb
quiz.explanation: Lan yaḍriba: “he will not strike”.

quiz.prompt: Lan taḍribū comes from taḍribūna. What is the sign of naṣb?
quiz.explanation: Taḍribūna is one of the five verbs: in naṣb its nūn is dropped.

quiz.prompt: The lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd) comes after…
quiz.explanation: Mā kāna llāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum: “God was not going to punish them”.

quiz.prompt: In uktub fa-taḥfaẓa, what puts taḥfaẓa in naṣb?
quiz.explanation: The answer with the fāʾ after a demand or a negation is one of the ten.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is in naṣb?
quiz.explanation: After kay the verb takes the fatḥa; lam najlis is in jazm, the others in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: On the Baṣran view, which of these governs by itself?
quiz.explanation: Only an, lan, idhan and kay govern by themselves; after the others an is understood.

text.original: فَالنَّوَاصِبُ عَشَرَةٌ، وَهِيَ: أَنْ، وَلَنْ، وَإِذًا، وَكَيْ، وَلَامُ كَيْ، وَلَامُ الْجُحُودِ، وَحَتَّى، وَالْجَوَابُ بِالْفَاءِ وَالْوَاوِ وَأَوْ.
text.en: The governors of naṣb (nawāṣib) are ten: an “that”, lan “will not”, idhan “in that case”, kay “so that”, the lām of kay [li- “so that”], the lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd), ḥattā “until”, and the answer with fa-, with wa- and with aw.

lessons.title: The governors of jazm
body: The book lists eighteen governors of jazm. The commentaries divide them into two groups. Six put one verb in jazm: lam, lammā, alam, alammā, the lām of command and of prayer, and the lā of prohibition and of prayer. The rest are the words of condition, which put two verbs in jazm, the condition (sharṭ) and its answer (jawāb): in, mā, man, mahmā, idh mā, ayy, matā, ayyāna, ayna, annā, ḥaythumā, kayfamā, and idhā in poetry only.

Lam negates the past, though the verb after it has the form of the present: lam yaḍrib, “he did not strike”. Lammā is “not yet”: the negation reaches up to now and is expected to end, as in wa-lammā yaʿlami llāhu, “while God has not yet known” (Q 3:142); the verb's sukūn takes a kasra there to join the next word. Alam and alammā are the same with the hamza of the question: a-lam nashraḥ laka ṣadraka, “did We not open your breast for you?” (Q 94:1).

The lām of command asks for an act: li-yajlis, “let him sit”; after fa- or wa- it loses its vowel, as in fa-l-yadʿu nādiyahu (Q 96:17). The lā of prohibition forbids: lā taḍrib, “do not strike”. The book adds “and of prayer” to both because the same forms are used when one asks God: li-yaqḍi ʿalaynā rabbuka, “let your Lord make an end of us” (Q 43:77); rabbanā lā tuʾākhidhnā, “our Lord, do not take us to task” (Q 2:286). The grammarians call that prayer (duʿāʾ), not command, out of courtesy.

In the condition both verbs are in jazm: in taḍrib aḍrib, “if you strike, I strike”: taḍrib is the condition, aḍrib its answer. Each word of condition adds its meaning: man “whoever”, mā and mahmā “whatever”, matā and ayyāna “whenever”, ayna, annā and ḥaythumā “wherever”, kayfamā “however”: aynamā takūnū yudrikkumu al-mawtu, “wherever you are, death will overtake you” (Q 4:78). In is a particle; most of the others are nouns.

Two notes the teachers add. Idhā puts the verb in jazm only in poetry; in prose the verb after it stays as it is. And kayfamā is counted among the governors of jazm by the Kūfans, whom the book follows here again; the Baṣrans do not count it. A beginner should also not confuse lam (jazm) with lan (naṣb): one letter apart, past and future, and different signs.

terms.en: the governors that put the present verb in jazm
the lām of command: li-yajlis, “let him sit”
the lā of prohibition: “do not”
the condition: the first verb after in, man …
the answer of the condition: the second verb
prayer: command or prohibition addressed to God

a-lam nashraḥ laka ṣadraka, “did We not open your breast for you?” (Q 94:1): alam
lā taḍrib, “do not strike”: the lā of prohibition
in taḍrib aḍrib, “if you strike, I strike”: two verbs in jazm, the condition and its answer
