tasks.prompt: Put each verb in jazm with the governor given: lam + yaktubu; lā of prohibition + taftaḥu; the lām of command + yajlisu; lam + yaktubūna.
tasks.arabic: لَمْ يَكْتُبُ — لَا تَفْتَحُ — لِـ يَجْلِسُ — لَمْ يَكْتُبُونَ
tasks.answer: Lam yaktub (sukūn); lā taftaḥ (sukūn); li-yajlis (sukūn); lam yaktubū (the nūn dropped).

tasks.prompt: In in taḍrib aḍrib, name the governor, the condition and the answer, and give the state and sign of each verb.
tasks.answer: In is the particle of condition. Taḍrib is the condition (sharṭ), in jazm by the sukūn; aḍrib is the answer (jawāb), in jazm by the sukūn. In governs both.

tasks.prompt: Parse a-lam nashraḥ (Q 94:1).
tasks.answer: A-: the hamza of the question. Lam: a particle of negation that puts the present in jazm. Nashraḥ: present verb (its nūn is the nūn of anaytu, “We”), in jazm by the sukūn; its doer is a hidden pronoun, “We”.

tasks.prompt: Lam yaḍrib and lan yaḍriba: what is the difference in meaning, in state and in sign?
tasks.answer: Lam yaḍrib is past in meaning (“he did not strike”), in jazm by the sukūn. Lan yaḍriba is future (“he will not strike”), in naṣb by the fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: Which of these puts two verbs in jazm?
quiz.explanation: The words of condition govern the condition and its answer; lam, lammā and the lā of prohibition govern one verb.

quiz.prompt: What does lammā mean?
quiz.explanation: Its negation reaches up to now and is expected to end: wa-lammā yaʿlami llāhu, “God has not yet known” (Q 3:142).

quiz.prompt: In in taḍrib aḍrib, what is aḍrib?
options: The answer of the condition, in jazm
quiz.explanation: Taḍrib is the condition, aḍrib its answer; both are majzūm.

quiz.prompt: When does idhā put the verb in jazm?
quiz.explanation: The book says: “and idhā in poetry only”.

quiz.prompt: Why does the book say “the lām of command and of prayer”?
options: Prayer has a lām of its own
The lām is only used in the prayer
Because the lām puts two verbs in jazm
The same form addressed to God is called prayer
quiz.explanation: Li-yaqḍi ʿalaynā rabbuka (Q 43:77): a command in form, called prayer out of courtesy.

quiz.prompt: Which governor is counted by the Kūfans, and by this book, but not by the Baṣrans?
quiz.explanation: Ibn Ājurrūm follows the Kūfans in counting kayfamā.

quiz.prompt: Lam yaktubū comes from yaktubūna. What is the sign of jazm?
quiz.explanation: The five verbs are in jazm by dropping the nūn.

text.original: وَالْجَوَازِمُ ثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ، وَهِيَ: لَمْ، وَلَمَّا، وَأَلَمْ، وَأَلَمَّا، وَلَامُ الْأَمْرِ وَالدُّعَاءِ، وَلَا فِي النَّهْيِ وَالدُّعَاءِ، وَإِنْ، وَمَا، وَمَنْ، وَمَهْمَا، وَإِذْمَا، وَأَيٌّ، وَمَتَى، وَأَيَّانَ، وَأَيْنَ، وَأَنَّى، وَحَيْثُمَا، وَكَيْفَمَا، وَإِذَا فِي الشِّعْرِ خَاصَّةً.
text.en: The governors of jazm (jawāzim) are eighteen: lam “did not”, lammā “has not yet”, a-lam “did … not?”, a-lammā “has … not yet?”, the lām of command and of prayer, lā in prohibition and in prayer, in “if”, mā “whatever”, man “whoever”, mahmā “whatever”, idhmā “if”, ayyun “whichever”, matā “whenever”, ayyāna “whenever”, ayna “wherever”, annā “wherever”, ḥaythumā “wherever”, kayfamā “however”, and idhā “when” in poetry only.

lessons.title: The nouns in rafʿ: the seven
body: With the verbs done, the book turns to the nouns, and from here to the end it is arranged by state: the nouns in rafʿ (marfūʿāt), the nouns in naṣb (manṣūbāt), the nouns in khafḍ (makhfūḍāt). This is the plan of the Ājurrūmiyya, and of the books built on it: first the signs, then the places where each state is found.

Seven nouns are in rafʿ: the doer (fāʿil); the object whose doer is not named, which later books call the deputy of the doer (nāʾib al-fāʿil); the subject (mubtadaʾ) and its predicate (khabar), counted as two; the noun of kāna and its sisters; the predicate of inna and its sisters; and the follower of a noun in rafʿ, which is of four kinds: the adjective (naʿt), the conjunction (ʿaṭf), the emphasis (tawkīd) and the substitute (badal).

Each item is a role in the sentence, not a kind of noun. The same word Zayd is a fāʿil in qāma Zaydun, a mubtadaʾ in Zaydun qāʾimun, the noun of kāna in kāna Zaydun qāʾiman; its state is rafʿ each time because each of these roles calls for rafʿ. That is why the student is asked, for every noun, “what is its role?” before “what is its ending?”.

Two items need care. From kāna, it is the noun (ism) that is listed here, because kāna gives rafʿ to its noun and naṣb to its predicate; from inna it is the predicate, because inna does the opposite. “Noun of kāna” means the subject of kāna, not a noun as a kind of word. And the followers (tawābiʿ) have no state of their own: they take the state of the word they follow, so they are listed again under naṣb and under khafḍ. Lessons 13 to 23 take the seven one by one.

terms.en: the nouns in rafʿ: seven roles
the doer
the noun (subject) of kāna
the predicate of inna
the follower, which takes the state of what it follows

examples.en: qāma Zaydun: Zayd in rafʿ as the doer
Zaydun qāʾimun: Zayd in rafʿ as the subject, qāʾimun as the predicate
kāna Zaydun qāʾiman, “Zayd was standing”: Zayd in rafʿ as the noun of kāna

tasks.prompt: Name every noun in rafʿ in these sentences and its role: Zaydun qāʾimun; kāna ʿAmrun shākhiṣan; inna Zaydan qāʾimun; ḍuriba Zaydun.
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ — كَانَ عَمْرٌو شَاخِصًا — إِنَّ زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ — ضُرِبَ زَيْدٌ
tasks.answer: Zaydun: mubtadaʾ; qāʾimun: khabar. ʿAmrun: the noun of kāna (shākhiṣan, its predicate, is in naṣb). Qāʾimun: the predicate of inna (Zaydan, its noun, is in naṣb). Zaydun: the object whose doer is not named (nāʾib al-fāʿil).

tasks.prompt: Recite the seven nouns in rafʿ, with the four followers.
tasks.answer: The fāʿil; the object whose doer is not named; the mubtadaʾ; its khabar; the noun of kāna and its sisters; the predicate of inna and its sisters; the follower of a noun in rafʿ: naʿt, ʿaṭf, tawkīd and badal.

tasks.prompt: Why does the list name the noun of kāna but the predicate of inna?
tasks.answer: Because kāna puts its noun in rafʿ and its predicate in naṣb, while inna puts its noun in naṣb and its predicate in rafʿ. Each list names the part that is in its state.

quiz.prompt: How many nouns in rafʿ does the book count?
quiz.explanation: Fāʿil, the object whose doer is not named, mubtadaʾ, khabar, the noun of kāna, the predicate of inna, and the follower.

quiz.prompt: Which part of the sentence with inna is in rafʿ?
quiz.explanation: Inna puts its noun in naṣb and its predicate in rafʿ: inna Zaydan qāʾimun.

quiz.prompt: Which part of the sentence with kāna is in rafʿ?
quiz.explanation: Kāna puts its noun in rafʿ and its predicate in naṣb: kāna Zaydun qāʾiman.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is not one of the four followers?
quiz.explanation: The followers are naʿt, ʿaṭf, tawkīd and badal; the ḥāl is one of the nouns in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Why are the followers listed under rafʿ and again under naṣb?
options: They take the state of the word they follow
They are always in rafʿ and naṣb at once
Because the book repeats itself by mistake
They have a state of their own
quiz.explanation: A follower of a noun in rafʿ is in rafʿ, of a noun in naṣb in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: The list of the nouns in rafʿ is a list of…
quiz.explanation: Fāʿil, mubtadaʾ and the rest are roles; the same noun can fill any of them.

quiz.prompt: In ḍuriba Zaydun, “Zayd was struck”, Zayd is…
options: the object whose doer is not named
quiz.explanation: With the doer left out, the object takes its place and its rafʿ.

text.original: الْمَرْفُوعَاتُ سَبْعَةٌ، وَهِيَ: الْفَاعِلُ، وَالْمَفْعُولُ الَّذِي لَمْ يُسَمَّ فَاعِلُهُ، وَالْمُبْتَدَأُ وَخَبَرُهُ، وَاسْمُ كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، وَخَبَرُ إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، وَالتَّابِعُ لِلْمَرْفُوعِ، وَهُوَ أَرْبَعَةُ أَشْيَاءَ: النَّعْتُ، وَالْعَطْفُ، وَالتَّوْكِيدُ، وَالْبَدَلُ.
text.en: The nouns in rafʿ (marfūʿāt) are seven: the fāʿil; the object whose doer is not named; the mubtadaʾ and its khabar; the noun of kāna and its sisters; the khabar of inna and its sisters; and that which follows a marfūʿ, which is four things: the adjective (naʿt), the conjunction (ʿaṭf), the emphasis (tawkīd) and the substitute (badal).

lessons.title: The doer (fāʿil)
body: The fāʿil is “the noun in rafʿ whose verb is mentioned before it”. Each part counts. A noun: a verb or a particle is never a fāʿil. In rafʿ: always. Its verb before it: in qāma Zaydun, “Zayd stood”, Zayd is the fāʿil; in Zaydun qāma, with Zayd first, he is not the fāʿil but a mubtadaʾ, and the fāʿil of qāma is a hidden pronoun, “he”. That is the first trap of this chapter, and the madrasa tests it again and again.

“Doer” is a word of grammar, not of the world. In ṭāba Muḥammadun nafsan, “Muḥammad was of good heart” (the book's example of tamyīz, p. 10), Muḥammad did nothing, yet he is the fāʿil of ṭāba. Whatever noun the verb is said of, coming after it, is its fāʿil.

The fāʿil is of two kinds, explicit (ẓāhir) and pronoun (muḍmar). The explicit fāʿil is shown with each kind of noun: qāma Zaydun, al-Zaydāni, al-Zaydūna, akhūka, with the present beside the past each time. Look at the verb: it is qāma for one, for two and for many. Before an explicit fāʿil the verb stays singular; one does not say qāmā al-Zaydāni in the language of the books.

The pronoun fāʿil is shown in the past verb ḍaraba with each person: ḍarabtu (I struck), ḍarabnā (we), ḍarabta (you, a man), ḍarabti (you, a woman), ḍarabtumā (you two), ḍarabtum (you, men), ḍarabtunna (you, women), ḍaraba (he), ḍarabat (she), ḍarabā (they two), ḍarabatā (they two, women), ḍarabū (they, men), ḍarabna (they, women). In most of them the doer is the ending you can see: -tu, -nā, -ta, -ū. In ḍaraba and ḍarabat it is hidden, “he” and “she”; the tāʾ of ḍarabat is the sign of the feminine from lesson 2, not the doer.

The madrasa reads such a sentence aloud in a fixed order: the word, its kind, its state, its sign, and why. Qāma akhūka: qāma, a past verb, fixed on the fatḥa; akhū, the fāʿil, in rafʿ, and the sign of its rafʿ is the wāw because it is one of the five nouns; -ka, a pronoun, fixed, in the place of khafḍ as the second term of the iḍāfa. This is “doing the iʿrāb”, and the tasks below ask for it.

terms.en: the noun in rafʿ whose verb comes before it
explicit: a noun that is not a pronoun
the pronoun
the hidden pronoun, as in ḍaraba, “he struck”

examples.en: qāma al-Zaydāni, “the two Zayds stood”: the verb stays singular before an explicit fāʿil
yaqūmu al-Zaydūna, “the Zayds stand”: the fāʿil in rafʿ by the wāw
ḍarabtu, “I struck”: the -tu is the fāʿil
ḍarabat, “she struck”: the doer is hidden; the tāʾ is the sign of the feminine

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of qāma akhūka.
tasks.answer: Qāma: a past verb, fixed on the fatḥa. Akhū: the fāʿil, in rafʿ; the sign of its rafʿ is the wāw, because it is one of the five nouns. -ka: a pronoun, fixed on the fatḥa, in the place of khafḍ as the second term of the iḍāfa (muḍāf ilayhi).

tasks.prompt: Find the fāʿil in each and say whether it is explicit or a pronoun: yaqūmu al-Zaydūna; ḍarabtu; ḍarabat; ṭāba Muḥammadun nafsan.
tasks.arabic: يَقُومُ الزَّيْدُونَ — ضَرَبْتُ — ضَرَبَتْ — طَابَ مُحَمَّدٌ نَفْسًا
tasks.answer: Al-Zaydūna: explicit, in rafʿ by the wāw. The -tu of ḍarabtu: a pronoun. In ḍarabat: a hidden pronoun, “she” (the tāʾ is only the sign of the feminine). Muḥammadun: explicit, in rafʿ by the ḍamma.

tasks.prompt: In Zaydun qāma, “Zayd, he stood”, why is Zayd not the fāʿil? What is the fāʿil?
tasks.answer: The fāʿil must come after its verb. Zayd comes before it, so he is a mubtadaʾ; the fāʿil of qāma is a hidden pronoun, “he”, referring to Zayd, and qāma with its fāʿil is the khabar.

tasks.prompt: Write the thirteen forms of ḍaraba that the book gives with a pronoun fāʿil, with their meanings.
tasks.answer: Ḍarabtu (I), ḍarabnā (we), ḍarabta (you, m.), ḍarabti (you, f.), ḍarabtumā (you two), ḍarabtum (you, m. pl.), ḍarabtunna (you, f. pl.), ḍaraba (he), ḍarabat (she), ḍarabā (they two, m.), ḍarabatā (they two, f.), ḍarabū (they, m.), ḍarabna (they, f.).

quiz.prompt: How does the book define the fāʿil?
options: The noun in rafʿ whose verb is mentioned before it
The first noun of every sentence
The noun in naṣb after the verb
quiz.explanation: Noun, in rafʿ, with its verb before it.

quiz.prompt: In Zaydun qāma, what is Zayd?
quiz.explanation: Coming before the verb he cannot be its fāʿil; the fāʿil of qāma is a hidden pronoun.

quiz.prompt: “The two Zayds stood” is…
quiz.explanation: Before an explicit fāʿil the verb stays singular.

quiz.prompt: What is the fāʿil in ḍarabat, “she struck”?
quiz.explanation: The quiescent tāʾ is the sign of the feminine; the doer is hidden.

quiz.prompt: In ṭāba Muḥammadun nafsan, Muḥammad did nothing. Is he the fāʿil?
options: Yes: the term belongs to grammar
quiz.explanation: The noun the verb is said of, after it, is its fāʿil, whether or not it acts.

quiz.prompt: Into which two kinds is the fāʿil divided?
quiz.explanation: Ẓāhir and muḍmar.

quiz.prompt: What is the fāʿil in ḍarabū?
quiz.explanation: The wāw of the plural is the pronoun fāʿil (the alif after it is only written).

text.original: الْفَاعِلُ هُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَرْفُوعُ الْمَذْكُورُ قَبْلَهُ فِعْلُهُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: ظَاهِرٍ وَمُضْمَرٍ.
text.en: The doer (fāʿil) is the noun in rafʿ whose verb is mentioned before it. It is of two divisions: an explicit noun (ẓāhir) and a pronoun (muḍmar).

text.original: فَالظَّاهِرُ نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ، وَيَقُومُ زَيْدٌ، وَقَامَ الزَّيْدَانِ، وَيَقُومُ الزَّيْدَانِ، وَقَامَ الزَّيْدُونَ، وَيَقُومُ الزَّيْدُونَ، وَقَامَ أَخُوكَ، وَيَقُومُ أَخُوكَ.
text.en: The explicit noun is as when you say: qāma Zaydun “Zayd stood”, yaqūmu Zaydun “Zayd stands”, qāma al-Zaydāni “the two Zayds stood”, yaqūmu al-Zaydāni “the two Zayds stand”, qāma al-Zaydūna “the Zayds stood”, yaqūmu al-Zaydūna “the Zayds stand”, qāma akhūka “your brother stood” and yaqūmu akhūka “your brother stands”.

text.original: وَالْمُضْمَرُ نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: ضَرَبْتُ، وَضَرَبْنَا، وَضَرَبْتَ، وَضَرَبْتِ، وَضَرَبْتُمَا، وَضَرَبْتُمْ، وَضَرَبْتُنَّ، وَضَرَبَ، وَضَرَبَتْ، وَضَرَبَا، وَضَرَبَتَا، وَضَرَبُوا، وَضَرَبْنَ.
text.en: The pronoun is as when you say: ḍarabtu “I struck”, ḍarabnā “we struck”, ḍarabta “you (m.) struck”, ḍarabti “you (f.) struck”, ḍarabtumā “you two struck”, ḍarabtum “you (m. pl.) struck”, ḍarabtunna “you (f. pl.) struck”, ḍaraba “he struck”, ḍarabat “she struck”, ḍarabā “they two struck”, ḍarabatā “they two (f.) struck”, ḍarabū “they (m.) struck” and ḍarabna “they (f.) struck”.

lessons.title: The object whose doer is not named
body: Sometimes the doer is left out: unknown, obvious, or not to be named. Then the object takes its place and its state. From ḍaraba ʿAmrun Zaydan, “ʿAmr struck Zayd”, one makes ḍuriba Zaydun, “Zayd was struck”: Zayd, who was the object in naṣb, is now in rafʿ. The book calls this noun “the object whose doer is not named” and defines it as “the noun in rafʿ whose doer is not mentioned with it”. Later books, such as the Alfiyya, speak of the deputy of the doer (nāʾib al-fāʿil).

The verb changes its form, and the book gives the rule in vowels. In the past, its first letter takes a ḍamma and the letter before the last a kasra: ḍaraba becomes ḍuriba, akrama becomes ukrima. In the present, its first letter takes a ḍamma and the letter before the last a fatḥa: yaḍribu becomes yuḍrabu, yukrimu becomes yukramu. Longer verbs change more letters; the ṣarf books (al-Amthila, al-ʿIzzī) give their passive forms in full.

Like the fāʿil, this noun is explicit or a pronoun. Explicit: ḍuriba Zaydun, yuḍrabu Zaydun, ukrima ʿAmrun, yukramu ʿAmrun. Pronoun: ḍuribtu, “I was struck”, ḍuribnā, “we were struck”, ḍuribta, “you were struck”, and so on through the persons, as with the fāʿil.

The trap is in the writing. Without vowels, ضرب زيد can be read ḍaraba Zaydun, “Zayd struck”, or ḍuriba Zaydun, “Zayd was struck”, and the two mean opposite things. Only the vowels of the verb tell them apart. That is one reason the madrasa insists on reading every text with full vocalisation, and why a student who cannot yet vowel a sentence is said not yet to have understood it.

terms.en: the object whose doer is not named
the deputy of the doer (the later name)
the passive verb, whose doer is unknown
the active verb

examples.en: ḍuriba Zaydun, “Zayd was struck”: the past with ḍamma first and kasra before the last letter
yuḍrabu Zaydun, “Zayd is struck”: the present with ḍamma first and fatḥa before the last letter
ukrima ʿAmrun, “ʿAmr was honoured”: the same rule in a four-letter verb
ḍuribtu, “I was struck”: the pronoun takes the doer's place

tasks.prompt: Leave out the doer and make the object take its place: kataba Zaydun al-darsa; yaftaḥu Zaydun al-bāba; akrama Zaydun ʿAmran.
tasks.arabic: كَتَبَ زَيْدٌ الدَّرْسَ — يَفْتَحُ زَيْدٌ الْبَابَ — أَكْرَمَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا
tasks.answer: Kutiba al-darsu, “the lesson was written”; yuftaḥu al-bābu, “the door is opened”; ukrima ʿAmrun, “ʿAmr was honoured”. Each object passes from naṣb to rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of ukrima ʿAmrun.
tasks.answer: Ukrima: a past verb in the passive, fixed on the fatḥa. ʿAmrun: the object whose doer is not named (nāʾib al-fāʿil), in rafʿ, and the sign of its rafʿ is the ḍamma. (The wāw written after ʿAmr only keeps it apart from ʿUmar in writing.)

tasks.prompt: Unvowelled, ضرب زيد has two readings. Give both with their meanings and say what Zayd is in each.
tasks.answer: Ḍaraba Zaydun, “Zayd struck”: Zayd is the fāʿil. Ḍuriba Zaydun, “Zayd was struck”: Zayd is the object whose doer is not named. Both are in rafʿ; only the verb's vowels tell the roles apart.

tasks.prompt: State the book's rule for the passive past and the passive present.
tasks.answer: Past: the first letter takes a ḍamma and the letter before the last a kasra (ḍuriba). Present: the first letter takes a ḍamma and the letter before the last a fatḥa (yuḍrabu).

quiz.prompt: What is the state of the object whose doer is not named?
quiz.explanation: It takes the place of the doer and its rafʿ: ḍuriba Zaydun.

quiz.prompt: How does the past verb change when its doer is not named?
options: First letter fatḥa, the last letter sukūn
First letter kasra, the letter before the last fatḥa
First letter ḍamma, the letter before the last kasra
quiz.explanation: Ḍaraba → ḍuriba; akrama → ukrima.

quiz.prompt: How does the present verb change?
options: First letter ḍamma, the letter before the last fatḥa
First letter ḍamma, the letter before the last kasra
First letter fatḥa, the letter before the last ḍamma
quiz.explanation: Yaḍribu → yuḍrabu; yukrimu → yukramu.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is passive?
quiz.explanation: Ḍamma on the first letter and kasra before the last: kutiba, “it was written”.

quiz.prompt: What do later books, such as the Alfiyya, call this noun?
options: The deputy of the doer (nāʾib al-fāʿil)
quiz.explanation: Nāʾib al-fāʿil: it stands in for the doer.

quiz.prompt: In ḍuribtu, “I was struck”, what takes the doer's place?
quiz.explanation: The pronoun kind: ḍuribtu, ḍuribnā, ḍuribta…

quiz.prompt: Why can ضرب زيد not be understood without vowels?
options: It may be active or passive
Zayd may be in naṣb or khafḍ
It may be a noun or a particle
It may be past or imperative
quiz.explanation: Ḍaraba Zaydun and ḍuriba Zaydun are written alike without vowels and mean opposite things.

text.original: وَهُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَرْفُوعُ الَّذِي لَمْ يُذْكَرْ مَعَهُ فَاعِلُهُ. فَإِنْ كَانَ الْفِعْلُ مَاضِيًا ضُمَّ أَوَّلُهُ وَكُسِرَ مَا قَبْلَ آخِرِهِ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مُضَارِعًا ضُمَّ أَوَّلُهُ وَفُتِحَ مَا قَبْلَ آخِرِهِ.
text.en: It is the noun in rafʿ with which its doer is not mentioned. If the verb is past, its first letter is given a ḍamma and the letter before its last is given a kasra; if it is muḍāriʿ, its first letter is given a ḍamma and the letter before its last is given a fatḥa.

text.original: وَهُوَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: ظَاهِرٍ وَمُضْمَرٍ. فَالظَّاهِرُ نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: ضُرِبَ زَيْدٌ، وَيُضْرَبُ زَيْدٌ، وَأُكْرِمَ عَمْرٌو، وَيُكْرَمُ عَمْرٌو. وَالْمُضْمَرُ نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: ضُرِبْتُ، وَضُرِبْنَا، وَضُرِبْتَ، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: It is of two divisions: an explicit noun and a pronoun. The explicit noun is as when you say: ḍuriba Zaydun “Zayd was struck”, yuḍrabu Zaydun “Zayd is struck”, ukrima ʿAmrun “ʿAmr was honoured” and yukramu ʿAmrun “ʿAmr is honoured”. The pronoun is as when you say: ḍuribtu “I was struck”, ḍuribnā “we were struck”, ḍuribta “you were struck”, and the like.

lessons.title: The subject and the predicate
body: The nominal sentence is made of a subject (mubtadaʾ) and a predicate (khabar): Zaydun qāʾimun, “Zayd is standing”. Arabic writes no “is”; the two nouns side by side make the statement. The mubtadaʾ is “the noun in rafʿ free of the verbal governors”: no verb and no particle stands before it. What puts it in rafʿ is then not a word but the fact of its being put first to be spoken of (al-ibtidāʾ), an abstract governor.

The khabar is “the noun in rafʿ predicated of it”. The words al-musnad ilayhi in the print are read by the commentators as “predicated of it”, the “it” being the mubtadaʾ: the khabar is what is said of the subject. Read carelessly, the phrase seems to say the opposite, and the commentaries stop to explain it.

The book's three examples show agreement: Zaydun qāʾimun, al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni, al-Zaydūna qāʾimūna. The khabar follows the mubtadaʾ in number, and in gender too (hiya qāʾimatun, “she is standing”). Usually the mubtadaʾ is definite and the khabar indefinite, as here.

The mubtadaʾ may be an explicit noun, as above, or one of the twelve separate pronouns: anā (I), naḥnu (we), anta (you, a man), anti (you, a woman), antumā (you two), antum (you, men), antunna (you, women), huwa (he), hiya (she), humā (they two), hum (they, men), hunna (they, women). Anā qāʾimun, “I am standing”; naḥnu qāʾimūna, “we are standing”.

The pronouns have fixed endings, so in the iʿrāb the madrasa says they are “in the place of rafʿ” (fī maḥall rafʿ): anā, a separate pronoun, fixed on the sukūn, in the place of rafʿ as mubtadaʾ; qāʾimun, its khabar, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. And remember the trap of lesson 13: in Zaydun qāma, Zayd comes first, so it is a mubtadaʾ, not a fāʿil.

terms.en: the subject: a noun in rafʿ with no verbal governor
the predicate: what is said of the subject
governors that are words
being put first: the abstract governor of the mubtadaʾ
the separate pronoun: anā, naḥnu …
in the place of rafʿ: said of a word with a fixed ending

examples.en: Zaydun qāʾimun, “Zayd is standing”: mubtadaʾ and khabar
al-Zaydūna qāʾimūna, “the Zayds are standing”: the khabar agrees in number
anā qāʾimun, “I am standing”: a pronoun as mubtadaʾ
naḥnu qāʾimūna, “we are standing”

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni.
tasks.answer: Al-Zaydāni: mubtadaʾ, in rafʿ, and the sign of its rafʿ is the alif, because it is a dual. Qāʾimāni: its khabar, in rafʿ, the sign the alif, because it is a dual.

tasks.prompt: Make the khabar qāʾim agree with each mubtadaʾ: al-muslimūna; hiya; antumā; anā.
tasks.answer: Al-muslimūna qāʾimūna; hiya qāʾimatun; antumā qāʾimāni; anā qāʾimun (or qāʾimatun, if the speaker is a woman).

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of anā qāʾimun, and explain “in the place of rafʿ”.
tasks.answer: Anā: a separate pronoun, fixed on the sukūn, in the place of rafʿ as mubtadaʾ. Qāʾimun: its khabar, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. A pronoun's ending never changes, so its state is said to be in its place (maḥall), not on its ending.

tasks.prompt: What governs the mubtadaʾ, according to the book's definition?
tasks.answer: No word: it is “free of the verbal governors”. Its rafʿ comes from an abstract governor, its being put first to be spoken of (al-ibtidāʾ).

quiz.prompt: What puts the mubtadaʾ in rafʿ?
options: Its being put first, an abstract governor
quiz.explanation: The mubtadaʾ is free of the verbal governors; its governor is the ibtidāʾ.

quiz.prompt: In al-Zaydūna qāʾimūna, what is the sign of rafʿ of the khabar?
quiz.explanation: Qāʾimūna is a sound masculine plural, in rafʿ by the wāw.

quiz.prompt: How many separate pronouns does the book count as mubtadaʾ?
quiz.explanation: Anā, naḥnu, anta, anti, antumā, antum, antunna, huwa, hiya, humā, hum, hunna.

quiz.prompt: Which is a correct nominal sentence?
quiz.explanation: The khabar agrees with the mubtadaʾ in number.

quiz.prompt: How do the commentators read al-musnad ilayhi in the definition of the khabar?
options: That to which something is predicated
quiz.explanation: The khabar is what is said of the mubtadaʾ; “it” is the mubtadaʾ.

quiz.prompt: In anā qāʾimun, anā is…
options: fixed, in the place of rafʿ, mubtadaʾ
in rafʿ by the ḍamma, mubtadaʾ
quiz.explanation: A pronoun's ending is fixed; its rafʿ is in its place.

quiz.prompt: Which word does the nominal sentence leave out that English needs?
quiz.explanation: Zaydun qāʾimun: two nouns side by side make the statement.

text.original: الْمُبْتَدَأُ هُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَرْفُوعُ الْعَارِي عَنِ الْعَوَامِلِ اللَّفْظِيَّةِ، وَالْخَبَرُ هُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَرْفُوعُ الْمُسْنَدُ إِلَيْهِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَالزَّيْدَانِ قَائِمَانِ، وَالزَّيْدُونَ قَائِمُونَ.
text.en: The subject (mubtadaʾ) is the noun in rafʿ that is free of the expressed governors (al-ʿawāmil al-lafẓiyya). The predicate (khabar) is the noun in rafʿ that is predicated of it, as when you say: Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing”, al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni “the two Zayds are standing” and al-Zaydūna qāʾimūna “the Zayds are standing”.

text.original: وَالْمُبْتَدَأُ قِسْمَانِ: ظَاهِرٌ وَمُضْمَرٌ. فَالظَّاهِرُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ ذِكْرُهُ، وَالْمُضْمَرُ اثْنَا عَشَرَ، وَهِيَ: أَنَا، وَنَحْنُ، وَأَنْتَ، وَأَنْتِ، وَأَنْتُمَا، وَأَنْتُمْ، وَأَنْتُنَّ، وَهُوَ، وَهِيَ، وَهُمَا، وَهُمْ، وَهُنَّ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: أَنَا قَائِمٌ، وَنَحْنُ قَائِمُونَ، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: The mubtadaʾ is of two divisions: an explicit noun and a pronoun. The explicit noun is what has been mentioned before. The pronoun is twelve [words]: anā “I”, naḥnu “we”, anta “you (m.)”, anti “you (f.)”, antumā “you two”, antum “you (m. pl.)”, antunna “you (f. pl.)”, huwa “he”, hiya “she”, humā “they two”, hum “they (m.)” and hunna “they (f.)”, as when you say: anā qāʾimun “I am standing” and naḥnu qāʾimūna “we are standing”, and the like.

lessons.title: The kinds of predicate
body: The khabar is single (mufrad) or not single. Here “single” means not a sentence and not like a sentence, which is not the same as the “singular” of the chapter on iʿrāb. Al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni and al-Zaydūna qāʾimūna have a dual and a plural khabar, and both are single in this sense, since the khabar is one word, not a sentence. Mixing the two meanings of mufrad is a common slip.

The khabar that is not single is of four kinds. A particle with its noun (al-jārr wa-l-majrūr): Zaydun fī al-dāri, “Zayd is in the house”. An adverb (ẓarf): Zaydun ʿindaka, “Zayd is with you”. A verb with its doer: Zaydun qāma abūhu, “Zayd, his father stood”. A subject with its predicate: Zaydun jāriyatuhu dhāhibatun, “Zayd, his slave-girl is going”.

The first two are called “like a sentence” (shibh al-jumla). The commentators explain that they hang on a word that is understood, such as mustaqirrun, “settled”, or istaqarra, “he settled”: Zaydun fī al-dāri is “Zayd is settled in the house”. The other two are full sentences, a verbal and a nominal one, standing as the khabar of the first noun.

A sentence that is a khabar needs a link (rābiṭ) back to the mubtadaʾ, usually a pronoun. In qāma abūhu it is the -hu of abūhu, “his”, in jāriyatuhu dhāhibatun the -hu of jāriyatuhu. Without it the sentence would not be about Zayd at all: Zaydun qāma ʿAmrun says nothing of Zayd and is wrong. When the verb's own doer is the pronoun, as in Zaydun ḍaraba ʿAmran, “Zayd struck ʿAmr”, the hidden “he” in ḍaraba is the link.

In the iʿrāb the whole sentence is “in the place of rafʿ” as the khabar: Zaydun, mubtadaʾ; qāma, a past verb; abū, its fāʿil, in rafʿ by the wāw; -hu, a pronoun in the place of khafḍ; and the sentence qāma abūhu, in the place of rafʿ, the khabar of Zayd. The student learns to say the inner sentence first and then its place in the outer one.

a particle of khafḍ with its noun
the adverb of time or place
like a sentence: the particle with its noun, and the adverb
the link back to the mubtadaʾ, usually a pronoun

examples.en: Zaydun fī al-dāri, “Zayd is in the house”: a particle with its noun
Zaydun ʿindaka, “Zayd is with you”: an adverb
Zaydun qāma abūhu, “Zayd, his father stood”: a verb with its doer
Zaydun jāriyatuhu dhāhibatun, “Zayd, his slave-girl is going”: a subject with its predicate

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of khabar in each: Zaydun fī al-masjidi; ʿAmrun abūhu qāʾimun; Zaydun ḍaraba ʿAmran; al-Zaydūna qāʾimūna.
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ — عَمْرٌو أَبُوهُ قَائِمٌ — زَيْدٌ ضَرَبَ عَمْرًا — الزَّيْدُونَ قَائِمُونَ
tasks.answer: Fī al-masjidi: a particle with its noun (like a sentence). Abūhu qāʾimun: a subject with its predicate (a nominal sentence). Ḍaraba ʿAmran: a verb with its doer, a hidden “he” (a verbal sentence). Qāʾimūna: single, though it is a plural.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of Zaydun qāma abūhu.
tasks.answer: Zaydun: mubtadaʾ, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. Qāma: a past verb, fixed on the fatḥa. Abū: its fāʿil, in rafʿ by the wāw (one of the five nouns). -hu: a pronoun, fixed, in the place of khafḍ as muḍāf ilayhi; it is the link. The sentence qāma abūhu is in the place of rafʿ as the khabar of Zayd.

tasks.prompt: Why is Zaydun qāma ʿAmrun wrong as “Zayd: ʿAmr stood”? Correct it in two ways.
tasks.answer: A sentence that is a khabar needs a link back to the mubtadaʾ, and here nothing refers to Zayd. Corrections: Zaydun qāma abūhu (the link -hu), or Zaydun qāma (the hidden “he” in qāma is the link).

tasks.prompt: Mufrad means “singular” in the chapter on the signs of iʿrāb and “single” in the chapter on the khabar. What does it exclude in each?
tasks.answer: In the signs of iʿrāb it excludes the dual, the plural and the five nouns. In the khabar it excludes the sentence and what is like a sentence (a particle with its noun, an adverb); a dual or plural khabar is still single.

quiz.prompt: What does “single” (mufrad) mean for the khabar?
options: Not a sentence and not like a sentence
quiz.explanation: Al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni has a single khabar, though it is a dual.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of khabar that is not single does the book give?
quiz.explanation: The particle with its noun, the adverb, the verb with its doer, the subject with its predicate.

quiz.prompt: What kind of khabar is in Zaydun ʿindaka?
quiz.explanation: ʿInda, “with, at”, is an adverb of place.

quiz.prompt: In Zaydun qāma abūhu, what is the link to Zayd?
quiz.explanation: A sentence khabar needs a link back to the mubtadaʾ; here the -hu of abūhu.

quiz.prompt: What is jāriyatuhu in Zaydun jāriyatuhu dhāhibatun?
options: A second mubtadaʾ, whose khabar is dhāhibatun
The khabar of Zayd on its own
quiz.explanation: Jāriyatuhu dhāhibatun is a nominal sentence, the khabar of Zayd.

quiz.prompt: Which two kinds are called “like a sentence” (shibh al-jumla)?
options: The verb with its doer, and the subject with its predicate
The particle with its noun, and the adverb
quiz.explanation: They hang on an understood word such as mustaqirrun, “settled”.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: The sentence that is a khabar needs a link back to Zayd: the -hu of abūhu.

text.original: وَالْخَبَرُ قِسْمَانِ: مُفْرَدٌ وَغَيْرُ مُفْرَدٍ. فَالْمُفْرَدُ نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَالزَّيْدَانِ قَائِمَانِ، وَالزَّيْدُونَ قَائِمُونَ.
text.en: The khabar is of two divisions: a single word (mufrad) and not a single word. The single word is as when you say: Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing”, al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni “the two Zayds are standing” and al-Zaydūna qāʾimūna “the Zayds are standing”.

text.original: وَغَيْرُ الْمُفْرَدِ أَرْبَعَةُ أَشْيَاءَ: الْجَارُّ وَالْمَجْرُورُ، وَالظَّرْفُ، وَالْفِعْلُ مَعَ فَاعِلِهِ، وَالْمُبْتَدَأُ مَعَ خَبَرِهِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ، وَزَيْدٌ عِنْدَكَ، وَزَيْدٌ قَامَ أَبُوهُ، وَزَيْدٌ جَارِيَتُهُ ذَاهِبَةٌ.
text.en: What is not a single word is four things: the particle of jarr with the word in jarr (al-jārr wa-l-majrūr), the adverb (ẓarf), the verb with its fāʿil, and the mubtadaʾ with its khabar, as when you say: Zaydun fī al-dāri “Zayd is in the house”, Zaydun ʿindaka “Zayd is with you”, Zaydun qāma abūhu “Zayd, his father stood” and Zaydun jāriyatuhu dhāhibatun “Zayd, his slave-girl is going”.

lessons.title: Kāna and its sisters
body: Three groups of words enter on a subject and its predicate and change their state: kāna and its sisters, inna and its sisters, and ẓanantu and its sisters. Later books call them the “cancellers” (nawāsikh), because they cancel the plain rafʿ of the nominal sentence. This lesson takes the first group.

Kāna and its sisters leave the subject in rafʿ, now called the noun (ism) of kāna, and put the predicate in naṣb, now called its khabar: Zaydun qāʾimun becomes kāna Zaydun qāʾiman, “Zayd was standing”, and ʿAmrun shākhiṣun becomes laysa ʿAmrun shākhiṣan, “ʿAmr is not setting out”. With other kinds of noun the signs follow the tables of lessons 4 to 8: kāna al-Zaydūna qāʾimīna, the noun in rafʿ by the wāw, the khabar in naṣb by the yāʾ.

The sisters add a time or a manner to the sentence: amsā, aṣbaḥa and aḍḥā (in the evening, the morning, the forenoon), ẓalla (through the day) and bāta (through the night), often simply “became”; ṣāra, “became”; laysa, “is not”. Four come with mā before them: mā zāla, mā infakka, mā fatiʾa, mā bariḥa. Each of them means “ceased”, and the mā negates it, so together they mean “did not cease, still was”: mā zāla Zaydun qāʾiman, “Zayd is still standing”. The last, mā dāma, means “as long as”.

“And what is conjugated from them”: the present and the imperative do the same work as the past, as the book's examples show, kāna, yakūnu, kun; aṣbaḥa, yuṣbiḥu, aṣbiḥ. Laysa has no present and no imperative, so it is the one sister that never changes its form.

These verbs are called incomplete (nāqiṣa) because they do not complete a statement with their noun alone: “Zayd was…” waits for its khabar. That is also why their noun is not called a fāʿil, nor their khabar an object. A beginner's slip is to put the noun of kāna in naṣb, by analogy with inna; the rule is the reverse, and the next lesson shows it.

terms.en: kāna and its sisters: rafʿ of the noun, naṣb of the khabar
the noun of kāna: the former subject, in rafʿ
the predicate of kāna, in naṣb
the incomplete verbs, which need a khabar
the cancellers: words that change the state of subject and predicate

examples.en: kāna Zaydun qāʾiman, “Zayd was standing”: the noun in rafʿ, the khabar in naṣb
laysa ʿAmrun shākhiṣan, “ʿAmr is not setting out”
kāna al-Zaydūna qāʾimīna, “the Zayds were standing”: wāw in the noun, yāʾ in the khabar
mā zāla Zaydun qāʾiman, “Zayd is still standing”: negated “ceasing” means continuing

tasks.prompt: Bring kāna into each sentence and give the new endings: Zaydun qāʾimun; al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni; al-muslimūna qāʾimūna.
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ — الزَّيْدَانِ قَائِمَانِ — الْمُسْلِمُونَ قَائِمُونَ
tasks.answer: Kāna Zaydun qāʾiman; kāna al-Zaydāni qāʾimayni; kāna al-muslimūna qāʾimīna. The noun stays in rafʿ (ḍamma, alif, wāw); the khabar goes into naṣb (fatḥa, yāʾ, yāʾ).

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of laysa ʿAmrun shākhiṣan.
tasks.answer: Laysa: an incomplete past verb, one of the sisters of kāna, fixed on the fatḥa. ʿAmrun: its noun, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. Shākhiṣan: its khabar, in naṣb by the fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Mā zāla is made of mā, “not”, and zāla, “ceased”. Why does it mean “still”? Translate mā zāla Zaydun qāʾiman.
tasks.answer: To deny ceasing is to affirm continuing: “he did not cease to be standing”, that is, “Zayd is still standing”. The same holds for mā infakka, mā fatiʾa and mā bariḥa.

tasks.prompt: Which sister has no present and no imperative, and which forms of kāna and aṣbaḥa does the book give?
tasks.answer: Laysa never changes its form. The book gives kāna, yakūnu, kun and aṣbaḥa, yuṣbiḥu, aṣbiḥ, and says that whatever is conjugated from these verbs works as they do.

quiz.prompt: What does kāna do to the subject and the predicate?
options: Naṣb of the noun, rafʿ of the khabar
Rafʿ of the noun, naṣb of the khabar
quiz.explanation: Kāna Zaydun qāʾiman: the noun stays in rafʿ, the khabar goes into naṣb.

quiz.prompt: In kāna al-Zaydūna qāʾimīna, what is the sign of naṣb of the khabar?
quiz.explanation: Qāʾimīna is a sound masculine plural, in naṣb by the yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: What does mā zāla mean?
quiz.explanation: The mā denies “ceasing”, and so the two together mean continuing.

quiz.prompt: Which sister of kāna has no present or imperative?
quiz.explanation: Laysa keeps one form; the others conjugate and govern in every form.

quiz.prompt: Why are kāna and its sisters called incomplete (nāqiṣa)?
options: Their noun alone does not complete the statement; they need a khabar
quiz.explanation: “Zayd was…” waits for its khabar.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: The noun of kāna in rafʿ, its khabar in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: What does mā dāma mean?
quiz.explanation: Mā dāma is the last of the sisters in the book's list: “as long as”.

text.original: وَهِيَ ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْيَاءَ: كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا، وَإِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا، وَظَنَّ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا.
text.en: They are three things: kāna and its sisters, inna and its sisters, and ẓanna and its sisters.

text.original: فَأَمَّا كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا فَإِنَّهَا تَرْفَعُ الِاسْمَ وَتَنْصِبُ الْخَبَرَ، وَهِيَ: كَانَ، وَأَمْسَى، وَأَصْبَحَ، وَأَضْحَى، وَظَلَّ، وَبَاتَ، وَصَارَ، وَلَيْسَ، وَمَا زَالَ، وَمَا انْفَكَّ، وَمَا فَتِئَ، وَمَا بَرِحَ، وَمَا دَامَ، وَمَا تَصَرَّفَ مِنْهَا، نَحْوُ: كَانَ، وَيَكُونُ، وَكُنْ، وَأَصْبَحَ، وَيُصْبِحُ، وَأَصْبِحْ، تَقُولُ: كَانَ زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا، وَلَيْسَ عَمْرٌو شَاخِصًا، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: As for kāna and its sisters, they put the noun in rafʿ and the khabar in naṣb. They are: kāna “was”, amsā “became in the evening”, aṣbaḥa “became in the morning”, aḍḥā “became in the forenoon”, ẓalla “remained all day”, bāta “spent the night”, ṣāra “became”, laysa “is not”, mā zāla, mā infakka, mā fatiʾa and mā bariḥa “did not cease”, mā dāma “as long as”, and whatever is conjugated from them, as kāna, yakūnu, kun, and aṣbaḥa, yuṣbiḥu, aṣbiḥ. You say: kāna Zaydun qāʾiman “Zayd was standing” and laysa ʿAmrun shākhiṣan “ʿAmr is not setting out”, and the like.

lessons.title: Inna and its sisters
body: Inna and its sisters do the reverse of kāna: they put the noun in naṣb and leave the khabar in rafʿ. Zaydun qāʾimun becomes inna Zaydan qāʾimun, “Zayd is indeed standing”; ʿAmrun shākhiṣun becomes layta ʿAmran shākhiṣun, “if only ʿAmr were setting out”. The pair to learn by heart is kāna Zaydun qāʾiman beside inna Zaydan qāʾimun.

There are six: inna, anna, lākinna, kaʾanna, layta and laʿalla, and the book gives each its meaning. Inna and anna are for emphasis (tawkīd). Lākinna is for correction (istidrāk): it sets right an impression left by what came before, qāma al-qawmu lākinna Zaydan jālisun, “the people stood, but Zayd is sitting”. Kaʾanna is for comparison (tashbīh): kaʾanna Zaydan asadun, “it is as if Zayd were a lion”. Layta is for wishing (tamannī), usually for what is impossible or far off. Laʿalla is for hope (tarajjī) and expectation (tawaqquʿ): hoping for what is wanted, or fearing what is feared.

Inna and anna mean the same but stand in different places. Inna begins a sentence. Anna comes inside one, and its clause takes the place of a noun: ʿalimtu anna Zaydan qāʾimun, “I knew that Zayd is standing”, where anna Zaydan qāʾimun stands for “Zayd's standing”, the object of ʿalimtu.

The madrasa calls these six the particles like the verb (al-ḥurūf al-mushabbaha bi-l-fiʿl): they are built on a fatḥa like the past verb, they carry a verb's meaning (“I emphasise”, “I wish”), and they govern two nouns as a transitive verb governs its doer and object, but in the opposite order, the one in naṣb first.

The trap is to take the noun of inna for a fāʿil or a mubtadaʾ and put it in rafʿ. It is still the subject in meaning, but its state is naṣb, with all the signs of naṣb: inna al-Zaydayni qāʾimāni, inna al-muslimīna qāʾimūna, inna abāka qāʾimun.

terms.en: inna and its sisters: naṣb of the noun, rafʿ of the khabar
the particles like the verb
emphasis: inna, anna
correction: lākinna
wishing: layta
hoping: laʿalla

examples.en: inna Zaydan qāʾimun, “Zayd is indeed standing”: the noun in naṣb, the khabar in rafʿ
layta ʿAmran shākhiṣun, “if only ʿAmr were setting out”
kaʾanna Zaydan asadun, “it is as if Zayd were a lion”
ʿalimtu anna Zaydan qāʾimun, “I knew that Zayd is standing”: anna inside a sentence
inna al-Zaydīna qāʾimūna, “the Zayds are indeed standing”: the noun in naṣb by the yāʾ

tasks.prompt: Bring inna into each sentence: Zaydun qāʾimun; al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni; al-muslimūna qāʾimūna; abūka qāʾimun.
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ — الزَّيْدَانِ قَائِمَانِ — الْمُسْلِمُونَ قَائِمُونَ — أَبُوكَ قَائِمٌ
tasks.answer: Inna Zaydan qāʾimun; inna al-Zaydayni qāʾimāni; inna al-muslimīna qāʾimūna; inna abāka qāʾimun. The noun goes into naṣb (fatḥa, yāʾ, yāʾ, alif); the khabar stays in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of layta ʿAmran shākhiṣun.
tasks.answer: Layta: a particle of wishing, one of the sisters of inna, fixed on the fatḥa. ʿAmran: its noun, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Shākhiṣun: its khabar, in rafʿ by the ḍamma.

tasks.prompt: Put the same sentence, Zaydun qāʾimun, after kāna and after inna, and state the difference in one sentence.
tasks.answer: Kāna Zaydun qāʾiman; inna Zaydan qāʾimun. Kāna keeps the noun in rafʿ and puts the khabar in naṣb; inna puts the noun in naṣb and keeps the khabar in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Translate and name the meaning of the particle: kaʾanna Zaydan asadun; laʿalla Zaydan qāʾimun; qāma al-qawmu lākinna Zaydan jālisun.
tasks.arabic: كَأَنَّ زَيْدًا أَسَدٌ — لَعَلَّ زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ — قَامَ الْقَوْمُ لَكِنَّ زَيْدًا جَالِسٌ
tasks.answer: “It is as if Zayd were a lion”: comparison (tashbīh). “Perhaps Zayd is standing”: hope or expectation (tarajjī, tawaqquʿ). “The people stood, but Zayd is sitting”: correction (istidrāk).

quiz.prompt: What do inna and its sisters do?
options: Rafʿ of the noun, naṣb of the khabar
Naṣb of the noun, rafʿ of the khabar
quiz.explanation: Inna Zaydan qāʾimun: the reverse of kāna.

quiz.prompt: What is the meaning of layta?
quiz.explanation: Layta is for tamannī, wishing, usually for what is far off.

quiz.prompt: Which particle is for comparison?
quiz.explanation: Kaʾanna Zaydan asadun: “as if Zayd were a lion”.

quiz.prompt: In inna al-Zaydīna qāʾimūna, al-Zaydīna is in…
options: naṣb by the yāʾ, as the noun of inna
quiz.explanation: The noun of inna is in naṣb; a sound masculine plural shows it by the yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Where does anna stand, as against inna?
options: Only at the beginning of a sentence
Only after a particle of khafḍ
Inside a sentence, its clause in the place of a noun
quiz.explanation: ʿAlimtu anna Zaydan qāʾimun: “I knew that Zayd is standing”.

quiz.prompt: Why are these six called the particles like the verb?
options: They are verbs in the past
They end in fatḥa, carry a verb's meaning and govern two nouns
quiz.explanation: So the madrasa explains their working on two nouns.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: The noun of inna in naṣb (one of the five nouns: alif), the khabar in rafʿ.

text.original: وَأَمَّا إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا فَإِنَّهَا تَنْصِبُ الِاسْمَ وَتَرْفَعُ الْخَبَرَ، وَهِيَ: إِنَّ، وَأَنَّ، وَلَكِنَّ، وَكَأَنَّ، وَلَيْتَ، وَلَعَلَّ، تَقُولُ: إِنَّ زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ، وَلَيْتَ عَمْرًا شَاخِصٌ. وَمَعْنَى إِنَّ وَأَنَّ لِلتَّوْكِيدِ، وَلَكِنَّ لِلِاسْتِدْرَاكِ، وَكَأَنَّ لِلتَّشْبِيهِ، وَلَيْتَ لِلتَّمَنِّي، وَلَعَلَّ لِلتَّرَجِّي وَلِلتَّوَقُّعِ.
text.en: As for inna and its sisters, they put the noun in naṣb and the khabar in rafʿ. They are: inna, anna, lākinna, kaʾanna, layta and laʿalla. You say: inna Zaydan qāʾimun “indeed Zayd is standing” and layta ʿAmran shākhiṣun “if only ʿAmr were setting out”. The meaning of inna and anna is emphasis (tawkīd), of lākinna correction (istidrāk) [“but”], of kaʾanna likening [“as if”], of layta wishing [“if only”], and of laʿalla hope and expectation [“perhaps”].

lessons.title: Ẓanantu and its sisters
body: The third group puts both parts in naṣb, “as their two objects”: Zaydun munṭaliqun becomes ẓanantu Zaydan munṭaliqan, “I thought Zayd was leaving”, and ʿAmrun shākhiṣun becomes khiltu ʿAmran shākhiṣan, “I imagined ʿAmr was setting out”. The book names them in the first person, ẓanantu, ḥasibtu, khiltu, as the madrasa likes to; any person works the same way.

These are full verbs with a doer of their own (the -tu of ẓanantu), so the two nouns after them are their objects, the first and the second. That is the difference from kāna, whose noun is in rafʿ, and from inna, a particle. In the print the book says they put “the noun and the khabar” in naṣb; most copies say “the mubtadaʾ and the khabar”. The sense is the same: the two parts of a nominal sentence.

By meaning the ten fall into groups, which the commentaries name. Verbs of thinking: ẓanantu (I thought), ḥasibtu (I reckoned), khiltu (I imagined), zaʿamtu (I claimed). Verbs of knowing: raʾaytu (I held, knew), ʿalimtu (I knew), wajadtu (I found). Verbs of making: ittakhadhtu (I took as) and jaʿaltu (I made). The first two groups are called the verbs of the heart (afʿāl al-qulūb), since what they name happens in the mind. Samiʿtu (I heard) is the odd one; many grammarians do not count it with them at all.

A trap: some of these verbs also have another meaning in which they take one object only. Raʾaytu Zaydan is “I saw Zayd”, with the eyes: one object, as in lesson 5. Raʾaytu Zaydan ʿāliman is “I held Zayd to be learned”: two objects, a sister of ẓanantu. The second noun shows which verb you have.
Put the three groups of this chapter side by side and the whole chapter is in one line: kāna Zaydun qāʾiman, inna Zaydan qāʾimun, ẓanantu Zaydan qāʾiman: rafʿ and naṣb, naṣb and rafʿ, naṣb and naṣb.

terms.en: ẓanantu and its sisters: naṣb of both parts
the verbs of the heart: thinking and knowing
the first object: the former subject
the second object: the former predicate

examples.en: ẓanantu Zaydan munṭaliqan, “I thought Zayd was leaving”: two objects in naṣb
khiltu ʿAmran shākhiṣan, “I imagined ʿAmr was setting out”
ʿalimtu Zaydan qāʾiman, “I knew Zayd to be standing”: a verb of knowing
ittakhadhtu Zaydan ṣadīqan, “I took Zayd as a friend”: a verb of making

tasks.prompt: Bring ẓanantu into each sentence: Zaydun munṭaliqun; al-Zaydāni qāʾimāni; ʿAmrun akhūka.
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ — الزَّيْدَانِ قَائِمَانِ — عَمْرٌو أَخُوكَ
tasks.answer: Ẓanantu Zaydan munṭaliqan; ẓanantu al-Zaydayni qāʾimayni; ẓanantu ʿAmran akhāka. Both parts go into naṣb, each with its own sign (fatḥa; yāʾ and yāʾ; fatḥa and alif).

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of ẓanantu Zaydan munṭaliqan.
tasks.answer: Ẓanantu: a past verb, fixed on the sukūn because of the moving pronoun; the -tu is its fāʿil, a pronoun fixed on the ḍamma in the place of rafʿ. Zaydan: its first object, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Munṭaliqan: its second object, in naṣb by the fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Raʾaytu Zaydan and raʾaytu Zaydan ʿāliman: translate both and say how many objects each has.
tasks.answer: “I saw Zayd”: seeing with the eyes, one object. “I held Zayd to be learned”: raʾaytu as a verb of knowing, a sister of ẓanantu, with two objects.

tasks.prompt: Write one sentence with each group of this chapter, using Zaydun qāʾimun, and name the state of both parts.
tasks.answer: Kāna Zaydun qāʾiman: rafʿ and naṣb. Inna Zaydan qāʾimun: naṣb and rafʿ. Ẓanantu Zaydan qāʾiman: naṣb and naṣb.

quiz.prompt: What do ẓanantu and its sisters do to the subject and predicate?
options: Rafʿ of the first, naṣb of the second
Naṣb of the first, rafʿ of the second
Put both in naṣb as two objects
quiz.explanation: Ẓanantu Zaydan munṭaliqan: both are objects of the verb.

quiz.prompt: What is the -tu of ẓanantu?
quiz.explanation: These are full verbs with a doer; the two nouns after them are their objects.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a verb of knowing?
quiz.explanation: Raʾaytu, ʿalimtu and wajadtu are of knowing; ẓanantu, ḥasibtu, khiltu and zaʿamtu of thinking.

quiz.prompt: Raʾaytu Zaydan, “I saw Zayd”: how many objects?
options: One: here it is seeing with the eyes
quiz.explanation: Only raʾaytu in the sense of knowing is a sister of ẓanantu and takes two objects.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
quiz.explanation: Both objects in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Ittakhadhtu and jaʿaltu belong to which group?
quiz.explanation: Ittakhadhtu Zaydan ṣadīqan: “I took Zayd as a friend”.

quiz.prompt: What are the verbs of thinking and knowing called?
quiz.explanation: Afʿāl al-qulūb: what they name happens in the mind.

text.original: وَأَمَّا ظَنَنْتُ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا فَإِنَّهَا تَنْصِبُ الِاسْمَ وَالْخَبَرَ عَلَى أَنَّهُمَا مَفْعُولَانِ لَهَا، وَهِيَ: ظَنَنْتُ، وَحَسِبْتُ، وَخِلْتُ، وَزَعَمْتُ، وَرَأَيْتُ، وَعَلِمْتُ، وَوَجَدْتُ، وَاتَّخَذْتُ، وَجَعَلْتُ، وَسَمِعْتُ، تَقُولُ: ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا مُنْطَلِقًا، وَخِلْتُ عَمْرًا شَاخِصًا، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: As for ẓanantu and its sisters, they put the noun and the khabar in naṣb, as their two objects. They are: ẓanantu “I thought”, ḥasibtu “I reckoned”, khiltu “I imagined”, zaʿamtu “I claimed”, raʾaytu “I saw”, ʿalimtu “I knew”, wajadtu “I found”, ittakhadhtu “I took [as]”, jaʿaltu “I made” and samiʿtu “I heard”. You say: ẓanantu Zaydan munṭaliqan “I thought Zayd [was] leaving” and khiltu ʿAmran shākhiṣan “I imagined ʿAmr [was] setting out”, and the like.

lessons.title: The adjective; definite and indefinite
body: Now come the four followers, and first the adjective (naʿt, called ṣifa in other books). It follows the noun it describes (the manʿūt) in its rafʿ, naṣb and khafḍ, and in its being definite or indefinite: qāma Zaydun al-ʿāqilu, “Zayd the sensible stood”; raʾaytu Zaydan al-ʿāqila; marartu bi-Zaydin al-ʿāqili. The adjective has no governor of its own; it simply takes the state of its noun. It also agrees in gender and number: rajulun ʿāqilun, “a sensible man”, imraʾatun ʿāqilatun, “a sensible woman”.

Because the adjective must match its noun in definiteness, the book stops here to say what a definite noun (maʿrifa) is. Five things: the pronoun (anā, anta); the proper name (Zayd, Makka); the “vague” noun, which is the demonstrative (hādhā, hādhihi, hāʾulāʾi); the noun with the article (al-rajul, al-ghulām); and what is joined (muḍāf) to one of these four: ghulāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's servant”, ghulāmuka, “your servant”.

The indefinite noun (nakira) is “every noun that is common in its kind, not belonging to one rather than another”: rajul is any man, faras any horse. The book gives a practical test: whatever can take the article is indefinite, as rajulun and farasun become al-rajulu and al-farasu.

Now a trap that this lesson solves. Zayd has no article, yet in qāma Zaydun al-ʿāqilu the adjective takes al-: Zayd is a proper name, so he is definite, and his adjective must be definite too. And al-rajulu al-ʿāqilu is not the same as al-rajulu ʿāqilun. In the first the adjective agrees in definiteness: “the sensible man”, a phrase. In the second it does not: ʿāqilun is a khabar, and the words make a sentence, “the man is sensible”.

terms.en: the adjective, which follows the noun it describes
the noun described
the definite noun: five kinds
the indefinite noun: common in its kind
the proper name
the vague noun: the demonstrative, hādhā

examples.arabic: قَامَ زَيْدٌ الْعَاقِلُ — رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا الْعَاقِلَ — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ الْعَاقِلِ
examples.en: the adjective follows Zayd in rafʿ, naṣb and khafḍ
ghulāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's servant”: definite by being joined to a proper name
al-rajulu al-ʿāqilu, “the sensible man”: an adjective, a phrase
al-rajulu ʿāqilun, “the man is sensible”: a khabar, a sentence

tasks.prompt: Describe rajulun with karīmun, “noble”, in the three states, after jāʾa, raʾaytu and marartu bi-.
tasks.answer: Jāʾa rajulun karīmun; raʾaytu rajulan karīman; marartu bi-rajulin karīmin. Both indefinite, the adjective in the state of its noun.

tasks.prompt: Definite or indefinite? If definite, which of the five kinds: hādhā; kitābuka; Makkatu; rajulun; al-ghulāmu; antum.
tasks.arabic: هَذَا — كِتَابُكَ — مَكَّةُ — رَجُلٌ — الْغُلَامُ — أَنْتُمْ
tasks.answer: Hādhā: definite, a vague noun (demonstrative). Kitābuka: definite, joined to a pronoun. Makkatu: definite, a proper name. Rajulun: indefinite (it can take al-). Al-ghulāmu: definite, with the article. Antum: definite, a pronoun.

tasks.prompt: Al-rajulu al-ʿāqilu and al-rajulu ʿāqilun: translate both and say why one is a phrase and the other a sentence.
tasks.answer: “The sensible man” and “the man is sensible”. In the first, al-ʿāqilu agrees with al-rajulu in definiteness, so it is an adjective and the two words are one phrase. In the second, ʿāqilun is indefinite after a definite noun, so it is the khabar of a nominal sentence.

tasks.prompt: Why does Zayd's adjective take the article in qāma Zaydun al-ʿāqilu, though Zayd has none?
tasks.answer: Zayd is a proper name, one of the five kinds of definite noun. The adjective follows its noun in definiteness, so it must be definite, and an adjective is made definite with al-.

quiz.prompt: In what does the adjective follow its noun, according to the book?
options: In rafʿ, naṣb, khafḍ, and definiteness or indefiniteness
In nothing: it has its own governor
quiz.explanation: Qāma Zaydun al-ʿāqilu, raʾaytu Zaydan al-ʿāqila, marartu bi-Zaydin al-ʿāqili.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of definite noun does the book name?
quiz.explanation: Pronoun, proper name, vague noun, noun with al-, and what is joined to one of these.

quiz.prompt: What is the “vague noun” (al-ism al-mubham)?
quiz.explanation: The book's examples of the vague noun are the demonstratives.

quiz.prompt: What is the book's test for an indefinite noun?
options: It can take the article al-
quiz.explanation: Rajulun can become al-rajulu, so it is indefinite.

quiz.prompt: Al-rajulu ʿāqilun means…
quiz.explanation: ʿĀqilun does not agree in definiteness, so it is the khabar, not an adjective.

quiz.prompt: Ghulāmu Zaydin is definite because…
options: it is joined to a proper name
quiz.explanation: What is joined (muḍāf) to one of the four definite kinds is definite.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct for “I passed by Zayd the sensible”?
quiz.explanation: In khafḍ like Zayd, and definite like him.

text.original: النَّعْتُ تَابِعٌ لِلْمَنْعُوتِ فِي رَفْعِهِ وَنَصْبِهِ وَخَفْضِهِ وَتَعْرِيفِهِ وَتَنْكِيرِهِ، تَقُولُ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ الْعَاقِلُ، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا الْعَاقِلَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ الْعَاقِلِ.
text.en: The adjective (naʿt) follows the word it describes (manʿūt) in its rafʿ, its naṣb and its khafḍ, and in its being definite or indefinite. You say: qāma Zaydun al-ʿāqilu “Zayd the intelligent stood”, raʾaytu Zaydan al-ʿāqila “I saw Zayd the intelligent” and marartu bi-Zaydin al-ʿāqili “I passed by Zayd the intelligent”.

text.original: وَالْمَعْرِفَةُ خَمْسَةُ أَشْيَاءَ: الِاسْمُ الْمُضْمَرُ نَحْوُ: أَنَا وَأَنْتَ، وَالِاسْمُ الْعَلَمُ نَحْوُ: زَيْدٍ وَمَكَّةَ، وَالِاسْمُ الْمُبْهَمُ نَحْوُ: هَذَا وَهَذِهِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ، وَالِاسْمُ الَّذِي فِيهِ الْأَلِفُ وَاللَّامُ نَحْوُ: الرَّجُلِ وَالْغُلَامِ، وَمَا أُضِيفَ إِلَى وَاحِدٍ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ.
text.en: The definite (maʿrifa) is five things: the pronoun, as anā “I” and anta “you”; the proper name (ʿalam), as Zaydin and Makkata “Zayd and Mecca”; the vague noun (mubham), as hādhā, hādhihi and hāʾulāʾi “this (m.), this (f.), these”; the noun in which there is the alif and lām, as al-rajuli and al-ghulāmi “the man and the boy”; and what is joined in iḍāfa to one of these four.

text.original: وَالنَّكِرَةُ كُلُّ اسْمٍ شَائِعٍ فِي جِنْسِهِ لَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ وَاحِدٌ دُونَ آخَرَ، وَتَقْرِيبُهُ: كُلُّ مَا صَلَحَ دُخُولُ الْأَلِفِ وَاللَّامِ عَلَيْهِ، نَحْوُ: الرَّجُلِ وَالْفَرَسِ.
text.en: The indefinite (nakira) is every noun that is spread through its kind (jins), so that no one of it has it rather than another. To put it simply: it is everything on which the alif and lām can come, as al-rajuli and al-farasi “the man and the horse”.

lessons.title: The conjunction (ʿaṭf)
body: The second follower is the word joined by a particle of conjunction (ʿaṭf). The book counts ten particles: wa-, fa-, thumma, aw, am, immā, bal, lā, lākin, and ḥattā “in some places”. The word after the particle (al-maʿṭūf) takes the state of the word before it (al-maʿṭūf ʿalayhi): qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun, raʾaytu Zaydan wa-ʿAmran, marartu bi-Zaydin wa-ʿAmrin.

Each particle has its meaning, which the commentaries give. Wa- joins without saying which came first. Fa- gives order with nothing between: qāma Zaydun fa-ʿAmrun, “Zayd stood, and then at once ʿAmr”. Thumma gives order with a delay: “and later ʿAmr”. Aw is “or”, for choice or doubt. Am asks which of two, after the hamza of the question: a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun?, “is Zayd with you, or ʿAmr?”. Immā is “either… or”, said twice: jāʾa immā Zaydun wa-immā ʿAmrun.

Bal turns away from the first to the second: mā qāma Zaydun bal ʿAmrun, “Zayd did not stand, rather ʿAmr”. Lā denies of the second what was affirmed of the first: qāma Zaydun lā ʿAmrun, “Zayd stood, not ʿAmr”. Lākin, after a negation, sets it right: mā qāma Zaydun lākin ʿAmrun. Ḥattā joins only “in some places”, when what follows it is the furthest part of what came before: qadima al-ḥujjāju ḥattā al-mushātu, “the pilgrims arrived, even those on foot”.

The rule covers all four states, jazm too, because ʿaṭf also joins verbs: lam yajlis wa-yaktub, “he did not sit and write”, where yaktub is in jazm because it is joined to a verb in jazm. The book gives examples of the noun only; the jazm is the same rule applied to the verb.

A wa- before a noun is not always ʿaṭf. The wa- of the oath (wa-llāhi) puts the noun in khafḍ, and the wa- “with” of lesson 34 (jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jaysha) puts it in naṣb whatever came before. The test is the state: in ʿaṭf the second word always has the state of the first.

terms.en: the conjunction: joining by a particle
the ten particles of conjunction
the word joined
the word it is joined to
order: the meaning of fa- and thumma

examples.arabic: قَامَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو — رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا وَعَمْرًا — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ وَعَمْرٍو
examples.en: ʿAmr follows Zayd in each state
mā qāma Zaydun bal ʿAmrun, “Zayd did not stand, rather ʿAmr”
qadima al-ḥujjāju ḥattā al-mushātu, “the pilgrims arrived, even those on foot”
lam yajlis wa-yaktub, “he did not sit and write”: a verb joined to a verb in jazm

tasks.prompt: Join al-Zaydāni to Zayd with wa- in each sentence: jāʾa Zaydun; raʾaytu Zaydan; marartu bi-Zaydin.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ — رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
tasks.answer: Jāʾa Zaydun wa-l-Zaydāni (rafʿ by the alif); raʾaytu Zaydan wa-l-Zaydayni (naṣb by the yāʾ); marartu bi-Zaydin wa-l-Zaydayni (khafḍ by the yāʾ).

tasks.prompt: What is the difference in meaning between qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun, qāma Zaydun fa-ʿAmrun and qāma Zaydun thumma ʿAmrun?
tasks.answer: With wa- both stood, and nothing is said of the order. With fa- ʿAmr stood after Zayd, at once. With thumma ʿAmr stood after Zayd, after a while.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of marartu bi-Zaydin wa-ʿAmrin.
tasks.answer: Marartu: a past verb, fixed on the sukūn; the -tu is its fāʿil, in the place of rafʿ. Bi-: a particle of khafḍ. Zaydin: in khafḍ by the bi-, the sign the kasra. Wa-: a particle of conjunction. ʿAmrin: joined to Zayd, in khafḍ by the kasra.

tasks.prompt: Join yaktubu to lam yajlis with wa-, and say why yaktubu changes.
tasks.answer: Lam yajlis wa-yaktub: yaktub is joined to a verb in jazm, so it takes jazm too, by the sukūn.

quiz.prompt: What state does the word after a particle of conjunction take?
options: The state of the word it is joined to
quiz.explanation: Rafʿ after rafʿ, naṣb after naṣb, khafḍ after khafḍ, jazm after jazm.

quiz.prompt: Which particle gives order with a delay?
quiz.explanation: Fa- is order at once, thumma order after a while, wa- no order.

quiz.prompt: Which particle asks “which of the two?” after the hamza of the question?
quiz.explanation: A-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun?

quiz.prompt: In mā qāma Zaydun bal ʿAmrun, who stood?
quiz.explanation: Bal turns from the first to the second: “not Zayd, rather ʿAmr”.

quiz.prompt: Why does the book mention jazm among the states of ʿaṭf?
options: Because nouns take jazm after wa-
Because the particles put verbs in jazm
quiz.explanation: Lam yajlis wa-yaktub: the verb joined to a verb in jazm is in jazm.

quiz.prompt: When is ḥattā a particle of conjunction?
options: “In some places”: when what follows it is the furthest part of what came before
quiz.explanation: Qadima al-ḥujjāju ḥattā al-mushātu: “even those on foot”.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: ʿAmr follows Zayd in naṣb.

text.original: وَحُرُوفُ الْعَطْفِ عَشَرَةٌ، وَهِيَ: الْوَاوُ، وَالْفَاءُ، وَثُمَّ، وَأَوْ، وَأَمْ، وَإِمَّا، وَبَلْ، وَلَا، وَلَكِنْ، وَحَتَّى فِي بَعْضِ الْمَوَاضِعِ.
text.en: The particles of ʿaṭf are ten: wa- “and”, fa- “and then”, thumma “then, later”, aw “or”, am “or”, immā “either … or”, bal “rather”, lā “not”, lākin “but”, and ḥattā “even” in some places.

text.original: فَإِنْ عَطَفْتَ بِهَا عَلَى مَرْفُوعٍ رَفَعْتَ، أَوْ عَلَى مَنْصُوبٍ نَصَبْتَ، أَوْ عَلَى مَخْفُوضٍ خَفَضْتَ، أَوْ عَلَى مَجْزُومٍ جَزَمْتَ، تَقُولُ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا وَعَمْرًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ وَعَمْرٍو.
text.en: If you join by them to a word in rafʿ, you put [the second] in rafʿ; to a word in naṣb, you put it in naṣb; to a word in khafḍ, you put it in khafḍ; to a word in jazm, you put it in jazm. You say: qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun “Zayd and ʿAmr stood”, raʾaytu Zaydan wa-ʿAmran “I saw Zayd and ʿAmr” and marartu bi-Zaydin wa-ʿAmrin “I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr”.

lessons.title: Emphasis (tawkīd)
body: The third follower is emphasis (tawkīd). It follows the word it emphasises (al-muʾakkad) in rafʿ, naṣb, khafḍ and definiteness, and it is made with known words: nafs (self), ʿayn (self, literally “eye”), kull (all), ajmaʿ (all), and the followers of ajmaʿ: aktaʿ, abtaʿ, abṣaʿ. The book's examples: qāma Zaydun nafsuhu, “Zayd himself stood”; raʾaytu al-qawma kullahum, “I saw the people, all of them”; marartu bi-l-qawmi ajmaʿīna, “I passed by the people, all together”.

The words do two different jobs. Nafs and ʿayn remove the thought that someone else was meant: jāʾa al-amīru nafsuhu, “the prince himself came”, not his messenger or his letter. Kull and ajmaʿ remove the thought that only some were meant: the whole people, not most of them. Aktaʿ, abtaʿ and abṣaʿ come only after ajmaʿ, to strengthen it, and are not used alone.

Nafs, ʿayn and kull carry a pronoun that refers back to the word emphasised and agrees with it: Zaydun nafsuhu, Hindun nafsuhā, al-qawmu kulluhum. That pronoun is why the emphasis is always definite: it is joined to a pronoun. Ajmaʿ takes the endings of its own kind of word: ajmaʿūna in rafʿ and ajmaʿīna in naṣb and khafḍ, with the wāw and yāʾ of the plural.

The Qurʾān joins the two kinds of all in one verse: fa-sajada al-malāʾikatu kulluhum ajmaʿūna, “so the angels bowed down, all of them together” (Q 15:30). Al-malāʾikatu is the fāʿil, in rafʿ; kulluhum follows it in rafʿ by the ḍamma; ajmaʿūna follows it in rafʿ by the wāw.

The book teaches the emphasis by these words, which the commentaries call emphasis by meaning (maʿnawī). They add the other kind, emphasis by repeating the word itself (lafẓī): jāʾa Zaydun Zaydun, “Zayd came, Zayd”. Either way the follower has no governor of its own: it takes the state of the word it strengthens.

terms.en: emphasis: a follower that strengthens the word before it
the word emphasised
self: not someone else
all: not only some
emphasis by repeating the word itself

examples.en: qāma Zaydun nafsuhu, “Zayd himself stood”
raʾaytu al-qawma kullahum, “I saw the people, all of them”
marartu bi-l-qawmi ajmaʿīna, “I passed by the people, all together”: ajmaʿīna in khafḍ by the yāʾ
fa-sajada al-malāʾikatu kulluhum ajmaʿūna (Q 15:30): two emphases in rafʿ

tasks.prompt: Emphasise Zayd with nafs in each sentence: qāma Zaydun; raʾaytu Zaydan; marartu bi-Zaydin.
tasks.arabic: قَامَ زَيْدٌ — رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
tasks.answer: Qāma Zaydun nafsuhu; raʾaytu Zaydan nafsahu; marartu bi-Zaydin nafsihi. Nafs takes Zayd's state and a pronoun, -hu, that refers to him.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of raʾaytu al-qawma kullahum.
tasks.answer: Raʾaytu: a past verb with its fāʿil, the -tu. Al-qawma: its object, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Kulla: emphasis of al-qawma, in naṣb by the fatḥa. -hum: a pronoun, fixed, in the place of khafḍ as muḍāf ilayhi.

tasks.prompt: In fa-sajada al-malāʾikatu kulluhum ajmaʿūna (Q 15:30), find the two words of emphasis and give the sign of each.
tasks.answer: Kulluhum: emphasis of al-malāʾikatu, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. Ajmaʿūna: a second emphasis, in rafʿ by the wāw, since it is inflected like a sound masculine plural.

tasks.prompt: What does nafsuhu add in jāʾa al-amīru nafsuhu, and what would kulluhum add after a plural?
tasks.answer: Nafsuhu removes the thought that someone else came for him (his messenger, his letter): the prince himself came. Kulluhum after a plural removes the thought that only some of them were meant.

quiz.prompt: In what does the emphasis follow the word emphasised, according to the book?
quiz.explanation: The book names the three states and definiteness.

quiz.prompt: What do nafs and ʿayn exclude?
options: That the act happened in the past
quiz.explanation: Jāʾa al-amīru nafsuhu: the prince himself, not his messenger.

quiz.prompt: Which words come only after ajmaʿ?
quiz.explanation: The followers of ajmaʿ strengthen it and are not used alone.

quiz.prompt: Marartu bi-l-qawmi ajmaʿīna: what is the sign of khafḍ of ajmaʿīna?
quiz.explanation: Ajmaʿ is inflected like a sound masculine plural: wāw in rafʿ, yāʾ in naṣb and khafḍ.

quiz.prompt: Why is the emphasis with nafs always definite?
options: It is joined to a pronoun
quiz.explanation: Nafsuhu, nafsuhā: joined to a pronoun, so definite.

quiz.prompt: What is jāʾa Zaydun Zaydun?
quiz.explanation: The commentaries add this second kind of emphasis to the one the book teaches.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: The emphasis takes Zayd's naṣb.

text.original: التَّوْكِيدُ تَابِعٌ لِلْمُؤَكَّدِ فِي رَفْعِهِ وَنَصْبِهِ وَخَفْضِهِ وَتَعْرِيفِهِ، وَيَكُونُ بِأَلْفَاظٍ مَعْلُومَةٍ، وَهِيَ: النَّفْسُ، وَالْعَيْنُ، وَكُلٌّ، وَأَجْمَعُ، وَتَوَابِعُ أَجْمَعَ، وَهِيَ: أَكْتَعُ، وَأَبْتَعُ، وَأَبْصَعُ، تَقُولُ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ نَفْسُهُ، وَرَأَيْتُ الْقَوْمَ كُلَّهُمْ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِالْقَوْمِ أَجْمَعِينَ.
text.en: The emphasis (tawkīd) follows the word emphasised (muʾakkad) in its rafʿ, its naṣb and its khafḍ, and in its being definite. It is made with known words: al-nafs “self”, al-ʿayn “self”, kull “all” and ajmaʿ “all together”, and the followers of ajmaʿ, which are aktaʿ, abtaʿ and abṣaʿ. You say: qāma Zaydun nafsuhu “Zayd himself stood”, raʾaytu al-qawma kullahum “I saw the people, all of them” and marartu bi-al-qawmi ajmaʿīna “I passed by the people, all together”.

lessons.title: The substitute (badal)
body: The last follower is the substitute (badal): “when a noun is put in place of a noun, or a verb in place of a verb, it follows it in all its iʿrāb”. The badal is the word that is really meant (al-maqṣūd bi-l-ḥukm); the word before it, the mubdal minhu, prepares the way. There is no particle between them, which is how a badal differs from ʿaṭf.

There are four kinds, and the book gives an example of each. The thing for the thing (badal al-shayʾ min al-shayʾ), where both name the same: jāʾanī Zaydun akhūka, “Zayd, your brother, came to me”. The part for the whole (badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull): akaltu al-raghīfa thuluthahu, “I ate the loaf, a third of it”. Inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl), something contained in the first or belonging to it: nafaʿanī Zaydun ʿilmuhu, “Zayd benefited me, his knowledge”. And the mistake (badal al-ghalaṭ): raʾaytu Zaydan al-farasa, “I saw Zayd, the horse”: “you meant to say the horse, made a mistake, and put Zayd in its place”.

In the part and the inclusion there is a pronoun that refers back to the first word: thuluthahu, “its third”; ʿilmuhu, “his knowledge”. It ties the badal to what it replaces. The badal of mistake belongs to speech, where a word slips out; the commentaries say it is not found in careful, eloquent language.

A verb can be a badal of a verb, and then it takes the verb's jazm or naṣb: wa-man yafʿal dhālika yalqa athāman, yuḍāʿaf lahu al-ʿadhābu, “whoever does that will meet the penalty: the punishment will be doubled for him” (Q 25:68–69). Yalqa is the answer of the condition, in jazm; yuḍāʿaf is its badal and is in jazm too.

The badal takes every sign of the word it replaces: raʾaytu Zaydan akhāka, marartu bi-Zaydin akhīka. A beginner sometimes reads akhūka as an adjective of Zayd; but “your brother” names a person, not a quality, and the badal can even be definite after an indefinite word. Its meaning is that of a second, clearer name for the same thing or a part of it.

terms.en: the substitute, the word really meant
the word replaced
the part for the whole
the badal of inclusion
the badal of a slip of the tongue

examples.en: jāʾanī Zaydun akhūka, “Zayd, your brother, came to me”: the thing for the thing
akaltu al-raghīfa thuluthahu, “I ate the loaf, a third of it”: the part for the whole
nafaʿanī Zaydun ʿilmuhu, “Zayd benefited me, his knowledge”: inclusion
raʾaytu Zaydan al-farasa, “I saw Zayd, the horse”: the mistake
yalqa athāman, yuḍāʿaf lahu al-ʿadhābu (Q 25:68–69): a verb as badal of a verb, both in jazm

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of badal: (a) katabtu al-kitāba niṣfahu, “I wrote the book, half of it”; (b) jāʾa al-amīru Zaydun; (c) aʿjabanī Zaydun ʿilmuhu.
tasks.arabic: كَتَبْتُ الْكِتَابَ نِصْفَهُ — جَاءَ الْأَمِيرُ زَيْدٌ — أَعْجَبَنِي زَيْدٌ عِلْمُهُ
tasks.answer: (a) The part for the whole, with the pronoun -hu. (b) The thing for the thing: the prince and Zayd are the same person. (c) Inclusion: his knowledge belongs to Zayd, with the pronoun -hu.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of akaltu al-raghīfa thuluthahu.
tasks.answer: Akaltu: a past verb with its fāʿil, the -tu. Al-raghīfa: its object, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Thuluthahu: a badal of the part for the whole, in naṣb by the fatḥa; the -hu is a pronoun in the place of khafḍ, referring to the loaf.

tasks.prompt: Put the book's first example into naṣb and khafḍ: raʾaytu … and marartu bi- … with Zaydun akhūka.
tasks.answer: Raʾaytu Zaydan akhāka; marartu bi-Zaydin akhīka. The badal takes every sign of the word it replaces: here the alif and the yāʾ of the five nouns.

tasks.prompt: In yalqa athāman, yuḍāʿaf lahu al-ʿadhābu (Q 25:68–69), why is yuḍāʿaf in jazm?
tasks.answer: Yalqa is the answer of the condition man yafʿal, in jazm. Yuḍāʿaf is a badal of it, a verb in place of a verb, and follows it in jazm.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of badal does the book give?
quiz.explanation: The thing for the thing, the part for the whole, inclusion, and mistake.

quiz.prompt: Akaltu al-raghīfa thuluthahu is a badal of…
quiz.explanation: A third is part of the loaf.

quiz.prompt: Nafaʿanī Zaydun ʿilmuhu is a badal of…
quiz.explanation: Knowledge is not a part of Zayd but something he has: inclusion (ishtimāl).

quiz.prompt: How does a badal differ from ʿaṭf?
options: There is no particle between the two words
quiz.explanation: The badal follows directly, without wa- or any other particle.

quiz.prompt: Can a verb be a badal?
options: Yes, of a verb, and it takes its state
quiz.explanation: Yalqa athāman yuḍāʿaf (Q 25:68–69): both verbs in jazm.

quiz.prompt: In the badal of part and of inclusion, what ties the badal to the first word?
options: A pronoun referring back to it
quiz.explanation: Thuluthahu, ʿilmuhu: the -hu refers to the loaf, to Zayd.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: The badal follows Zayd in khafḍ; akh, one of the five nouns, shows it by the yāʾ.

text.original: الْبَدَلُ إِذَا أُبْدِلَ اسْمٌ مِنِ اسْمٍ أَوْ فِعْلٌ مِنْ فِعْلٍ تَبِعَهُ فِي جَمِيعِ إِعْرَابِهِ، وَهُوَ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَقْسَامٍ: بَدَلُ الشَّيْءِ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ، وَبَدَلُ الْبَعْضِ مِنَ الْكُلِّ، وَبَدَلُ الِاشْتِمَالِ، وَبَدَلُ الْغَلَطِ.
text.en: The substitute (badal): when a noun is substituted for a noun, or a verb for a verb, it follows it in all its iʿrāb. It is of four divisions: the substitute of the thing for the thing [itself], the substitute of the part for the whole, the substitute of inclusion (ishtimāl), and the substitute of mistake.

text.original: نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ أَخُوكَ، وَأَكَلْتُ الرَّغِيفَ ثُلُثَهُ، وَنَفَعَنِي زَيْدٌ عِلْمُهُ، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا الْفَرَسَ، أَرَدْتَ أَنْ تَقُولَ الْفَرَسَ فَغَلِطْتَ فَأَبْدَلْتَ زَيْدًا مِنْهُ.
text.en: As when you say: jāʾanī Zaydun akhūka “Zayd, your brother, came to me”, akaltu al-raghīfa thuluthahu “I ate the loaf, a third of it”, nafaʿanī Zaydun ʿilmuhu “Zayd benefited me, his knowledge”, and raʾaytu Zaydan al-farasa “I saw Zayd, the horse”: you meant to say “the horse”, made a mistake, and so replaced Zayd with it.

lessons.title: The nouns in naṣb: the list
body: The second half of the nouns: those in naṣb. The book announces fifteen: the object (mafʿūl bihi), the maṣdar, the adverb of time, the adverb of place, the state (ḥāl), the specification (tamyīz), the excepted (mustathnā), the noun of lā, the one called (munādā), the predicate of kāna and its sisters, the noun of inna and its sisters, the object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), the object of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu), and the follower of a noun in naṣb, of four kinds: adjective, conjunction, emphasis and substitute.

Count them and you find fourteen. Our print announces fifteen but leaves out one item that other copies have: the two objects of ẓanantu and its sisters (lesson 19). The count of fifteen is right for the full list; our print simply lacks that line, and the student who learns this text should know the missing item.

Most of these are what the grammarians call additions (faḍla): the core of the sentence, a verb with its doer or a subject with its predicate, is complete without them, and they add an object, a time, a place, a manner, a reason. The nouns in rafʿ, by contrast, are mostly the pillars (ʿumda) of the sentence. The exceptions are the predicate of kāna and the noun of inna, which belong to the core but are in naṣb because of the word that governs them.

Later books group five of these as the five objects: the object proper (mafʿūl bihi), the absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, the book's maṣdar), the object in which (mafʿūl fīhi, the book's two adverbs), the object for which (mafʿūl lahu, the book's object of purpose) and the object with which (mafʿūl maʿahu). The Ājurrūmiyya gives them their older, plainer names. The lessons that follow take the list in the book's order; the predicate of kāna, the noun of inna and the followers were explained among the nouns in rafʿ.

an addition: what the core sentence can do without
a pillar of the sentence
the five objects of the later books

jāʾa Zaydun rākiban, “Zayd came riding”: the ḥāl, an addition
qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan, “the people stood, except Zayd”: the excepted

tasks.answer: Zaydan: the object. Rākiban: the ḥāl. Qāʾiman: the predicate of kāna. Zaydan: the noun of inna.

The core sentence is complete without them
quiz.explanation: A verb with its doer is complete; the object, the time or the manner is added.

text.original: الْمَنْصُوبَاتُ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ، وَهِيَ: الْمَفْعُولُ بِهِ، وَالْمَصْدَرُ، وَظَرْفُ الزَّمَانِ، وَظَرْفُ الْمَكَانِ، وَالْحَالُ، وَالتَّمْيِيزُ، وَالْمُسْتَثْنَى، وَاسْمُ لَا، وَالْمُنَادَى، وَخَبَرُ كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، وَاسْمُ إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، وَالْمَفْعُولُ مِنْ أَجْلِهِ، وَالْمَفْعُولُ مَعَهُ، وَالتَّابِعُ لِلْمَنْصُوبِ، وَهُوَ أَرْبَعَةُ أَشْيَاءَ: النَّعْتُ، وَالْعَطْفُ، وَالتَّوْكِيدُ، وَالْبَدَلُ.
text.en: The nouns in naṣb (manṣūbāt) are fifteen: the direct object (mafʿūl bihi), the maṣdar, the adverb of time, the adverb of place, the ḥāl, the tamyīz, the excepted (mustathnā), the noun of lā, the one called (munādā), the khabar of kāna and its sisters, the noun of inna and its sisters, the object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), the object of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu), and that which follows a manṣūb, which is four things: the naʿt, the ʿaṭf, the tawkīd and the badal.

lessons.title: The object (mafʿūl bihi)
body: The object is “the noun in naṣb on which the act falls”: ḍarabtu Zaydan, “I struck Zayd”; rakibtu al-farasa, “I rode the horse”. The striking reaches Zayd, the riding the horse. Only a transitive verb (mutaʿaddī) has such an object. An intransitive verb (lāzim), such as qāma or jalasa, reaches a noun only through a particle: marartu bi-Zaydin, where Zayd is in khafḍ by the bi-, not an object in naṣb.

Like the doer, the object is explicit or a pronoun, and the pronoun is attached (muttaṣil) or separate (munfaṣil). The book gives the twelve attached ones on ḍaraba: ḍarabanī (he struck me), ḍarabanā (us), ḍarabaka, ḍarabaki (you, man, woman), ḍarabakumā, ḍarabakum, ḍarabakunna, ḍarabahu (him), ḍarabahā (her), ḍarabahumā, ḍarabahum, ḍarabahunna. In ḍarabanī the nūn before the -ī is not part of the pronoun; the grammarians call it the nūn of protection (nūn al-wiqāya), which keeps the verb's last vowel from becoming a kasra.

The separate ones are the twelve forms of iyyā-: iyyāya, iyyānā, iyyāka, iyyāki, iyyākumā, iyyākum, iyyākunna, iyyāhu, iyyāhā, iyyāhumā, iyyāhum, iyyāhunna. They are used when the object cannot be attached, above all when it comes before its verb: iyyāka naʿbudu, “You alone we worship” (Q 1:5). Putting the object first adds the sense of “only”.

The trap is to confuse the pronoun that is the doer with the pronoun that is the object, since both are attached to the end of the verb. -tu, -ta, -ti are always doers (ḍarabtu, “I struck”); -nī, -ka, -hu are always objects (ḍarabanī, “he struck me”). -nā can be either, and the vowel before it decides: ḍarabnā, with sukūn, is “we struck”; ḍarabanā, with fatḥa, is “he struck us”.

In the iʿrāb an attached object pronoun is “fixed, in the place of naṣb, the object”: ḍarabahu: ḍaraba, a past verb, fixed on the fatḥa; its doer a hidden “he”; -hu, an attached pronoun, fixed on the ḍamma, in the place of naṣb as its object.

terms.en: the object: the noun on which the act falls
transitive: a verb that takes an object
intransitive: a verb without an object
the attached pronoun: -nī, -ka, -hu
the separate pronoun: iyyāka, iyyāhu
the nūn of protection in ḍarabanī
