tasks.prompt: Find the object in each, if there is one: rakibtu al-farasa; qāma Zaydun; marartu bi-Zaydin; ḍarabahum.
tasks.arabic: رَكِبْتُ الْفَرَسَ — قَامَ زَيْدٌ — مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ — ضَرَبَهُمْ
tasks.answer: Al-farasa: object, in naṣb. Qāma Zaydun: no object (qāma is intransitive). Marartu bi-Zaydin: no object in naṣb; Zayd is in khafḍ by bi-. Ḍarabahum: -hum, an attached pronoun in the place of naṣb, the object.

tasks.prompt: Translate ḍarabnā and ḍarabanā and say what the -nā is in each.
tasks.answer: Ḍarabnā, “we struck”: -nā is the doer (sukūn before it). Ḍarabanā, “he struck us”: -nā is the object, and the doer is a hidden “he” (fatḥa before it).

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of ḍarabanī.
tasks.answer: Ḍaraba: a past verb, fixed on the fatḥa. The nūn: the nūn of protection. The -ī: an attached pronoun, fixed on the sukūn, in the place of naṣb as the object. The doer is a hidden pronoun, “he”.

tasks.prompt: Why does Q 1:5 say iyyāka naʿbudu and not naʿbuduka?
tasks.answer: The object is put before its verb, and an attached pronoun cannot stand before a verb, so the separate iyyāka is used. Putting the object first adds restriction: “You alone we worship”.

The noun in naṣb on which the act falls
The noun that does the act

quiz.prompt: In ḍarabanī, what is the nūn?
quiz.explanation: It protects the verb's last vowel; the pronoun is the -ī.

quiz.prompt: Which pronoun is always an object?
quiz.explanation: -tu, -ta and -ti are doers; -nī, -ka and -hu are objects.

quiz.prompt: Ḍarabanā means…
quiz.explanation: With fatḥa before -nā it is the object; with sukūn (ḍarabnā), the doer.

quiz.prompt: When is a separate object pronoun (iyyā-) used?
options: When the object cannot be attached, as when it comes first

quiz.explanation: Ḍarabanī to ḍarabahunna: twelve.

quiz.prompt: Does qāma, “he stood”, take an object?
quiz.explanation: An intransitive verb reaches a noun only through a particle, or not at all.

text.original: وَهُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَنْصُوبُ الَّذِي يَقَعُ بِهِ الْفِعْلُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا، وَرَكِبْتُ الْفَرَسَ. وَهُوَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: ظَاهِرٍ وَمُضْمَرٍ. فَالظَّاهِرُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ ذِكْرُهُ، وَالْمُضْمَرُ قِسْمَانِ: مُتَّصِلٌ وَمُنْفَصِلٌ.
text.en: It is the noun in naṣb on which the action falls, as ḍarabtu Zaydan “I struck Zayd” and rakibtu al-farasa “I rode the horse”. It is of two divisions: an explicit noun and a pronoun. The explicit noun is what has been mentioned before. The pronoun is of two divisions: attached (muttaṣil) and separate (munfaṣil).

text.original: فَالْمُتَّصِلُ اثْنَا عَشَرَ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: ضَرَبَنِي، وَضَرَبَنَا، وَضَرَبَكَ، وَضَرَبَكِ، وَضَرَبَكُمَا، وَضَرَبَكُمْ، وَضَرَبَكُنَّ، وَضَرَبَهُ، وَضَرَبَهَا، وَضَرَبَهُمَا، وَضَرَبَهُمْ، وَضَرَبَهُنَّ.
text.en: The attached are twelve, as when you say: ḍarabanī “he struck me”, ḍarabanā “he struck us”, ḍarabaka “he struck you (m.)”, ḍarabaki “he struck you (f.)”, ḍarabakumā “he struck you two”, ḍarabakum “he struck you (m. pl.)”, ḍarabakunna “he struck you (f. pl.)”, ḍarabahu “he struck him”, ḍarabahā “he struck her”, ḍarabahumā “he struck them two”, ḍarabahum “he struck them (m.)” and ḍarabahunna “he struck them (f.)”.

text.original: وَالْمُنْفَصِلُ اثْنَا عَشَرَ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: إِيَّايَ، وَإِيَّانَا، وَإِيَّاكَ، وَإِيَّاكِ، وَإِيَّاكُمَا، وَإِيَّاكُمْ، وَإِيَّاكُنَّ، وَإِيَّاهُ، وَإِيَّاهَا، وَإِيَّاهُمَا، وَإِيَّاهُمْ، وَإِيَّاهُنَّ.
text.en: The separate are twelve, as when you say: iyyāya “me”, iyyānā “us”, iyyāka “you (m.)”, iyyāki “you (f.)”, iyyākumā “you two”, iyyākum “you (m. pl.)”, iyyākunna “you (f. pl.)”, iyyāhu “him”, iyyāhā “her”, iyyāhumā “them two”, iyyāhum “them (m.)” and iyyāhunna “them (f.)”.

lessons.title: The maṣdar in naṣb
body: The maṣdar, the verbal noun, is defined here as “the noun in naṣb that comes third in the conjugation of the verb”: ḍaraba, yaḍribu, ḍarban. This is the order in which the madrasa recites every verb, past, present, maṣdar, and in which al-Amthila and the other ṣarf primers open their tables. The definition borrows ṣarf to explain a point of naḥw.

What the chapter means is the maṣdar used in naṣb with its own verb, which later books call the absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq): qataltuhu qatlan, “I killed him a killing”. It adds to the verb in three ways that the commentaries name: it emphasises it (ḍarabtu ḍarban, “I really struck”), it shows its kind (ḍarabtu ḍarban shadīdan, “I struck a hard striking”), or its number (ḍarabtu ḍarbatayni, “I struck twice”).

The book divides it into two. Verbal (lafẓī): the maṣdar has the letters of its verb, qataltuhu qatlan. By meaning (maʿnawī): it has the meaning of its verb but other letters, jalastu quʿūdan, “I sat a sitting”, where quʿūd is the maṣdar of qaʿada, “to sit”, not of jalasa; and qumtu wuqūfan, “I stood a standing”, where wuqūf belongs to waqafa.

A note from ṣarf: the maṣdar of the bare three-letter verb is learnt by hearing, not by rule (ḍarb, qatl, quʿūd, wuqūf all have different shapes), which is why the conjugation tool gives no maṣdar for the bare verb. The augmented verbs have regular maṣdars: akrama, yukrimu, ikrāman, so akramtuhu ikrāman, “I honoured him greatly”.

In the iʿrāb: qataltuhu qatlan: qataltu, a past verb with its doer; -hu, the object; qatlan, a maṣdar in naṣb (an absolute object), by the fatḥa. Do not confuse it with an object: in ḍarabtu ḍarban nobody is struck called “striking”; the maṣdar repeats the act itself.

terms.en: the verbal noun: third in the conjugation
the absolute object: the maṣdar in naṣb with its verb
the maṣdar with the letters of its verb
the maṣdar with its verb's meaning only
learnt by hearing, not by rule

examples.en: ḍaraba, yaḍribu, ḍarban: the maṣdar comes third
qataltuhu qatlan, “I killed him a killing”: verbal
jalastu quʿūdan, “I sat a sitting”: by meaning, from another root
akramtuhu ikrāman, “I honoured him greatly”: the regular maṣdar of akrama

tasks.prompt: Verbal or by meaning? qataltuhu qatlan; qumtu wuqūfan; ḍarabtu ḍarban; jalastu quʿūdan.
tasks.arabic: قَتَلْتُهُ قَتْلًا — قُمْتُ وُقُوفًا — ضَرَبْتُ ضَرْبًا — جَلَسْتُ قُعُودًا
tasks.answer: Qatlan: verbal (the letters of qatala). Wuqūfan: by meaning (from waqafa, not qāma). Ḍarban: verbal. Quʿūdan: by meaning (from qaʿada, not jalasa).

tasks.prompt: Add the maṣdar of akrama to akramtu Zaydan, and say what it adds.
tasks.answer: Akramtu Zaydan ikrāman, “I honoured Zayd greatly”. The maṣdar ikrāman emphasises the verb; it is an absolute object in naṣb by the fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of qataltuhu qatlan.
tasks.answer: Qatala: a past verb; the -tu, its doer, a pronoun in the place of rafʿ; the -hu, its object, a pronoun in the place of naṣb; qatlan: a maṣdar in naṣb (absolute object), the sign the fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Why does the book say the maṣdar “comes third in the conjugation”? Show it on qatala, whose maṣdar the book gives.
tasks.answer: The madrasa recites every verb in the order past, present, maṣdar; the maṣdar is the third. On qatala: qatala, yaqtulu, qatlan.

quiz.prompt: How does the book define the maṣdar?
options: The first form of the verb
The noun in naṣb that comes third in the conjugation of the verb
The noun that does the act
quiz.explanation: Ḍaraba, yaḍribu, ḍarban.

quiz.prompt: Jalastu quʿūdan is a maṣdar…
quiz.explanation: Quʿūd is from qaʿada; it shares the meaning of jalasa, not its letters.

quiz.prompt: Qataltuhu qatlan is a maṣdar…
quiz.explanation: Qatl has the letters of qatala.

quiz.prompt: What do later books call the maṣdar in naṣb with its own verb?
quiz.explanation: Mafʿūl muṭlaq, one of the five objects.

quiz.prompt: Why does the conjugation tool give no maṣdar for the bare verb?
options: The bare verb has no maṣdar
Its maṣdar is learnt by hearing, not by rule
quiz.explanation: Ḍarb, qatl, quʿūd: different shapes, known by hearing. The augmented verbs have regular maṣdars.

quiz.prompt: What is the maṣdar of akrama?
quiz.explanation: Akrama, yukrimu, ikrāman.

quiz.prompt: Which of these does a maṣdar in naṣb not do, according to the commentaries?
options: Name the place of the act
quiz.explanation: The place is given by the adverb of place, not by the maṣdar.

text.original: الْمَصْدَرُ هُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَنْصُوبُ الَّذِي يَجِيءُ ثَالِثًا فِي تَصْرِيفِ الْفِعْلِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: ضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ ضَرْبًا.
text.en: The maṣdar is the noun in naṣb that comes third in the conjugation of the verb, as when you say: ḍaraba yaḍribu ḍarban “he struck, he strikes, a striking”.

text.original: وَهُوَ قِسْمَانِ: لَفْظِيٌّ وَمَعْنَوِيٌّ. فَإِنْ وَافَقَ لَفْظُهُ لَفْظَ فِعْلِهِ فَهُوَ لَفْظِيٌّ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: قَتَلْتُهُ قَتْلًا، وَإِنْ وَافَقَ مَعْنَى فِعْلِهِ دُونَ لَفْظِهِ فَهُوَ مَعْنَوِيٌّ، نَحْوُ: جَلَسْتُ قُعُودًا، وَقُمْتُ وُقُوفًا.
text.en: It is of two divisions: in wording (lafẓī) and in meaning (maʿnawī). If its wording agrees with the wording of its verb, it is lafẓī, as when you say: qataltuhu qatlan “I killed him, a killing”. If it agrees with the meaning of its verb but not with its wording, it is maʿnawī, as jalastu quʿūdan “I sat, a sitting down” and qumtu wuqūfan “I stood, a standing up”.

lessons.title: The adverbs of time and place
body: The adverb (ẓarf, literally “vessel”) is the noun of a time or a place in naṣb “with fī understood”: jalastu al-yawma, “I sat today”, means jalastu fī al-yawmi, “I sat in the day”. The time or place is a vessel in which the act happens; later books call it the object in which (mafʿūl fīhi).

The book lists nouns of time: al-yawma (today), al-laylata (tonight), ghudwatan and bukratan (early in the morning), saḥaran (before dawn), ghadan (tomorrow), ʿatamatan (in the dark of the evening), ṣabāḥan (in the morning), masāʾan (in the evening), abadan (ever, for ever), amadan (for a long time) and ḥīnan (for a while). And nouns of place: amāma, quddāma (in front of), khalfa, warāʾa (behind), fawqa (above), taḥta (under), ʿinda (at, with), maʿa (with), izāʾa, ḥidhāʾa (facing, opposite), tilqāʾa (towards), hunā (here) and thamma (there). “And what is like them”: the lists are examples, not the whole.

The test is the understood fī. If fī can be put before the noun without changing the meaning, and it is not said, the noun is an adverb in naṣb. Once fī is said, as in jalastu fī al-yawmi, the noun is in khafḍ by the particle and is not an adverb in this chapter's sense. And a noun of time that is not a vessel for an act is no adverb at all: in al-yawmu ṭawīlun, “the day is long”, al-yawmu is a mubtadaʾ in rafʿ.

Most adverbs of place are joined to a noun after them: jalastu amāma al-shaykhi, “I sat in front of the shaykh”, where amāma is in naṣb and al-shaykh in khafḍ as the second term of the iḍāfa. Some never change their ending: hunā and thamma are fixed, and their naṣb is in their place. You have met an adverb already as a khabar: Zaydun ʿindaka, “Zayd is with you” (lesson 16).

terms.en: the adverb, a “vessel” of time or place
the adverb of time
the adverb of place
with fī understood
the object in which (the later name)

examples.en: jalastu al-yawma, “I sat today”: an adverb of time
akhruju ghadan, “I go out tomorrow”
jalastu amāma al-shaykhi, “I sat in front of the shaykh”: an adverb of place joined to a noun
Zaydun ʿindaka, “Zayd is with you”: an adverb as khabar

tasks.prompt: Find the adverb and say whether it is of time or of place: jalastu taḥta al-shajarati; akhruju ghadan; Zaydun ʿindaka; jalastu ṣabāḥan.
tasks.arabic: جَلَسْتُ تَحْتَ الشَّجَرَةِ — أَخْرُجُ غَدًا — زَيْدٌ عِنْدَكَ — جَلَسْتُ صَبَاحًا
tasks.answer: Taḥta: place (joined to al-shajarati). Ghadan: time. ʿInda: place (here the khabar). Ṣabāḥan: time.

tasks.prompt: Say jalastu al-yawma with fī. What happens to al-yawm, and is it still an adverb?
tasks.answer: Jalastu fī al-yawmi: al-yawm is now in khafḍ by the particle fī. It is no longer an adverb in naṣb; the adverb is a noun in naṣb with fī understood, not said.

tasks.prompt: Is al-yawm an adverb in al-yawmu ṭawīlun, “the day is long”? Explain.
tasks.answer: No. It is not the time in which an act happens but the thing spoken about: it is a mubtadaʾ in rafʿ, and ṭawīlun its khabar.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of jalastu amāma al-shaykhi.
tasks.answer: Jalastu: a past verb with its doer, the -tu. Amāma: an adverb of place in naṣb by the fatḥa, and it is the first term of an iḍāfa. Al-shaykhi: the second term of the iḍāfa (muḍāf ilayhi), in khafḍ by the kasra.

quiz.prompt: What is an adverb of time?
options: A noun of time after fī
A noun of time in naṣb with fī understood
quiz.explanation: Jalastu al-yawma: “in the day” without the fī being said.

quiz.prompt: In jalastu fī al-yawmi, al-yawmi is…
options: in khafḍ by fī, not an adverb
quiz.explanation: Once fī is said, the noun is governed by it.

quiz.prompt: Which is an adverb of place?
quiz.explanation: Taḥta, “under”; the other three are of time.

quiz.prompt: What do later books call the adverb?
quiz.explanation: The time or place in which the act happens.

quiz.prompt: In al-yawmu ṭawīlun, al-yawmu is…
quiz.explanation: It is spoken about, not a vessel for an act.

quiz.prompt: What does “ẓarf” literally mean?
quiz.explanation: The time or place holds the act as a vessel holds what is in it.

quiz.prompt: Hunā, “here”, never changes its ending. How is its naṣb given in the iʿrāb?
options: It is in the place of naṣb
quiz.explanation: A word with a fixed ending is in the place (maḥall) of its state.

text.original: ظَرْفُ الزَّمَانِ هُوَ اسْمُ الزَّمَانِ الْمَنْصُوبُ بِتَقْدِيرِ فِي، نَحْوُ: الْيَوْمَ، وَاللَّيْلَةَ، وَغُدْوَةً، وَبُكْرَةً، وَسَحَرًا، وَغَدًا، وَعَتَمَةً، وَصَبَاحًا، وَمَسَاءً، وَأَبَدًا، وَأَمَدًا، وَحِينًا، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: The adverb of time (ẓarf al-zamān) is the noun of time in naṣb with fī “in” understood, as al-yawma “today”, al-laylata “tonight”, ghudwatan “early in the morning”, bukratan “at daybreak”, saḥaran “before dawn”, ghadan “tomorrow”, ʿatamatan “at nightfall”, ṣabāḥan “in the morning”, masāʾan “in the evening”, abadan “for ever”, amadan “for a long time” and ḥīnan “for a while”, and the like.

text.original: وَظَرْفُ الْمَكَانِ هُوَ اسْمُ الْمَكَانِ الْمَنْصُوبُ بِتَقْدِيرِ فِي، نَحْوُ: أَمَامَ، وَخَلْفَ، وَقُدَّامَ، وَوَرَاءَ، وَفَوْقَ، وَتَحْتَ، وَعِنْدَ، وَمَعَ، وَإِزَاءَ، وَحِذَاءَ، وَتِلْقَاءَ، وَهُنَا، وَثَمَّ، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: The adverb of place (ẓarf al-makān) is the noun of place in naṣb with fī understood, as amāma “in front of”, khalfa “behind”, quddāma “before”, warāʾa “behind”, fawqa “above”, taḥta “below”, ʿinda “at”, maʿa “with”, izāʾa “opposite”, ḥidhāʾa “facing”, tilqāʾa “towards”, hunā “here” and thamma “there”, and the like.

lessons.title: The state (ḥāl)
body: The ḥāl is “the noun in naṣb that explains what was vague of states (hayʾāt)”: jāʾa Zaydun rākiban, “Zayd came riding”. “Zayd came” leaves open how he came; rākiban answers the question kayfa?, “how?”. The ḥāl is usually a participle, a word of the shape rākib (riding) or musraj (saddled), which describes a state at the time of the act.

The ḥāl may describe the doer or the object. In jāʾa Zaydun rākiban it describes Zayd, the doer. In rakibtu al-farasa musrajan, “I rode the horse saddled”, it describes the horse, the object. The book's third example, laqītu ʿAbda llāhi rākiban, “I met ʿAbd Allāh riding”, can be read both ways, the speaker riding or ʿAbd Allāh riding; the commentaries point out that the context must decide.

Three conditions follow. The ḥāl is always indefinite: rākiban, never al-rākiba. It comes only after the speech is complete: jāʾa Zaydun is already a full sentence, and rākiban is an addition to it. And its owner (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl), the word it describes, is always definite: Zayd, the horse, ʿAbd Allāh.

These conditions are what tell a ḥāl from an adjective. Jāʾa Zaydun rākiban, “Zayd came riding”, is a ḥāl: indefinite, in naṣb, telling how. Jāʾa Zaydun al-rākibu, “Zayd the rider came”, is an adjective: definite like Zayd, in rafʿ like him, telling which Zayd. And jāʾa rajulun rākibun, “a riding man came”, is an adjective too, since its owner rajulun is indefinite and so cannot have a ḥāl in the book's rule.

In the iʿrāb: rākiban, a ḥāl in naṣb, the sign the fatḥa. When you meet a noun in naṣb after a complete sentence, ask first “how?”: if it answers, it is a ḥāl; if it answers “in what respect?”, it is the tamyīz of the next lesson.

terms.en: the state: a noun in naṣb that tells how
the owner of the ḥāl, the word it describes
a state, a manner
the completeness of the sentence

examples.en: jāʾa Zaydun rākiban, “Zayd came riding”: the ḥāl describes the doer
rakibtu al-farasa musrajan, “I rode the horse saddled”: it describes the object
laqītu ʿAbda llāhi rākiban, “I met ʿAbd Allāh riding”: either may be riding
jāʾa Zaydun al-rākibu, “Zayd the rider came”: an adjective, not a ḥāl

tasks.prompt: Find the ḥāl and its owner: jāʾa Zaydun rākiban; rakibtu al-farasa musrajan; kharaja Zaydun musriʿan, “Zayd went out hurrying”.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ رَاكِبًا — رَكِبْتُ الْفَرَسَ مُسْرَجًا — خَرَجَ زَيْدٌ مُسْرِعًا
tasks.answer: Rākiban, owner Zayd (the doer). Musrajan, owner al-faras (the object). Musriʿan, owner Zayd (the doer).

tasks.prompt: Ḥāl or adjective? (a) jāʾa Zaydun rākiban; (b) jāʾa Zaydun al-rākibu; (c) jāʾa rajulun rākibun.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ رَاكِبًا — جَاءَ زَيْدٌ الرَّاكِبُ — جَاءَ رَجُلٌ رَاكِبٌ
tasks.answer: (a) Ḥāl: indefinite, in naṣb, its owner definite. (b) Adjective: definite and in rafʿ like Zayd. (c) Adjective: its noun is indefinite, so it agrees with it in rafʿ and indefiniteness.

tasks.prompt: Give the two readings of laqītu ʿAbda llāhi rākiban.
tasks.answer: “I met ʿAbd Allāh while I was riding” (the owner is the -tu, the doer) and “I met ʿAbd Allāh while he was riding” (the owner is ʿAbd Allāh, the object). The context decides.

tasks.prompt: State the three conditions of the ḥāl in the book.
tasks.answer: It is always indefinite; it comes only after the speech is complete; its owner is always definite.

quiz.prompt: What question does the ḥāl answer?
quiz.explanation: Jāʾa Zaydun rākiban: how did Zayd come? Riding.

quiz.prompt: The ḥāl is always…
quiz.explanation: Rākiban, never al-rākiba.

quiz.prompt: Its owner (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl) is always…
quiz.explanation: Zayd, the horse, ʿAbd Allāh: all definite.

quiz.prompt: In rakibtu al-farasa musrajan, whose state is musrajan?
quiz.explanation: Saddled describes the horse, the object.

quiz.prompt: Jāʾa Zaydun al-rākibu: what is al-rākibu?
quiz.explanation: Definite and in rafʿ like Zayd: an adjective.

quiz.prompt: When does the ḥāl come, according to the book?
options: Only after the speech is complete
quiz.explanation: Jāʾa Zaydun is complete; rākiban is added.

quiz.prompt: Why is laqītu ʿAbda llāhi rākiban open to two readings?
options: ʿAbd Allāh may be the doer
The ḥāl may describe the doer or the object
quiz.explanation: Either the speaker or ʿAbd Allāh may be riding.

text.original: الْحَالُ هُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَنْصُوبُ الْمُفَسِّرُ لِمَا انْبَهَمَ مِنَ الْهَيْئَاتِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ رَاكِبًا، وَرَكِبْتُ الْفَرَسَ مُسْرَجًا، وَلَقِيتُ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ رَاكِبًا، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: The state (ḥāl) is the noun in naṣb that explains what is unclear of manners, as when you say: jāʾa Zaydun rākiban “Zayd came riding”, rakibtu al-farasa musrajan “I rode the horse saddled” and laqītu ʿAbd Allāhi rākiban “I met ʿAbd Allāh riding”, and the like.

text.original: وَلَا يَكُونُ الْحَالُ إِلَّا نَكِرَةً، وَلَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا بَعْدَ تَمَامِ الْكَلَامِ، وَلَا يَكُونُ صَاحِبُهَا إِلَّا مَعْرِفَةً.
text.en: The ḥāl is only indefinite; it comes only after the speech is complete; and the one it belongs to is only definite.

lessons.title: The specification (tamyīz)
body: The tamyīz is “the noun in naṣb that explains what was vague of things (dhawāt)”. Where the ḥāl tells how, the tamyīz tells what, or in what respect. Taṣabbaba Zaydun ʿaraqan, “Zayd poured with sweat”: Zayd poured, but poured what? Sweat. Ishtaraytu ʿishrīna ghulāman, “I bought twenty slaves”: twenty what? Slaves.

The book's examples fall into two groups, which the commentaries name. The tamyīz of a relation: the meaning of the whole sentence is vague until it comes. Taṣabbaba Zaydun ʿaraqan (it was his sweat that poured), tafaqqaʾa Bakrun shaḥman, “Bakr burst with fat”, ṭāba Muḥammadun nafsan, “Muḥammad was of good heart”, and the comparisons Zaydun akramu minka aban, “Zayd is nobler than you in his father”, and ajmalu minka wajhan, “more handsome than you in face”. In the first three the real subject is hidden in the tamyīz: taṣabbaba Zaydun ʿaraqan is “Zayd's sweat poured”.

The tamyīz of a single word: a number or a measure is vague until we know what is counted. Ishtaraytu ʿishrīna ghulāman, malaktu tisʿīna naʿjatan, “I owned ninety ewes”. After the numbers from eleven to ninety-nine the counted thing is a single noun in naṣb: ʿishrīna ghulāman, not ghilmānan.

The conditions are two: the tamyīz is always indefinite, and it comes only after the speech is complete. These it shares with the ḥāl, and so the two are easy to confuse: both are indefinite nouns in naṣb added to a complete sentence. The question decides. Jāʾa Zaydun rākiban answers “how did he come?”: a ḥāl. Ṭāba Zaydun nafsan answers “in what respect was he good?”: a tamyīz.

terms.en: the specification: a noun in naṣb that tells what
a thing, an essence (pl. dhawāt)
the specification of a relation
the specification of a single word: numbers, measures

examples.en: taṣabbaba Zaydun ʿaraqan, “Zayd poured with sweat”: the tamyīz of a relation
ṭāba Muḥammadun nafsan, “Muḥammad was of good heart”
Zaydun akramu minka aban, “Zayd is nobler than you in his father”
ishtaraytu ʿishrīna ghulāman, “I bought twenty slaves”: the tamyīz of a number

tasks.prompt: Find the tamyīz and say what was vague before it: tafaqqaʾa Bakrun shaḥman; malaktu tisʿīna naʿjatan; ajmalu minka wajhan.
tasks.arabic: تَفَقَّأَ بَكْرٌ شَحْمًا — مَلَكْتُ تِسْعِينَ نَعْجَةً — أَجْمَلُ مِنْكَ وَجْهًا
tasks.answer: Shaḥman: Bakr burst, but with what? (a relation). Naʿjatan: ninety of what? (a number). Wajhan: more handsome in what respect? (a relation, in a comparison).

tasks.prompt: Ḥāl or tamyīz? jāʾa Zaydun rākiban; ṭāba Zaydun nafsan.
tasks.arabic: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ رَاكِبًا — طَابَ زَيْدٌ نَفْسًا
tasks.answer: Rākiban is a ḥāl: it answers “how did he come?”. Nafsan is a tamyīz: it answers “in what respect was he good?”.

tasks.prompt: Rewrite taṣabbaba Zaydun ʿaraqan so that the sweat is the doer, and explain what this shows.
tasks.answer: Taṣabbaba ʿaraqu Zaydin, “Zayd's sweat poured”. It shows that the tamyīz of a relation holds the real subject of the verb, which the sentence has moved into the tamyīz to say it more strongly.

tasks.prompt: Complete with a tamyīz: ishtaraytu ʿishrīna … (kitāb, “book”).
tasks.answer: Ishtaraytu ʿishrīna kitāban: after twenty the counted thing is a single noun, indefinite, in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: What does the tamyīz explain?
options: What was vague of states: how
What was vague of things: what, in what respect
quiz.explanation: The ḥāl explains states (hayʾāt), the tamyīz things (dhawāt).

quiz.prompt: In ishtaraytu ʿishrīna ghulāman, what is the tamyīz?
quiz.explanation: Twenty what? Slaves.

quiz.prompt: Ṭāba Zaydun nafsan: nafsan is…
quiz.explanation: Good in what respect? In heart (nafs). Not the nafs of emphasis, which follows its noun's state.

quiz.prompt: What do the ḥāl and the tamyīz share?
options: Both are indefinite, in naṣb, after complete speech
quiz.explanation: The question (how? or what?) tells them apart.

quiz.prompt: After the numbers eleven to ninety-nine, the counted thing is…
quiz.explanation: ʿIshrīna ghulāman, tisʿīna naʿjatan.

quiz.prompt: Zaydun akramu minka aban means…
options: “Zayd is nobler than you in his father”
quiz.explanation: Aban specifies the respect in which Zayd is nobler.

quiz.prompt: Which two conditions does the book give for the tamyīz?
options: In rafʿ, and after a number
quiz.explanation: The tamyīz is always indefinite and comes after the speech is complete.

text.original: التَّمْيِيزُ هُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَنْصُوبُ الْمُفَسِّرُ لِمَا انْبَهَمَ مِنَ الذَّوَاتِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: تَصَبَّبَ زَيْدٌ عَرَقًا، وَتَفَقَّأَ بَكْرٌ شَحْمًا، وَطَابَ مُحَمَّدٌ نَفْسًا، وَاشْتَرَيْتُ عِشْرِينَ غُلَامًا، وَمَلَكْتُ تِسْعِينَ نَعْجَةً، وَزَيْدٌ أَكْرَمُ مِنْكَ أَبًا، وَأَجْمَلُ مِنْكَ وَجْهًا.
text.en: The specification (tamyīz) is the noun in naṣb that explains what is unclear of things, as when you say: taṣabbaba Zaydun ʿaraqan “Zayd poured with sweat”, tafaqqaʾa Bakrun shaḥman “Bakr burst with fat”, ṭāba Muḥammadun nafsan “Muḥammad was glad of soul”, ishtaraytu ʿishrīna ghulāman “I bought twenty boys”, malaktu tisʿīna naʿjatan “I owned ninety ewes”, Zaydun akramu minka aban “Zayd is nobler than you in father” and ajmalu minka wajhan “more handsome than you in face”.

text.original: وَلَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا نَكِرَةً، وَلَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا بَعْدَ تَمَامِ الْكَلَامِ.
text.en: It is only indefinite, and it comes only after the speech is complete.

lessons.title: The exception with illā
body: Exception (istithnāʾ) takes something out of a statement: qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan, “the people stood, except Zayd”. The book names eight words of exception: illā, ghayr, siwā, suwā, sawāʾ, khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā. It calls them all particles, though the commentaries note that ghayr and the three forms of siwā are nouns, and that khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā can be verbs; the next lesson shows why that matters.

Three words are needed for everything that follows. The excepted (al-mustathnā): Zayd. That from which he is excepted (al-mustathnā minhu): al-qawm, the people. And the kind of statement: affirmative (mūjab) or negative (manfī), and complete (tāmm), when the mustathnā minhu is mentioned, or incomplete (nāqiṣ), when it is not.

First rule: after illā in a complete, affirmative statement the excepted is in naṣb, and nothing else is allowed: qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan; kharaja al-nāsu illā ʿAmran, “the people went out, except ʿAmr”.

Second rule: in a complete, negative statement two things are allowed: the excepted may follow the mustathnā minhu as its substitute (badal), or be in naṣb as an exception. Mā qāma aḥadun illā Zaydun, “no one stood except Zayd”, with Zayd in rafʿ as a badal of aḥadun, the doer; or mā qāma aḥadun illā Zaydan, in naṣb. The commentaries say the badal is the better of the two.

The beginner's mistake is to put every word after illā in naṣb. Look first at the statement: is the mustathnā minhu mentioned, and is the statement negated? The third case, the incomplete statement, comes in the next lesson, and there illā governs nothing at all.

terms.en: exception: taking something out of a statement
the excepted
that from which it is excepted
complete: the mustathnā minhu is mentioned
affirmative and negative

examples.en: qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan, “the people stood, except Zayd”: complete, affirmative: naṣb
kharaja al-nāsu illā ʿAmran, “the people went out, except ʿAmr”
mā qāma aḥadun illā Zaydun, “no one stood except Zayd”: badal, in rafʿ
mā qāma aḥadun illā Zaydan: the same, with naṣb as an exception

tasks.prompt: Name the mustathnā minhu and the kind of statement, then give the state of the excepted: (a) qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan; (b) mā qāma aḥadun illā Zaydun.
tasks.arabic: قَامَ الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا — مَا قَامَ أَحَدٌ إِلَّا زَيْدٌ
tasks.answer: (a) Mustathnā minhu al-qawm; complete and affirmative; Zayd in naṣb, the only choice. (b) Mustathnā minhu aḥad; complete and negative; Zayd in rafʿ as a badal of aḥad (naṣb, illā Zaydan, is also allowed).

tasks.prompt: Give the two ways of saying “no one went out except ʿAmr” and say which the commentaries prefer.
tasks.answer: Mā kharaja aḥadun illā ʿAmrun (badal, in rafʿ like aḥad) and mā kharaja aḥadun illā ʿAmran (naṣb as an exception). The badal is preferred.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan.
tasks.answer: Qāma: a past verb, fixed on the fatḥa. Al-qawmu: its doer, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. Illā: a particle of exception. Zaydan: the excepted, in naṣb by the fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: How many words of exception does the book name?
quiz.explanation: Illā, ghayr, siwā, suwā, sawāʾ, khalā, ʿadā, ḥāshā.

quiz.prompt: In qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan, what is al-qawm?
quiz.explanation: Zayd is taken out of the people.

quiz.prompt: After illā in a complete, affirmative statement, the excepted is…
quiz.explanation: Qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan.

quiz.prompt: Mā qāma aḥadun illā Zaydun: why is Zayd in rafʿ?
options: As a badal of aḥad, the doer
quiz.explanation: In a complete, negative statement the excepted may follow the mustathnā minhu as its badal.

quiz.prompt: What makes a statement “complete” (tāmm) in this chapter?
quiz.explanation: Qāma al-qawmu: the people are named.

quiz.prompt: Which is not allowed?
quiz.explanation: In a complete, affirmative statement only naṣb is allowed.

quiz.prompt: Which of the eight do the commentaries say are nouns?
options: Ghayr and the forms of siwā
quiz.explanation: The book calls them all particles; ghayr, siwā, suwā and sawāʾ are nouns.

text.original: وَحُرُوفُ الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ ثَمَانِيَةٌ، وَهِيَ: إِلَّا، وَغَيْرُ، وَسِوَى، وَسُوَى، وَسَوَاءُ، وَخَلَا، وَعَدَا، وَحَاشَا.
text.en: The particles of exception are eight: illā “except”, ghayr, siwā, suwā and sawāʾ “other than”, and khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā “save”.

text.original: فَالْمُسْتَثْنَى بِإِلَّا يُنْصَبُ إِذَا كَانَ الْكَلَامُ مُوجَبًا تَامًّا، نَحْوُ: قَامَ الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا، وَخَرَجَ النَّاسُ إِلَّا عَمْرًا. وَإِنْ كَانَ الْكَلَامُ مَنْفِيًّا تَامًّا جَازَ فِيهِ الْبَدَلُ وَالنَّصْبُ عَلَى الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ، نَحْوُ: مَا قَامَ أَحَدٌ إِلَّا زَيْدٌ، وَإِلَّا زَيْدًا.
text.en: The word excepted with illā is in naṣb when the speech is affirmative and complete, as qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan “the people stood except Zayd” and kharaja al-nāsu illā ʿAmran “the people went out except ʿAmr”. If the speech is negative and complete, both the badal and naṣb by exception are allowed in it, as mā qāma aḥadun illā Zaydun and illā Zaydan “no one stood except Zayd”.

lessons.title: The incomplete exception; ghayr, siwā, khalā
body: When the statement is incomplete (nāqiṣ), the mustathnā minhu is not mentioned, and illā governs nothing. The word after it takes the state that its governor before illā requires, as if illā were not there: mā qāma illā Zaydun, “only Zayd stood”, Zayd in rafʿ as the doer of qāma; mā ḍarabtu illā Zaydan, “I struck only Zayd”, in naṣb as the object; mā marartu illā bi-Zaydin, “I passed only by Zayd”, in khafḍ by the bi-. The book says it is “according to the governors”.

Such a statement is always negated (or a question), and its meaning is restriction (ḥaṣr): “none but Zayd”. Later books call it the emptied exception (al-istithnāʾ al-mufarragh), because the governor before illā is left free, emptied, to work on the word after it. To parse it, cover illā with your finger and read the sentence again: mā qāma Zaydun shows at once that Zayd is the doer.

After ghayr, siwā, suwā and sawāʾ the excepted is in khafḍ, “and nothing else”: qāma al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin, “the people stood, except Zayd”. Here the book uses the word majrūr, the later term, beside its usual khafḍ. The reason is that these four are nouns, and the excepted is the second term of an iḍāfa with them. Ghayr itself then takes the state that the excepted would have after illā: in naṣb in qāma al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin, as in qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan.

After khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā the excepted may be in naṣb or in khafḍ: qāma al-qawmu khalā Zaydan or khalā Zaydin, ʿadā ʿAmran or ʿadā ʿAmrin, ḥāshā Zaydan or ḥāshā Zaydin. The commentaries explain the choice: taken as verbs, these three put the excepted in naṣb as their object; taken as particles of khafḍ, they put it in khafḍ. When mā comes before them (mā khalā, mā ʿadā) they are verbs, and only naṣb is allowed.
So the whole chapter is one table. After illā: naṣb, or badal or naṣb, or according to the governor. After ghayr and the siwā words: khafḍ only. After khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā: naṣb or khafḍ.

terms.en: incomplete: the mustathnā minhu is not mentioned
the emptied exception (the later name)
restriction: “none but…”
nouns of exception: the excepted after them is in khafḍ
verbs or particles: naṣb or khafḍ after them

examples.en: mā qāma illā Zaydun, “only Zayd stood”: Zayd is the doer
mā ḍarabtu illā Zaydan, “I struck only Zayd”: Zayd is the object
mā marartu illā bi-Zaydin, “I passed only by Zayd”: Zayd is in khafḍ by bi-
qāma al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin, “the people stood, except Zayd”

tasks.prompt: Replace illā with ghayr in qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan. Give the state of ghayr and of Zayd.
tasks.answer: Qāma al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin. Ghayra is in naṣb, the state Zayd had after illā; Zaydin is in khafḍ as the second term of the iḍāfa with ghayr.

tasks.prompt: Say “the people stood, except ʿAmr” with ḥāshā in both allowed ways, and explain each.
tasks.answer: Qāma al-qawmu ḥāshā ʿAmran: ḥāshā taken as a verb, ʿAmr its object in naṣb. Qāma al-qawmu ḥāshā ʿAmrin: ḥāshā taken as a particle of khafḍ, ʿAmr in khafḍ.

tasks.prompt: Turn qāma Zaydun, “Zayd stood”, into a restriction, “only Zayd stood”, and parse Zayd.
tasks.answer: Mā qāma illā Zaydun. Zaydun is the doer of qāma, in rafʿ by the ḍamma; mā negates and illā restricts, but neither governs it.

options: The doer of qāma, in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: In the incomplete statement illā governs nothing; read it as mā qāma Zaydun.

quiz.prompt: After ghayr, the excepted is…
quiz.explanation: Ghayr is a noun; the excepted is the second term of an iḍāfa with it.

quiz.prompt: After khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā, the excepted may be…
quiz.explanation: As verbs they take an object in naṣb; as particles they put it in khafḍ.

quiz.prompt: What is the meaning of the incomplete exception?
quiz.explanation: Mā qāma illā Zaydun: only Zayd stood.

quiz.prompt: In qāma al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin, why is ghayr in naṣb?
options: Because of qāma, as its object
Because ghayr is always in naṣb
It takes the state the excepted would have after illā
quiz.explanation: Compare qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan.

quiz.prompt: Mā ḍarabtu illā Zaydan: Zayd is in naṣb because…
options: he is the object of ḍarabtu
quiz.explanation: The incomplete statement: the word after illā takes the state its governor requires.

quiz.prompt: When mā comes before khalā (mā khalā), the excepted is…
quiz.explanation: With mā they are verbs, so only naṣb.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ الْكَلَامُ نَاقِصًا كَانَ عَلَى حَسَبِ الْعَوَامِلِ، نَحْوُ: مَا قَامَ إِلَّا زَيْدٌ، وَمَا ضَرَبْتُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا، وَمَا مَرَرْتُ إِلَّا بِزَيْدٍ.
text.en: If the speech is incomplete, [the word excepted] goes by the governors, as mā qāma illā Zaydun “none stood but Zayd”, mā ḍarabtu illā Zaydan “I struck none but Zayd” and mā marartu illā bi-Zaydin “I passed by none but Zayd”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمُسْتَثْنَى بِغَيْرٍ وَسِوَى وَسُوَى وَسَوَاءٍ مَجْرُورٌ لَا غَيْرُ. وَالْمُسْتَثْنَى بِخَلَا وَعَدَا وَحَاشَا يَجُوزُ نَصْبُهُ وَجَرُّهُ، نَحْوُ: قَامَ الْقَوْمُ خَلَا زَيْدًا وَزَيْدٍ، وَعَدَا عَمْرًا وَعَمْرٍو، وَحَاشَا زَيْدًا وَزَيْدٍ.
text.en: As for the word excepted with ghayr, siwā, suwā and sawāʾ, it is majrūr and nothing else. The word excepted with khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā may be in naṣb or in jarr, as qāma al-qawmu khalā Zaydan and Zaydin “the people stood, save Zayd”, ʿadā ʿAmran and ʿAmrin, and ḥāshā Zaydan and Zaydin.

lessons.title: The lā that denies the whole kind
body: This lā denies a whole kind: lā rajula fī al-dāri, “there is no man in the house”, not one, of any sort. It puts the indefinite noun in naṣb without tanwīn, on two conditions: it comes directly before the noun, and lā is not repeated. Its noun is in naṣb and the khabar after it (here fī al-dāri) in rafʿ, so lā works like inna; the madrasa adds that a single noun after it is fixed on the fatḥa, which is why it has no tanwīn. The Qurʾān opens al-Baqara with it: lā rayba fīhi, “there is no doubt in it” (Q 2:2).

If something comes between lā and the noun, lā no longer governs it: the noun must be in rafʿ, and lā must be repeated. Lā fī al-dāri rajulun wa-lā imraʾatun, “there is in the house neither man nor woman”. Here fī al-dāri stands between, so rajulun and imraʾatun are in rafʿ and lā is said twice.

If lā is repeated with the noun directly after it, both ways are allowed: to make it govern, lā rajula fī al-dāri wa-lā imraʾata, or to leave it ungoverning, lā rajulun fī al-dāri wa-lā imraʾatun. The book says “if you wish”. The commentaries add a difference of meaning: with naṣb the denial is of the whole kind; with rafʿ it can deny one only, so that one could go on, “but two men”.

Two traps. This lā governs only indefinite nouns; with a definite noun, such as a proper name, it cannot govern, and the noun is in rafʿ with lā repeated: lā Zaydun fī al-dāri wa-lā ʿAmrun. And lā rajula has no tanwīn: the student who says lā rajulan has confused it with a noun in naṣb by a verb. Note too that our print gives “rafʿ is required” where other copies add “and tanwīn”; the editor added the word in brackets, and the sense is the same.

terms.en: the lā that denies the whole kind
the noun of lā, in naṣb without tanwīn
coming directly before, with nothing between
repetition of lā
leaving lā without effect

examples.en: lā rajula fī al-dāri, “there is no man in the house”: naṣb without tanwīn
lā rayba fīhi, “there is no doubt in it” (Q 2:2)

examples.arabic: لَا فِي الدَّارِ رَجُلٌ وَلَا امْرَأَةٌ
examples.en: separated: rafʿ, and lā repeated

examples.arabic: لَا رَجُلَ فِي الدَّارِ وَلَا امْرَأَةَ
examples.en: repeated: lā may govern…

examples.arabic: لَا رَجُلٌ فِي الدَّارِ وَلَا امْرَأَةٌ
examples.en: …or not, as you wish

tasks.prompt: Give the state of the noun after lā in each and say which rule applies: lā rajula fī al-dāri; lā fī al-dāri rajulun wa-lā imraʾatun; lā rajulun fī al-dāri wa-lā imraʾatun.
tasks.arabic: لَا رَجُلَ فِي الدَّارِ — لَا فِي الدَّارِ رَجُلٌ وَلَا امْرَأَةٌ — لَا رَجُلٌ فِي الدَّارِ وَلَا امْرَأَةٌ
tasks.answer: Rajula: naṣb without tanwīn, lā directly before it and not repeated. Rajulun: rafʿ required, because fī al-dāri separates it from lā, and lā is repeated. Rajulun: rafʿ, allowed because lā is repeated (naṣb, lā rajula … wa-lā imraʾata, is allowed too).

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of lā rayba fīhi (Q 2:2).
tasks.answer: Lā: the lā that denies the whole kind, working like inna. Rayba: its noun, fixed on the fatḥa in the place of naṣb (the book: in naṣb without tanwīn). Fīhi: fī, a particle of khafḍ, and -hi, a pronoun in the place of khafḍ; the two together stand in the place of rafʿ as the khabar of lā.

tasks.prompt: Put fī al-dāri between lā and the noun in lā rajula fī al-dāri, and correct the rest of the sentence.
tasks.answer: Lā fī al-dāri rajulun wa-lā imraʾatun: once separated, the noun must be in rafʿ, and lā must be repeated.

tasks.prompt: Why can one not say lā Zayda fī al-dāri?
tasks.answer: This lā governs only an indefinite noun, since it denies a whole kind; Zayd is a proper name, definite. One says lā Zaydun fī al-dāri wa-lā ʿAmrun, with rafʿ and lā repeated.

quiz.prompt: What does lā do to an indefinite noun directly after it, when it is not repeated?
options: Puts it in naṣb without tanwīn
Puts it in rafʿ with tanwīn
quiz.explanation: Lā rajula fī al-dāri.

quiz.prompt: If something comes between lā and the noun…
options: rafʿ and the repetition of lā are required
quiz.explanation: Lā fī al-dāri rajulun wa-lā imraʾatun.

quiz.prompt: If lā is repeated with the noun directly after it…
options: both naṣb and rafʿ are allowed
quiz.explanation: Lā rajula … wa-lā imraʾata, or lā rajulun … wa-lā imraʾatun.

quiz.prompt: In lā rayba fīhi (Q 2:2), rayba is…
options: the noun of lā, without tanwīn
quiz.explanation: The lā that denies the whole kind; fīhi is its khabar.

quiz.prompt: Which is wrong?
options: Lā fī al-dāri rajulun wa-lā imraʾatun
Lā rajulun fī al-dāri wa-lā imraʾatun
quiz.explanation: The noun of lā has no tanwīn.

quiz.prompt: Which other governor does this lā work like?
quiz.explanation: Its noun in naṣb, its khabar in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: Why can this lā not govern Zayd?
options: Zayd is definite; lā denies an indefinite kind
quiz.explanation: With a definite noun: rafʿ and lā repeated.

text.original: اعْلَمْ أَنَّ لَا تَنْصِبُ النَّكِرَةَ مِنْ غَيْرِ تَنْوِينٍ إِذَا بَاشَرَتِ النَّكِرَةَ وَلَمْ تَتَكَرَّرْ لَا، نَحْوُ: لَا رَجُلَ فِي الدَّارِ.
text.en: Know that lā puts the indefinite noun in naṣb without tanwīn when it comes directly before the indefinite and lā is not repeated, as lā rajula fī al-dāri “there is no man in the house”.

text.original: وَإِنْ لَمْ تُبَاشِرْهَا وَجَبَ الرَّفْعُ وَوَجَبَ تَكْرَارُ لَا، نَحْوُ: لَا فِي الدَّارِ رَجُلٌ وَلَا امْرَأَةٌ. وَإِنْ تَكَرَّرَتْ جَازَ إِعْمَالُهَا وَإِلْغَاؤُهَا، نَحْوُ: لَا رَجُلَ فِي الدَّارِ وَلَا امْرَأَةَ، وَإِنْ شِئْتَ قُلْتَ: لَا رَجُلٌ فِي الدَّارِ وَلَا امْرَأَةٌ.
text.en: If it does not come directly before it, rafʿ is necessary and the repetition of lā is necessary, as lā fī al-dāri rajulun wa-lā imraʾatun “in the house there is neither a man nor a woman”. If it is repeated, you may let it govern or leave it without effect, as lā rajula fī al-dāri wa-lā imraʾata “there is no man in the house and no woman”; and if you wish, you say: lā rajulun fī al-dāri wa-lā imraʾatun.

lessons.title: The one called (munādā)
body: The munādā is the one called with yā, “O”. The book gives five kinds. The single proper name (al-mufrad al-ʿalam): yā Zaydu. The meant indefinite (al-nakira al-maqṣūda): yā rajulu, said to a particular man in front of you. The unmeant indefinite (al-nakira ghayr al-maqṣūda): yā rajulan, as a blind man calls out to whoever may hear. The joined noun (al-muḍāf): yā ʿAbda llāhi. And the noun like the joined (al-mushabbah bi-l-muḍāf), a noun followed by a word that completes its meaning: yā ṭāliʿan jabalan, “O you climbing a mountain”.

The first two are fixed on the ḍamma without tanwīn: yā Zaydu, yā rajulu. The other three are in naṣb, “and nothing else”: yā rajulan, yā ʿAbda llāhi, yā ṭāliʿan jabalan. Why naṣb at all? The grammarians explain that yā stands for a verb, “I call”, so the one called is its object; the first two are fixed, and their naṣb is in their place.

Here “single” (mufrad) has a third meaning: not joined to a following word and not like the joined, so a dual or a plural can be single too. Such a noun is fixed on what it takes in rafʿ: yā Zaydāni, “O two Zayds”, with the alif, and yā Zaydūna, “O Zayds”, with the wāw. The beginner who has learnt mufrad as “singular” in the chapter on iʿrāb and as “not a sentence” in the chapter on the khabar learns now a third use of the same word.

The difference between yā rajulu and yā rajulan is one of meaning made audible. The man you address and point to has become definite by being called: yā rajulu, with ḍamma, as a proper name has it. The unknown man, any man at all, stays indefinite: yā rajulan, in naṣb with tanwīn. The madrasa student hears the speaker's intention in the vowel.

terms.en: the one called
the single proper name
the meant indefinite: a particular person addressed
the unmeant indefinite: anyone
like the joined noun: completed by what follows

examples.en: yā Zaydu, “O Zayd”: fixed on the ḍamma
yā rajulu, “O man” (a particular man): fixed on the ḍamma
yā ʿAbda llāhi, “O ʿAbd Allāh”: joined, in naṣb
yā ṭāliʿan jabalan, “O you climbing a mountain”: like the joined, in naṣb
yā Zaydāni, “O two Zayds”: single in this chapter's sense, fixed on the alif

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of munādā and its ending: yā Muḥammadu; yā ʿAbda llāhi; yā rajulu (to a man in front of you); yā ṭāliʿan jabalan.
tasks.arabic: يَا مُحَمَّدُ — يَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ — يَا رَجُلُ — يَا طَالِعًا جَبَلًا
tasks.answer: Yā Muḥammadu: single proper name, fixed on the ḍamma. Yā ʿAbda llāhi: joined, in naṣb. Yā rajulu: meant indefinite, fixed on the ḍamma. Yā ṭāliʿan jabalan: like the joined, in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Call two men named Zayd, and several men named Zayd. Why is the ending not a ḍamma?
tasks.answer: Yā Zaydāni and yā Zaydūna. Both are single in this chapter's sense (not joined), so they are fixed on what they take in rafʿ: the alif of the dual and the wāw of the plural.

tasks.prompt: Yā rajulu and yā rajulan: when is each said?
tasks.answer: Yā rajulu to a particular man you are addressing (the meant indefinite, fixed on the ḍamma). Yā rajulan to anyone who may hear, as a blind man calls for help (the unmeant indefinite, in naṣb).

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of yā Zaydu.
tasks.answer: Yā: a particle of calling. Zaydu: munādā, a single proper name, fixed on the ḍamma in the place of naṣb.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of munādā does the book give?
quiz.explanation: Single proper name, meant indefinite, unmeant indefinite, joined, like the joined.

quiz.prompt: Yā Zaydu: what is the ending of Zayd?
options: Fixed on the ḍamma, without tanwīn
quiz.explanation: The single proper name is fixed on the ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: Which munādā is in naṣb?
options: Yā rajulu, to a man in front of you
quiz.explanation: The joined noun is in naṣb; the others are fixed.

quiz.prompt: What does “single” (mufrad) mean in this chapter?
options: Not joined and not like the joined
quiz.explanation: So yā Zaydāni and yā Zaydūna are single too.

quiz.prompt: A blind man calls out yā rajulan to anyone who may hear. Why naṣb?
quiz.explanation: No particular man is meant, so it stays indefinite, in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Why is the munādā in naṣb in principle?
options: Yā stands for “I call”, and the one called is its object
Because yā is a particle of khafḍ
quiz.explanation: The first two kinds are fixed in the place of that naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Yā ṭāliʿan jabalan is…
quiz.explanation: Jabalan completes the meaning of ṭāliʿan, as a second term completes the first.

text.original: الْمُنَادَى خَمْسَةُ أَنْوَاعٍ: الْمُفْرَدُ الْعَلَمُ، وَالنَّكِرَةُ الْمَقْصُودَةُ، وَالنَّكِرَةُ غَيْرُ الْمَقْصُودَةِ، وَالْمُضَافُ، وَالْمُشَبَّهُ بِالْمُضَافِ.
text.en: The one called (munādā) is of five kinds: the single proper name (al-mufrad al-ʿalam), the intended indefinite (al-nakira al-maqṣūda), the unintended indefinite, the muḍāf, and that which resembles the muḍāf.

text.original: فَأَمَّا الْمُفْرَدُ الْعَلَمُ وَالنَّكِرَةُ الْمَقْصُودَةُ فَيُبْنَيَانِ عَلَى الضَّمِّ مِنْ غَيْرِ تَنْوِينٍ، نَحْوُ: يَا زَيْدُ، وَيَا رَجُلُ، وَالثَّلَاثَةُ الْبَاقِيَةُ مَنْصُوبَةٌ لَا غَيْرُ.
text.en: As for the single proper name and the intended indefinite, they are fixed on the ḍamma (yubnayāni ʿalā al-ḍamm), without tanwīn, as yā Zaydu “O Zayd” and yā rajulu “O man”. The remaining three are in naṣb and nothing else.

lessons.title: The objects of purpose and of accompaniment
body: The object of purpose (al-mafʿūl min ajlihi, “the object for whose sake”) is “the noun in naṣb mentioned to explain the cause of the act”: qāma Zaydun ijlālan li-ʿAmrin, “Zayd stood out of respect for ʿAmr”; qaṣadtuka ibtighāʾa maʿrūfika, “I came to you seeking your kindness”. It answers li-mādhā?, “why?”. It is usually a maṣdar, as both examples are, and the sense can be given with li-: qāma Zaydun li-ijlāli ʿAmrin. Later books call it the object for which (mafʿūl lahu).

The object of accompaniment (al-mafʿūl maʿahu) is “the noun in naṣb mentioned to explain with whom the act was done”. It comes after a wāw that means “with”: jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jaysha, “the prince came with the army”; istawā al-māʾu wa-l-khashabata, “the water came level with the post”.

The trap is the wāw. In jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jayshu, with rafʿ, the wāw is the wāw of ʿaṭf: the prince came and the army came, both doers. In jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jaysha, with naṣb, it is the wāw of accompaniment: the army is what the prince came with. In the second example of the book ʿaṭf is impossible, since the post did not “come level” with anything: it stood still while the water rose. So only naṣb is right there.

The book then closes the chapter of the nouns in naṣb: the predicate of kāna and its sisters and the noun of inna and its sisters “were mentioned among the nouns in rafʿ”, in the chapter on what enters the subject and predicate, and so were the followers. With the five objects now complete, the student can name every noun in naṣb he meets: the object (what?), the absolute object (the act itself), the adverb (when? where?), the object of purpose (why?) and the object of accompaniment (with what?).

terms.en: the object of purpose: why the act was done
the object of accompaniment: with what it was done
the wāw meaning “with”
the object for which (the later name)

examples.en: qāma Zaydun ijlālan li-ʿAmrin, “Zayd stood out of respect for ʿAmr”
qaṣadtuka ibtighāʾa maʿrūfika, “I came to you seeking your kindness”
jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jaysha, “the prince came with the army”
istawā al-māʾu wa-l-khashabata, “the water came level with the post”: ʿaṭf is impossible

tasks.prompt: Name the noun in naṣb and its kind: qāma Zaydun ijlālan li-ʿAmrin; jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jaysha; jalastu al-yawma; ḍarabtu Zaydan.
tasks.arabic: قَامَ زَيْدٌ إِجْلَالًا لِعَمْرٍو — جَاءَ الْأَمِيرُ وَالْجَيْشَ — جَلَسْتُ الْيَوْمَ — ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا
tasks.answer: Ijlālan: object of purpose (why?). Al-jaysha: object of accompaniment (with what?). Al-yawma: adverb of time (when?). Zaydan: the object (whom?).

tasks.prompt: Jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jayshu and jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jaysha: what is the difference?
tasks.arabic: جَاءَ الْأَمِيرُ وَالْجَيْشُ — جَاءَ الْأَمِيرُ وَالْجَيْشَ
tasks.answer: With rafʿ the wāw is ʿaṭf: the army is a second doer, and both came. With naṣb the wāw means “with”: the army is the object of accompaniment, what the prince came with.

tasks.prompt: Why is only naṣb right in istawā al-māʾu wa-l-khashabata?
tasks.answer: With ʿaṭf the post would be a second doer of istawā, as if it too rose level; but the post stood still and the water rose to it. So the wāw can only mean “with”, and al-khashabata is an object of accompaniment in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Give the full iʿrāb of qāma Zaydun ijlālan li-ʿAmrin.
tasks.answer: Qāma: a past verb, fixed on the fatḥa. Zaydun: its doer, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. Ijlālan: object of purpose, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Li-: a particle of khafḍ. ʿAmrin: in khafḍ by li-, the sign the kasra.

quiz.prompt: What question does the object of purpose answer?
quiz.explanation: Qāma Zaydun ijlālan li-ʿAmrin: why did he stand? Out of respect.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jaysha, al-jaysha is…
options: joined to the prince by ʿaṭf
quiz.explanation: With naṣb the wāw means “with”.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾa al-amīru wa-l-jayshu, with rafʿ, the wāw is…
quiz.explanation: Both are doers of jāʾa.

quiz.prompt: Why can istawā al-māʾu wa-l-khashabata not be ʿaṭf?
options: The post did not rise level; only the water did
Because the wāw is the oath
quiz.explanation: Only “with” makes sense, so naṣb is required.

quiz.prompt: The object of purpose is usually…
quiz.explanation: Ijlālan, ibtighāʾa: both maṣdars.

quiz.prompt: Where did the book treat the predicate of kāna and the noun of inna?
quiz.explanation: In the chapter on what enters the subject and predicate.

quiz.prompt: Which object answers “when? where?”
quiz.explanation: Jalastu al-yawma; jalastu amāma al-shaykhi.

text.original: وَهُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَنْصُوبُ الَّذِي يُذْكَرُ بَيَانًا لِسَبَبِ وُقُوعِ الْفِعْلِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ إِجْلَالًا لِعَمْرٍو، وَقَصَدْتُكَ ابْتِغَاءَ مَعْرُوفِكَ.
text.en: It is the noun in naṣb that is mentioned to make clear the cause of the action, as when you say: qāma Zaydun ijlālan li-ʿAmrin “Zayd stood out of respect for ʿAmr” and qaṣadtuka ibtighāʾa maʿrūfika “I came to you seeking your kindness”.

text.original: وَهُوَ الِاسْمُ الْمَنْصُوبُ الَّذِي يُذْكَرُ لِبَيَانِ مَنْ فُعِلَ مَعَهُ الْفِعْلُ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: جَاءَ الْأَمِيرُ وَالْجَيْشَ، وَاسْتَوَى الْمَاءُ وَالْخَشَبَةَ.
text.en: It is the noun in naṣb that is mentioned to make clear with whom the action was done, as when you say: jāʾa al-amīru wa-al-jaysha “the prince came with the army” and istawā al-māʾu wa-al-khashabata “the water rose level with the post”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا خَبَرُ كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا وَاسْمُ إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا فَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ ذِكْرُهُمَا فِي الْمَرْفُوعَاتِ، وَكَذَلِكَ التَّوَابِعُ فَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَتْ هُنَالِكَ.
text.en: As for the khabar of kāna and its sisters and the noun of inna and its sisters, they have been mentioned among the nouns in rafʿ; and so have the followers: they came before, there.

lessons.title: The nouns in khafḍ
body: The last chapter is the shortest, because the nouns in khafḍ are only three: the noun in khafḍ by a particle, the noun in khafḍ by iḍāfa, and the follower of a noun in khafḍ (the adjective, conjunction, emphasis or substitute of lessons 20 to 23).

The particles are those of lesson 2, now given as governors: min (from), ilā (to), ʿan (away from, about), ʿalā (on), fī (in), rubba (many a), bi- (with, by), ka- (like), li- (for, belonging to), the particles of the oath, wa-, bi- and ta-, and mudh and mundhu (since). Ta- is used in an oath by God only: ta-llāhi. Mudh and mundhu give the start of a time: mā raʾaytuhu mundhu yawmi al-jumuʿati, “I have not seen him since Friday”. Other copies add the wāw of rubba, as in wa-laylin, “and many a night”; our editor put it in brackets, and it is left out of our text.

Iḍāfa joins two nouns so that the second completes the first: ghulāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's servant”. The first term (al-muḍāf) loses its tanwīn and takes whatever state its role gives it: jāʾa ghulāmu Zaydin, raʾaytu ghulāma Zaydin, marartu bi-ghulāmi Zaydin. The second term (al-muḍāf ilayhi) is always in khafḍ. And the first term never takes the article: one says ghulāmu Zaydin, not al-ghulāmu Zaydin.

The book divides iḍāfa by the particle it implies. With the sense of li-, “belonging to”: ghulāmu Zaydin is a servant belonging to Zayd. With the sense of min, “made of”: thawbu khazzin, “a garment of silk”, bābu sājin, “a door of teak”, khātamu ḥadīdin, “a ring of iron”. Later books add a third, with the sense of fī, “in”: makru al-layli, “scheming by night” (Q 34:33).

With this the Ājurrūmiyya is complete. A student who knows it by heart can take a plain sentence and say, for every word, its kind, its state, its sign and its governor, which is what the madrasa means by knowing naḥw at the first level. On the North-African path the next books, Qaṭr al-nadā and the Alfiyya, take the same chapters again at greater depth.

terms.en: the nouns in khafḍ: three
joining two nouns, the second completing the first
the first term, which loses its tanwīn
the second term, always in khafḍ
since: particles of khafḍ for time

examples.en: mā raʾaytuhu mundhu yawmi al-jumuʿati, “I have not seen him since Friday”: mundhu puts its noun in khafḍ
ta-llāhi, “by God”: the tāʾ of the oath, used with the name of God only
ghulāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's servant”: iḍāfa with the sense of li-
thawbu khazzin, “a garment of silk”; khātamu ḥadīdin, “a ring of iron”: with the sense of min

tasks.prompt: Find every noun in khafḍ and say what put it there: marartu bi-ghulāmi Zaydin al-ʿāqili.
tasks.answer: Ghulāmi: in khafḍ by the particle bi-. Zaydin: in khafḍ by iḍāfa, the second term. Al-ʿāqili: in khafḍ as a follower, the adjective of Zayd (or of the servant; both are in khafḍ and definite).

tasks.prompt: With the sense of li- or of min? kitābu Zaydin; khātamu ḥadīdin; bābu sājin; ghulāmu ʿAmrin.
tasks.arabic: كِتَابُ زَيْدٍ — خَاتَمُ حَدِيدٍ — بَابُ سَاجٍ — غُلَامُ عَمْرٍو
tasks.answer: Kitābu Zaydin: li- (a book belonging to Zayd). Khātamu ḥadīdin: min (a ring made of iron). Bābu sājin: min (a door made of teak). Ghulāmu ʿAmrin: li- (a servant belonging to ʿAmr).

tasks.prompt: Put ghulāmu Zaydin as the doer, as the object, and after bi-.
tasks.answer: Jāʾa ghulāmu Zaydin; raʾaytu ghulāma Zaydin; marartu bi-ghulāmi Zaydin. The first term changes with its role; Zaydin stays in khafḍ as the second term.

tasks.prompt: Using the whole book, give the iʿrāb of inna ghulāma Zaydin fī al-dāri.
tasks.answer: Inna: a particle of emphasis, working on the subject and predicate. Ghulāma: its noun, in naṣb by the fatḥa, the first term of an iḍāfa. Zaydin: the second term, in khafḍ by the kasra. Fī: a particle of khafḍ. Al-dāri: in khafḍ by fī. Fī al-dāri, a particle with its noun, stands in the place of rafʿ as the khabar of inna.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of noun in khafḍ does the book give?
quiz.explanation: By a particle, by iḍāfa, and the follower.

quiz.prompt: In ghulāmu Zaydin, which word is always in khafḍ?
quiz.explanation: The first term takes the state of its role; the second is always in khafḍ.

quiz.prompt: Thawbu khazzin implies which particle?
options: Li-: a garment belonging to silk
Min: a garment made of silk
quiz.explanation: The book gives thawbu khazzin, bābu sājin and khātamu ḥadīdin for the sense of min.

quiz.prompt: The tāʾ of the oath is used with…
quiz.explanation: Ta-llāhi; with other nouns the wāw or the bāʾ is used.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: The first term loses its tanwīn and never takes the article; the second is in khafḍ.

quiz.prompt: Which particles does the book add here that it did not give among the signs of the noun?
quiz.explanation: In our print, mudh and mundhu come only in this last chapter.

quiz.prompt: In raʾaytu ghulāma Zaydin, why is ghulāma in naṣb?
options: It is the second term of the iḍāfa
It is the object of raʾaytu
quiz.explanation: The first term takes the state of its role in the sentence.

text.original: الْمَخْفُوضَاتُ ثَلَاثَةٌ: مَخْفُوضٌ بِالْحَرْفِ، وَمَخْفُوضٌ بِالْإِضَافَةِ، وَتَابِعٌ لِلْمَخْفُوضِ.
text.en: The nouns in khafḍ (makhfūḍāt) are three: in khafḍ by a particle, in khafḍ by iḍāfa, and following a word in khafḍ.

text.original: فَأَمَّا الْمَخْفُوضُ بِالْحَرْفِ فَهُوَ مَا يُخْفَضُ بِمِنْ، وَإِلَى، وَعَنْ، وَعَلَى، وَفِي، وَرُبَّ، وَالْبَاءِ، وَالْكَافِ، وَاللَّامِ، وَبِحُرُوفِ الْقَسَمِ، وَهِيَ: الْوَاوُ، وَالْبَاءُ، وَالتَّاءُ، وَبِمُذْ وَمُنْذُ.
text.en: As for the word in khafḍ by a particle, it is what is put in khafḍ by min, ilā, ʿan, ʿalā, fī, rubba, bi-, ka- and li-; by the particles of oath, which are wa-, bi- and ta-; and by mudh and mundhu “since”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا مَا يُخْفَضُ بِالْإِضَافَةِ فَنَحْوُ قَوْلِكَ: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ، وَهُوَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: مَا يُقَدَّرُ بِاللَّامِ نَحْوُ: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ، وَمَا يُقَدَّرُ بِمِنْ نَحْوُ: ثَوْبُ خَزٍّ، وَبَابُ سَاجٍ، وَخَاتَمُ حَدِيدٍ، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ.
text.en: As for what is put in khafḍ by iḍāfa, it is as when you say: ghulāmu Zaydin “Zayd's boy”. It is of two divisions: one understood with li- “of, belonging to”, as ghulāmu Zaydin, and one understood with min “of, made of”, as thawbu khazzin “a garment of silk”, bābu sājin “a door of teak” and khātamu ḥadīdin “a ring of iron”, and the like.
